voices.who: The anonymous continuator of the Song of the Albigensian Crusade, a partisan of Toulouse, on the epitaph at Carcassonne that called Simon de Montfort a saint and martyr (in Paul Meyer's 1879 French translation of the Occitan). Gloss: 'I have heard that it must be so: if by killing men and shedding blood, losing souls, consenting to murders, following wicked counsel, setting fires, destroying barons, shaming Parage [the southern nobility's code of honour], seizing lands by force, making pride triumph, stirring up evil and quenching good, killing women and slaughtering children, a man can win Jesus Christ in this world, then he must wear a crown and shine in heaven!'
voices.doc: La Chanson de la croisade contre les Albigeois, laisse CCVIII (lines 8688–8696), tr. Paul Meyer, vol. II (1879), p. 430

voices.text: et aussitôt le cri et le tumulte s'élèvent : on court vers la ville avec les armes tranchantes, et alors commence le massacre et l'effroyable boucherie. Les barons, les dames, les petits enfants, les hommes, les femmes, dépouillés et nus, sont passés au fil de l'épée. Les chairs, le sang, les cervelles, les troncs, les membres, les corps ouverts et pourfendus, les foies, les courées, mis en morceaux, brisés, gisent par les places comme s'il en avait plu. Du sang répandu, la terre, le sol, la rive sont rougis. Il ne reste homme ni femme jeune ou vieux : aucune créature n'échappe, à moins de s'être tenue cachée. La ville est détruite, le feu l'embrase.
voices.who: The anonymous Toulousain continuator of the Song, on the sack of Marmande by the crusade of Prince Louis, after its commander had been spared (Meyer's 1879 French translation). He was not inside the town; Meyer judges the scene arranged but the massacre itself confirmed by the royal chronicler Guillaume le Breton. Gloss: 'the shouting begins; they run at the town with blades, and the massacre and the dreadful butchery begin. Barons, ladies, little children, men and women, stripped naked, are put to the sword. Flesh, blood, brains, limbs, bodies split open, livers and entrails lie in the squares as if they had rained down; the earth and the river bank are red with blood. No man or woman, young or old, is left; no creature escapes unless it stayed hidden. The town is destroyed and set on fire.'
voices.doc: La Chanson de la croisade contre les Albigeois, laisse CCXII (lines 9305–9321), tr. Paul Meyer, vol. II (1879), p. 462

voices.text: Roma, ben ancse a hom auzit retraire Quel cap sem vos te, per quel faitz soven raire; Per que cug e cre qu'ops vos auria traire, Roma, del cervel, Quar de mal capel Etz vos e Cistel, qu'a Bezers fezetz faire Mout estranh mazel.
voices.who: Guilhem Figueira, a tailor's son and troubadour from Toulouse exiled by the crusade, in his song against Rome, D'un sirventes far, said to have been written in Toulouse during the crusaders' siege of 1229 (Old Occitan). Rough gloss: 'Rome, it has always been said that your head is empty, which is why you keep it shaved; so I believe you need some brain put into you, Rome, for you and Cîteaux are of an evil cap, you who at Béziers had a most terrible slaughter done.'
voices.doc: D'un sirventes far, stanza 22 (lines 148–154), in Emil Levy, Guilhem Figueira, ein provenzalischer Troubadour (Berlin, 1880), p. 42

witness.text: Voilà pourquoi [les habitants] furent à Béziers détruits et mis à mal : tous ils (les croisés) les occirent : ils ne peuvent leur faire pis. Ils massacraient tous ceux qui s'étaient réfugiés dans le moûtier; rien ne put les sauver, ni croix, ni autel, ni crucifix; et ces fous ribauds mendiants massacraient les clercs, et femmes et enfants, tellement que je ne crois pas qu'un seul en soit échappé. Dieu reçoive les âmes, s'il lui plaît, en paradis! car je ne pense pas que jamais, depuis le temps des Sarrazins, si sauvage massacre ait été résolu ni accompli.
witness.who: William of Tudela, a Navarrese cleric who supported the crusade and wrote the first part of the Song (Meyer's 1879 French translation of the Occitan). Just before this he says the crusade's leaders had agreed that any town that resisted would be put to the sword, so that fear would make the others surrender. Gloss: 'That is why the people of Béziers were destroyed: the crusaders killed them all. They massacred everyone who had fled into the church; neither cross, nor altar, nor crucifix could save them; the mad beggar-ribalds killed the clergy, women and children, so that I do not think one escaped. May God receive their souls in paradise! I do not think so savage a massacre has been decided or done since the time of the Saracens.'

witness.text: When they discovered, from the admissions of some of them, that there were Catholics mingled with the heretics, they said to the abbot, “Sir, what shall we do, for we cannot distinguish between the faithful and the heretics.” The abbot, like the others, was afraid that many, in fear of death, would pretend to be Catholics, and after their departure, would return to their heresy, and is said to have replied: “Kill them all; for the Lord knoweth them that are His (2 Tim. ii. 19)!” and so countless numbers in that town were slain.
witness.who: Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk in the Rhineland who approved of the crusade, writing a decade or more later and far from Béziers; the Latin says only that the abbot 'dixisse fertur', is said to have said, 'Caedite eos. Novit enim Dominus qui sunt eius.' (Dialogue on Miracles, Book V, ch. 21, tr. H. von E. Scott and C. C. Swinton Bland, 1929) The word 'all' in 'Kill them all' is the 1929 translators'; the Latin 'Caedite eos' means 'Kill them'. Caesarius also misdates the campaign to 1211.

official.text: dum tractaretur cum baronibus de liberatione illorum qui in civitate ipsa catholici censebantur, ribaldi et alii viles et inermes personae, non exspectato mandato principum, in civitatem fecerant insultum, et mirantibus nostris, cum clamaretur: Ad arma, ad arma, quasi sub duarum vel trium horarum spatio, transcensis fossatis ac muro, capta est civitas Biterrensis, nostrique non parcentes ordini, sexui, vel aetati, fere viginti millia hominum in ore gladii peremerunt
official.who: Arnaud Amaury, abbot of Cîteaux, and Milo, the papal legates leading the crusade, reporting to Pope Innocent III (Latin, Innocent III's register, book XII, letter 108, in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 216, 1855). Gloss: 'while we were still negotiating with the barons to free those in the city held to be Catholics, the camp followers and other low, unarmed people attacked the city without waiting for the princes' orders; to our amazement, with cries of "To arms, to arms!", within two or three hours they had crossed the ditches and the wall and Béziers was taken, and our men, sparing neither rank nor sex nor age, put almost twenty thousand people to the sword.' The letter goes on to call the sack divine vengeance, and recalls that the townspeople had once murdered their own lord in the church of the Magdalene.

stories.warn: The official and Occitan voices are given in their original Latin and Old Occitan or in Paul Meyer's 1879 French translation, with the site's own plain glosses. The Song is partisan: its first author supported the crusade, its continuator was a Toulouse loyalist who was not present at Marmande. Caesarius wrote at second hand, years later, and only reports what Arnaud 'is said' to have said.
stories.note: Research in progress: no words of Cathar believers themselves are quoted yet. Their testimony survives mainly in inquisition registers (e.g. the Doat collection and Jacques Fournier's register, edited by Jean Duvernoy in 1965); a pre-1931 public-domain printing of such a deposition (e.g. in Döllinger's Beiträge zur Sektengeschichte, 1890) still needs to be found and checked. Even then it would be the inquisitor's record ('as recorded by the inquisitor').
disputed: How many died at Béziers? The legates' own letter says almost 20,000 were put to the sword; Peter of les Vaux-de-Cernay (as quoted by Meyer) says up to 7,000 were killed in the church of the Magdalene alone; Caesarius says the city was said to have held more than 100,000 men. Among modern historians, Christopher Tyerman says the true figure was almost certainly far less, and Laurence Marvin argues that clearly most of the population and buildings survived and the city went on as a major town.

Did Arnaud Amaury say 'Kill them all'? Only Caesarius reports it, years later and at a distance, and he writes 'is said to have replied'; Britannica says the legate 'allegedly' said it, and Marvin calls it apocryphal, noting that the legate may not even have known what was happening until it was over. Other historians cited by Wikipedia hold that, whether or not the words were spoken, they captured the spirit of the assault.

Was the massacre ordered or spontaneous? The legates told the pope that the camp followers attacked without waiting for orders while talks were still going on; William of Tudela says the crusade's leaders had already agreed that any town that resisted would be put to the sword to frighten the others into surrender.

Violence on the other side. The crusade's immediate cause was the killing of the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau in 1208, in which Raymond VI was implicated. Meyer's notes record that in 1218 the people of Avignon, partisans of Toulouse, captured the prince of Orange and put him to death (in Pope Honorius's words, cut to pieces), and that Raymond VII had the captured crusader captains Foucaut and Jean beheaded in 1220. In 1242 men from Montségur murdered two inquisitors and their companions at Avignonet.

How reliable is the Song's account of Marmande? Meyer judged that the continuator was not inside the town and that the council scene was arranged, but that the massacre itself is confirmed by the French royal chronicler Guillaume le Breton, who wrote that the crusaders killed all the townspeople with their women and children, up to five thousand.
stories.blind: The record of Béziers belongs almost wholly to the winners: the legates who reported to the pope, Cistercian and northern clerical chroniclers, and William of Tudela, who backed the crusade even while he mourned its victims. The southern side survives in the Song's anonymous continuator and in troubadours like Guilhem Figueira, voices of the Toulouse court and the southern nobility. The Cathars themselves, and the ordinary Catholic townspeople killed alongside them, left almost nothing in their own words; what they believed comes down to us mainly through the questions and records of the inquisitors who hunted them.
reading: Paul Meyer, La Chanson de la croisade contre les Albigeois, vol. II, translation (1879, archive.org)
Caesarius of Heisterbach, The Dialogue on Miracles, vol. I, tr. Scott & Bland (1929, archive.org)
Emil Levy, Guilhem Figueira, ein provenzalischer Troubadour (1880, archive.org)

stories.title: The ten days of Yangzhou
stories.where: Yangzhou, Jiangsu, China (approximate)
facts: Shi Kefa, a Ming loyalist general, was president of the Board of War at Nanking when Peking fell in 1644; the new court of the Prince of Fu sent him to command at Yangzhou, where he tried in vain to reconcile the Four Guardian Generals, who were warring among themselves and outraging the people of their districts.
https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Eminent_Chinese_of_the_Ch%27ing_Period/Shih_K%27o-fa
The Qing regent Dorgon wrote to Shi Kefa asking him to surrender; Shi declined, and his reply was circulated among later generations.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Kefa

The forces of the Manchu prince Dodo surrounded Yangzhou on 13 May 1645 and took it after a seven days' siege; Shi failed in an attempt at suicide, rejected every offer of amity and was killed, and the Manchus then plundered and slaughtered the inhabitants for ten days, from 20 to 29 May.
https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Eminent_Chinese_of_the_Ch%27ing_Period/Shih_K%27o-fa

The Qing army included Han Chinese bannermen; Wikipedia describes homes burned with refugees inside, women raped and killed in the streets and bodies burned in piles, and says the massacre served as a warning to the rest of Jiangnan of what resistance would cost.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangzhou_massacre

Wang Xiuchu's eyewitness Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou was not published under the Qing; copies survived and reached Japan, and accounts of the Yangzhou, Jiading and Jiangyin massacres were later republished by anti-Qing writers before the Taiping Rebellion and the 1911 revolution.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangzhou_massacre

Shi's body was never found and only his garments were buried at Mei-hua-ling outside Yangzhou; the Qianlong emperor later gave him the posthumous name Chung-cheng (Zhongzheng), and in 1768 a temple to his memory was built beside the tomb.
https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Eminent_Chinese_of_the_Ch%27ing_Period/Shih_K%27o-fa

voices.text: 越次早，督鎮牌諭至，內有『一人當之，不累百姓』之語，聞者莫不感泣。
voices.who: Wang Xiuchu, a townsman of Yangzhou, describing the placard Shi Kefa had posted the day the city fell (in short: next morning the commander's placard came, with the words 'I alone will bear it; the common people shall not be made to suffer'; everyone who heard it wept, moved)
voices.doc: Wang Xiuchu, Yangzhou shiri ji (A Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou), as printed in the Mingji baishi huibian, transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 一卒提刀前導，一卒橫槊後逐，一卒居中，或左或右以防逃逸。數十人如驅牛羊，稍不前即加捶撻，或即殺之；諸婦女長索繋頸，累累如貫珠，一步一跌，遍身泥土；滿地皆嬰兒，或襯馬蹄，或籍人足，肝腦塗地，泣聲盈埜。
voices.who: Wang Xiuchu, being marched off with his brothers and some fifty other captives (in short: one soldier went ahead with a sword, one behind with a lance, one in the middle to stop anyone escaping; several dozen of us were driven like oxen and sheep, and whoever lagged was beaten or killed on the spot; the women had a long rope tied round their necks, strung together like pearls, stumbling at every step and covered in mud; babies lay all over the ground under horses' hooves and people's feet, their brains spattered on the earth, and weeping filled the fields)
voices.doc: Wang Xiuchu, Yangzhou shiri ji (A Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou), as printed in the Mingji baishi huibian, transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 忽聞隔墻吾弟哀號聲，又聞舉刀砍擊聲，凡三擊，遂寂然。少間，復聞仲兄哀懇曰：「吾有金在家地窖中，放我取獻。」一擊復寂然。
voices.who: Wang Xiuchu, hiding in a loft after escaping the killing ground (in short: through the wall I suddenly heard my younger brother cry out, then a blade striking, three blows, then silence; a little later I heard my second brother beg, 'I have gold in a cellar at home; let me go and fetch it for you'; one blow, and silence again)
voices.doc: Wang Xiuchu, Yangzhou shiri ji (A Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou), as printed in the Mingji baishi huibian, transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 查焚尸簿載數，其八十萬餘，其落井投河、閉門焚縊者不與焉，被擄者不與焉。
voices.who: Wang Xiuchu, after the monks were ordered to burn the dead (in short: the register of burned corpses counted more than 800,000, not counting those who threw themselves into wells and rivers or shut their doors and burned or hanged themselves, nor those carried off); historians consider the figure greatly exaggerated (see Disputed)
voices.doc: Wang Xiuchu, Yangzhou shiri ji (A Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou), as printed in the Mingji baishi huibian, transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 自四月二十五日起，至五月五日止，共十日。其間皆身所親歷，目所親睹，故漫記之如此，遠處風聞者不載也。
voices.who: Wang Xiuchu, closing his record; of the eight members of his close family caught up in the sack, he writes, three were left (in short: from the 25th of the fourth month to the 5th of the fifth, ten days in all; I lived through all of it myself and saw it with my own eyes, so I have written it down as it was; what I only heard of from far away I have left out)
voices.doc: Wang Xiuchu, Yangzhou shiri ji (A Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou), as printed in the Mingji baishi huibian, transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 法北望陵廟，無涕可揮；身蹈大戮，罪應萬死；所以不即從先帝於地下者，實惟社稷之故。
voices.who: Shi Kefa, Ming commander-in-chief and so an official of the losing state, killed when the city fell, in his reply to the Qing regent Dorgon (in short: looking north to the imperial tombs I have no tears left to shed; I have earned the gravest punishment and deserve ten thousand deaths; I did not follow the late emperor into the grave at once only for the sake of the dynasty's altars)
voices.doc: Shi Kefa, Fu Duo'ergun shu (Reply to Dorgon), Chinese Wikisource, supplemented from the Nanjiang yishi

official.text: 今若擁號稱尊，便是天有二日，儼為敵國。予將簡西行之銳卒，轉旆東征；且擬釋彼重誅，命為前導。
official.who: Dorgon, Prince Regent of the Qing, in his letter to Shi Kefa, which presents the Manchus as avengers of the Ming emperor against the rebel Li Zicheng (in short: if you now set up an emperor of your own, there will be two suns in the sky and you will be an enemy state; I will take the picked troops I was sending west, turn my banners east, and may even pardon the rebel and make him my vanguard). The letter is preserved in the Qing draft history, Qing shi gao

official.text: 四月，師進次泗州，渡淮趨揚州，遣兵部尚書漢岱等先驅，得舟三百餘，圍七日，克之，殺明大學士史可法。
official.who: The Qing shi gao (Draft History of the Qing), biography of Dodo, compiled by the Qing History Office of the Republic of China and published 1928 from Qing records (in short: in the fourth month the army advanced to Sizhou, crossed the Huai and made for Yangzhou; it sent the President of the Board of War Handai ahead, seized more than 300 boats, besieged the city seven days, took it, and killed the Ming Grand Secretary Shi Kefa). The official record says nothing of the killing of the townspeople

official.text: 至若史可法之支撐殘局、力矢孤忠，終蹈一死以殉；又如劉宗周、黃道周等之立朝謇諤、抵觸僉壬，及遭際時艱，臨危授命：均足稱一代完人，為褒揚所當及。其他或死守城池、或身殞行陣與夫俘擒駢戮、視死如歸者，爾時王旅徂征，自不得不申法令，以明順逆；而事後平情而論，若而人者皆無愧於疾風勁草，即自盡以全名節，其心亦並可矜憐！
official.who: The Qianlong emperor, edict ordering posthumous honours for Ming loyalists, printed at the head of the Qinding Shengchao xunjie zhuchen lu (Record of the Martyred Officials of the Fallen Dynasty, 1776) (in short: Shi Kefa, who held up a collapsing cause with solitary loyalty and died for it, and others like him, were perfect men of their age and deserve praise; as for those who died defending cities, in battle, or executed as captives, at that time, while the royal army was on campaign, the law had to be enforced to show who submitted and who rebelled; but judged calmly afterwards, they were all like hardy grass in a gale, and even those who killed themselves to keep their honour deserve pity)
official.date: 10th day of the 11th month of Qianlong 40 (winter 1775–76)

official.text: 夫可法，明臣也。其不屈，正也。不載其語，不有失忠臣之心乎？
official.who: The Qianlong emperor, essay on Shi Kefa's reply to Dorgon, which he had searched for in the palace archives and ordered printed (in short: Shi Kefa was a Ming minister, and his refusal to yield was right; not to record his words would fail a loyal minister's heart). Reprinted in Li Yao's Nanjiang yishi (1830)

stories.note: Research in progress: P. Aucourt's French translation of the memoir, 'Journal d'un bourgeois de Yang-tcheou (1645)' (Bulletin de l'École française d'Extrême-Orient, 1907), is public domain and could supply a checked European-language version; it has not yet been examined.
stories.warn: The memoir, Shi Kefa's letter and the Qing documents are quoted in classical Chinese from Chinese Wikisource transcriptions of public-domain texts; the plain-English summaries in 'who' are the site's own, not translations. The only pre-1931 English version, in Backhouse and Bland's Annals and Memoirs of the Court of Peking (1914), was checked against the Chinese and is not quoted: it departs from Wang's text in places (it has the captive women tied together 'at the knees' where Wang wrote that a long rope was tied round their necks, and softens a Qing soldier's boast that not one of tens of thousands of women seized in Korea had lost her chastity), it calls the author unknown, and Backhouse is known to have forged other Chinese documents. Chinese tradition holds that Dorgon's letter may have been drafted by Li Wen and Shi's reply by Hou Fangyu. The memoir describes rape and the killing of children.
disputed: How many died? Wang says the register of corpses burned by the monks counted more than 800,000, not counting suicides and captives. Wikipedia reports that modern historians consider this an extreme exaggeration: Lynn Struve, following a 1964 study by Zhang Defang, notes that the city then probably held no more than 300,000 people and the whole prefecture about 800,000. Backhouse and Bland (1914) put the population at over a million and the dead at more than half a million. Wikipedia also says the killing was over by the sixth day, despite the memoir's title.

Silence and revival. The Qing draft history records only that Dodo's army besieged Yangzhou seven days, took it and killed Shi Kefa. Wang's record was not published under the Qing and survived in copies that reached Japan; late-Qing anti-Manchu writers republished it, and Wikipedia says such atrocity accounts were used by revolutionaries in 1911 to fuel massacres of Manchus, so the memoir has served as propaganda as well as testimony.

The Ming side's own record. Wang does not spare it: two of the Ming soldiers billeted in his house trampled everything and cost over a thousand cash a day; he says Yangzhou men guided the Qing soldiers to rich houses; on the first day of the fifth month the troops of the Ming Earl of Xingping (an interlinear note identifies him as Gao Jie, but Gao Jie had been murdered at Suiyang months before, as the appendix printed with the memoir says, and the title had passed to his young son, so these were his old army) re-entered the city and took every last thread and grain; and on the tenth day he could not tell whether the plunderers were Qing soldiers, Ming garrison troops or rioters. An appendix printed with the memoir blames Gao Jie's army for earlier killing around the city and blames Shi Kefa's own decisions, quoting a friend who said Shi had ruined the south-east; Hummel's biography likewise says the Ming generals at Yangzhou were outraging the people of their districts.

Hero or lesson? The Qing state that killed Shi Kefa made him a model of loyalty: Qianlong praised his solitary loyalty, blamed the Prince of Fu for not trusting him, and honoured him with a posthumous name, while saying that the killing of loyalists had been necessary at the time to show the difference between submission and rebellion.
stories.blind: Wang Xiuchu, a townsman who survived by hiding and paying, is almost the only voice of Yangzhou's people; he names his brothers but not the women he saw seized and raped, and those women, the children, the captives carried off and the soldiers of both armies have no words of their own. The Qing official record is silent on the killing, and the Ming words that survive are those of officials.
reading: Shih K'o-fa, in Eminent Chinese of the Ch'ing Period (1943, Wikisource)
揚州十日記 Yangzhou shiri ji, Chinese text (Wikisource)
Backhouse and Bland, Annals and Memoirs of the Court of Peking (1914), ch. VII, 'The Sack of Yang Chou-fu' (archive.org; a loose translation)

stories.title: Le Grand Dérangement: the expulsion of the Acadians
stories.where: Grand-Pré and the Minas Basin, Nova Scotia, Canada
facts: The Acadians had lived in what is now Nova Scotia since the founding of Port-Royal in 1604, farming dyked marshland around the Bay of Fundy with the Mi'kmaq as friends and allies; sovereignty passed to Britain after 1713, and in 1730 the British persuaded them to swear, if not allegiance, at least neutrality in any war between Britain and France.
https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/la-deportation-des-acadiens

Many Acadians refused an unconditional oath because it might commit their men to fight France and look to their Mi'kmaq neighbours like accepting the British claim to Acadia; others refused because they were anti-British, and over the decades some took part in French military operations and helped supply the French fortresses of Louisbourg and Beauséjour.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_the_Acadians

After Fort Beauséjour fell in June 1755, Governor Charles Lawrence noted some 270 Acadian militia among its inhabitants; in July 1755 he pressed Acadian delegates in Halifax to take an unqualified oath of allegiance, and when they refused he imprisoned them and ordered the deportation.
https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/la-deportation-des-acadiens

On 5 September 1755 Lieutenant-Colonel John Winslow had the men and boys of the Grand-Pré district gathered in the church to hear the order; the plan was to capture as many men as possible, breach the dykes and burn the houses and crops, and between 1755 and 1763 approximately 10,000 Acadians were deported to the English colonies, France and the Caribbean.
https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/la-deportation-des-acadiens

Of some 3,100 Acadians deported after the fall of Louisbourg in 1758 an estimated 1,649 died by drowning or disease, a death rate of 53 per cent; thousands died of disease or starvation aboard the ships.
https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/la-deportation-des-acadiens

Some Acadians fought back, among them Joseph Broussard dit Beausoleil, who led retaliatory raids on British troops, and many hid in the forests, where they were hunted for five years; their lands went to New England settlers, and when Acadians were allowed to return after 1764 they settled far from their old homes.
https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/la-deportation-des-acadiens

voices.text: It appears, Sir, that your Excellency doubts the sincerity with which we have promised to be faithful to his Britannic Majesty. We most humbly beg your Excellency to consider our past conduct. You will see, that, very far from violating the oath we have taken, we have maintained it in its entirety, in spite of the solicitations and the dreadful threats of another power. [...] It is not the gun which an inhabitant possesses, that will induce him to revolt, nor the privation of the same gun that will make him more faithful; but his conscience alone must induce him to maintain his oath.
voices.who: The inhabitants of Minas, Pisiquid and the River Canard, memorial to Governor Charles Lawrence after their guns and canoes were seized, signed by their deputies and others
voices.doc: Selections from the Public Documents of the Province of Nova Scotia, ed. Thomas B. Akins (Halifax, 1869), pp. 247-249, 'translated from the French' by Benjamin Curren

voices.text: we were transported into the English Colonies, and this was done in so much haste, and with so little regard to our necessities and the tenderest ties of nature, that from the most social enjoyments and affluent circumstances, many found themselves destitute of the necessaries of life: Parents were separated from children, and husbands from wives, some of whom have not to this day met again; and we were so crowded in the transport vessels, that we had not room even for all our bodies to lay down at once, and consequently were prevented from carrying with us proper necessaries, especially for the support and comfort of the aged and weak, many of whom quickly ended their misery with their lives.
voices.who: The late French inhabitants of Nova Scotia formerly settled on the Bay of Minas, now residing in Pennsylvania, petition to King George
voices.doc: Thomas C. Haliburton, An Historical and Statistical Account of Nova-Scotia, vol. I (Halifax, 1829), p. 194

voices.text: The miseries we have since endured are scarce sufficiently to be expressed, being reduced for a livelihood to toil and hard labour in a southern clime, so disagreeable to our constitutions, that most of us have been prevented, by sickness, from procuring the necessary subsistance for our families; and therefore are threatened with that which we esteem the greatest aggravation of all our sufferings, even of having our children forced from us, and bound out to strangers [...] We have already seen in this Province of Pennsylvania two hundred and fifty of our people, which is more than half the number that were landed here, perish through misery and various diseases.
voices.who: Same petition of the Acadians in Pennsylvania to King George
voices.doc: Thomas C. Haliburton, An Historical and Statistical Account of Nova-Scotia, vol. I (Halifax, 1829), p. 195

witness.text: Upon an impartial review of the transactions of this period, it must be admitted, that the transportation of the Acadians to distant colonies, with all the marks of ignominy and guilt peculiar to convicts, was cruel; and although such a conclusion could not then be drawn, yet subsequent events have disclosed that their expulsion was unnecessary.
witness.who: Thomas Chandler Haliburton, Nova Scotian lawyer and historian, writing two generations later in An Historical and Statistical Account of Nova-Scotia, vol. I, p. 195

official.text: They were asked, what Excuse they could make for their Presumption in this Paragraph, and treating the Government with such Indignity and Contempt as to Expound to them the nature of Fidelity, and to prescribe what would be the Security proper to be relied on by the Government for their Sincerity.
official.who: Minutes of the Nova Scotia Council, Halifax, on the Minas deputies' memorial and its sentence about guns and conscience; the next day, when the deputies would not take the oath without consulting their people, the Council declared it 'could no longer look on them as Subjects to His Britannick Majesty but as Subjects of the King of France' (Akins, Selections, 1869, pp. 254-256)

official.text: After mature Consideration, it was unanimously Agreed That, to prevent as much as possible their Attempting to return and molest the Settlers that may be set down on their Lands, it would be most proper to send them to be distributed amongst the several Colonies on the Continent, and that a sufficient Number of Vessels should be hired with all possible Expedition for that purpose.
official.who: Nova Scotia Council under Lieutenant-Governor Charles Lawrence, minutes signed by Lawrence (Akins, Selections, 1869, p. 267)

official.text: The Part of Duty I am now upon is what thoh Necessary is Very Disagreable to my natural make & Temper as I Know it Must be Grevious to you who are of the Same Specia. But it is not my Buisness to annimedvert, but to obey Such orders as I receive and therefore without Hessitation Shall Deliver you his Majesty's orders and Instructions vizt. That your Lands & Tennements, Cattle of all Kinds and Live Stock of all Sortes are Forfitted to the Crown with all other your Effects Saving your money and Household Goods and you your Selves to be removed from this his Province.
official.who: Lieutenant-Colonel John Winslow, address read through interpreters to the men held in the church at Grand-Pré, as entered in his journal (Collections of the Nova Scotia Historical Society, vol. III, 1883, pp. 94-95)

official.text: order ye Prisoners to March, they all answered they would No go without their Fathers. I Told them that was a word I did not understand for that the Kings Command was to me absolute & Should be absolutely obeyed & That I Did not Love to use Harsh Means but that the time Did not admit of Parlies or Delays and Then ordered the whole Troops to Fix their Bayonets and advance Towards the French [...] and went of Praying, Singing & Crying being Met by the women & Children all the way (which is 1½ mile) with Great Lamentations upon their Knees praying &c.
official.who: John Winslow's journal, on marching the first 141 young men of Grand-Pré to the transports (Collections of the Nova Scotia Historical Society, vol. III, 1883)

today.text: Whereas the deportation of the Acadian people, commonly known as the Great Upheaval, continued until 1763 and had tragic consequences, including the deaths of many thousands of Acadians - from disease, in shipwrecks, in their places of refuge and in prison camps in Nova Scotia and England as well as in the British colonies in America; Whereas We acknowledge these historical facts and the trials and suffering experienced by the Acadian people during the Great Upheaval;
today.who: Royal Proclamation designating 28 July as 'A Day of Commemoration of the Great Upheaval' (SI/2003-188), issued in the name of Queen Elizabeth II as Queen of Canada; it states that it is not a recognition of legal or financial responsibility

stories.warn: The 1755 memorial was written in French; the card quotes the 1869 English translation printed by the Nova Scotia government. The Pennsylvania petition is quoted as Haliburton printed it in 1829, without a date. Winslow's journal keeps his own eighteenth-century spelling ('thoh', 'Specia' for species, 'annimedvert' for animadvert), which is reproduced as printed. Officials call the Acadians 'the French' and 'Recusants', and the memorial calls the Mi'kmaq 'savages'; these are the documents' words.
disputed: Neutral or not. The Acadians' deputies insisted they had kept their oath of fidelity despite French threats, and the Pennsylvania petition admits only 'some weak and false-hearted persons', twelve of them outlawed by Governor Shirley, while denying that they took part in the killing of Major Noble and his men at Grand-Pré, of which they say they had warned; the Nova Scotia Council treated their refusal of the unconditional oath as proof of insincerity. Some 270 Acadian militia were found at Beauséjour in 1755, some Acadians had joined French military operations and supplied Louisbourg and Beauséjour, and historians note that some Acadians labelled 'neutral' were not; the expulsion nonetheless made no distinction between those who stayed neutral and those who took up arms.

Ethnic cleansing or wartime removal. John Mack Faragher compares the expulsion to ethnic cleansing and points to anti-Catholic laws and the land handed to Protestant settlers; John Grenier says Faragher overstates the religious motive, and Naomi Griffiths and A. J. B. Johnston see it as comparable to other deportations of the age, driven by a perceived military threat, and not ethnic cleansing. The event is widely called a crime against humanity, while the use of 'genocide' is debated. The Canadian Encyclopedia judges it as unnecessary on military grounds as it was inhumane; Haliburton already called it cruel and unnecessary in 1829.

How many were deported and died. The Canadian Encyclopedia gives approximately 10,000 deported between 1755 and 1763, and 1,649 dead of some 3,100 deported after 1758; Wikipedia gives about 11,500 deported of an estimated 14,100 Acadians, of whom 5,000 died, including almost 1,000 when the Duke William, Violet and Ruby sank in 1758. The Pennsylvania exiles wrote that 250 of their people, more than half of those landed there, had died; Haliburton says 415 were sent to Pennsylvania.
stories.blind: The Acadians who speak here are their deputies and elders, men writing formal petitions to governors and the king, in documents later selected by a Nova Scotia records commissioner who said in his preface that the necessity of the removal had not been clearly understood; the women and children appear only in Winslow's journal, on their knees by the road. The thousands who died at sea or in the colonies, and the Mi'kmaq, allies and kin of many Acadians who fought the British for decades, have almost no words of their own in this record.
reading: T. B. Akins (ed.), Selections from the Public Documents of the Province of Nova Scotia (1869, scan)
Journal of Colonel John Winslow, Collections of the Nova Scotia Historical Society, vol. III (1883, scan)
T. C. Haliburton, An Historical and Statistical Account of Nova-Scotia, vol. I (1829, scan)
The Canadian Encyclopedia, Acadian Expulsion (the Great Upheaval)
Royal Proclamation of 2003 (SI/2003-188), Justice Laws Website

stories.title: The Eora and the First Fleet: smallpox, reprisals and Pemulwuy's war
stories.where: Sydney Cove (Warrane), Port Jackson, New South Wales, Australia
facts: The Eora are the traditional owners of the lands around Sydney Harbour; nearly 1,500 people arrived on the First Fleet, with limited food, foreign animals and firearms.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/pemulwuy

In 1789, some 16 months after the fleet arrived, an epidemic that the colonists called smallpox devastated the Aboriginal people around Sydney while sparing the British (Collins records one North American sailor who caught it and died); Governor Phillip estimated that perhaps half had died, and Bennelong also believed that half the Eora of the Sydney district had died.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_in_Australia

In December 1790 the Bidjigal man Pemulwuy was involved in the spearing of Governor Phillip's gamekeeper John McIntyre (spelt McEntire by Tench), a man the Eora feared and hated; Phillip called for a punitive raid by soldiers equipped with bags for heads, and when that party came back without corpses he sent it out again.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/pemulwuy

From 1792 Pemulwuy led raids on the farms spreading over Bidjigal land, in which huts were burnt, maize taken and travellers attacked; by April 1794 the violence between Aboriginal people and farmers was frequent and extensive, and in the 'Battle of Toongabbie' a settlers' reprisal party cut off the head of a slain warrior and carried it to Sydney.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/pemulwuy

On 1 May 1801 Governor King ordered that Aboriginal people near Parramatta, Georges River and Prospect could be shot on sight, and in November outlawed Pemulwuy with rewards for his death or capture; on or just before 2 June 1802 he was shot dead, and his head was cut off and sent to Sir Joseph Banks in England, where its whereabouts are now unknown.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/pemulwuy

A letter Bennelong drafted in 1796 addressed to a 'Mr. Phillips' (perhaps meant for former Governor Phillip, whose wife had nursed him in England), thanking Mrs Phillips for her care and asking for stockings and a handkerchief, is the first known text in English by an Aboriginal Australian (dictated to a scribe).
https://web.archive.org/web/20201021021051/https://aiatsis.gov.au/bennelongs-letter

voices.text: Sir, I am very well. I hope you are very well. I live at the governor's. I have every day dinner there. I have not my wife; another black man took her away. We have had muzzy doings; he speared me in the back, but I better now; his name is Carroway. All my friends alive and well. Not me go to England no more. I am at home now.
voices.who: Bennelong (Baneelon, Bannelong), Wangal man, letter dictated to a scribe and addressed to 'Mr. Phillips, Steward to Lord Sidney'; AIATSIS notes that no such steward has been found and that it may have been meant for former Governor Phillip, whose second wife nursed Bennelong when he was ill in England; signed 'Bannelong'
voices.doc: Letter from Bennelong, Sydney Cove, to Mr Phillips (original lost; text from the copy printed by F. X. von Zach, Monatliche Correspondenz, 1801), transcription on the AIATSIS page
voices.lic: Public domain (letter of 1796; printed 1801); transcription as given by AIATSIS, an Australian Government body

voices.text: He looked anxiously around him in the different coves we visited; not a vestige on the sand was to be found of human foot; the excavations in the rocks were filled with the putrid bodies of those who had fallen victims to the disorder; not a living person was any where to be met with. It seemed as if, flying from the contagion, they had left the dead to bury the dead. He lifted up his hands and eyes in silent agony for some time; at last he exclaimed, 'All dead! all dead!' and then hung his head in mournful silence, which he preserved during the remainder of our excursion.
voices.who: The Eora man held at the settlement, whom Collins does not name but who is identified as Arabanoo, seized by the colonists at Manly Cove on 31 December 1788 and held at Sydney, on being taken round the harbour during the 1789 epidemic, as recorded by David Collins, the colony's judge-advocate (Arabanoo himself died of the disease in May 1789)
voices.doc: David Collins, An Account of the English Colony in New South Wales, vol. I (London, 1798), appendix on the natives

voices.text: Bennillong told us, that his friend Cole-be's tribe being reduced by its effects to three persons, Cole-be, the boy Nan-bar-ray, and some one else, they found themselves compelled to unite with some other tribe, not only for their personal protection, but to prevent the extinction of their tribe.
voices.who: Bennelong, on what the 1789 epidemic did to the Cadigal clan of his friend Colbee, as recorded by David Collins
voices.doc: David Collins, An Account of the English Colony in New South Wales, vol. I (London, 1798), appendix on the natives

voices.text: These two people inquired kindly how his excellency did, and seemed pleased to hear that he was likely to recover. They said that they were inhabitants of Rose Hill, and expressed great dissatisfaction at the number of white men who had settled in their former territories. In consequence of which declaration, the detachment at that post was reinforced on the following day.
voices.who: Two Aboriginal men of the Rose Hill (Parramatta) district, speaking a week after Governor Phillip was speared at Manly, as recorded by Watkin Tench, captain of marines
voices.doc: Watkin Tench, A Complete Account of the Settlement at Port Jackson (London, 1793), ch. VIII

voices.text: In passing along we shot some ducks, which Boladeree refused to swim for when requested, and told us in a surly tone that they swam for what was killed, and had the trouble of fetching it ashore, only for the white men to eat it. This reproof was, I fear, too justly founded; for of the few ducks we had been so fortunate as to procure, little had fallen to their share except the offals, and now and then a half-picked bone.
voices.who: Boladeree (Ballederry), an Eora man guiding an exploring party up the Hawkesbury, as recorded by Watkin Tench, who agrees with him
voices.doc: Watkin Tench, A Complete Account of the Settlement at Port Jackson (London, 1793), ch. XIV (travelling diaries)

witness.text: On inspection, it appeared that all the parties had died a natural death: pustules, similar to those occasioned by the small pox, were thickly spread on the bodies; but how a disease, to which our former observations had led us to suppose them strangers, could at once have introduced itself, and have spread so widely, seemed inexplicable.
witness.who: Watkin Tench, captain of marines in the First Fleet, on the bodies found in the coves of the harbour in April 1789, A Complete Account of the Settlement at Port Jackson, ch. IV (he was a colonist, not a neutral observer)

witness.text: An armed party was directly sent out, who, coming up with them, killed four men and one woman, badly wounded a child, and took four men prisoners. It might have been supposed that these punishments, following the enormities so immediately, would have taught the natives to keep at a greater distance; but nothing seemed to deter them from prosecuting the revenge they had vowed against the settlers for the injuries they had received at their hands.
witness.who: David Collins, judge-advocate and secretary of the colony, on the Hawkesbury River after Aboriginal people stripped outlying settlers' huts, An Account of the English Colony in New South Wales, vol. I

official.text: Several tribes of the natives still continuing to throw spears at any man they meet unarmed, by which several have been killed, or dangerously wounded, the governor, in order to deter the natives from such practices in future, has ordered out a party to search for the man who wounded the convict McEntire, in so dangerous a manner on Friday last, though no offence was offered on his part, in order to make a signal example of that tribe. [...] A party, consisting of two captains, two subalterns, and forty privates, with a proper number of non-commissioned officers from the garrison, with three days provisions, etc. are to be ready to march to-morrow morning at day-light, in order to bring in six of those natives who reside near the head of Botany Bay; or, if that should be found impracticable, to put that number to death.
official.who: Governor Arthur Phillip, public order after the spearing of McEntire, as printed by Watkin Tench (ch. XII), who was chosen to lead the party; Tench adds that Phillip's spoken orders were 'to cut off and bring in the heads of the slain; for which purpose hatchets and bags would be furnished' (the order first named ten to be killed and two taken; Tench persuaded Phillip to make it six)

official.text: Decided measures therefore became necessary to prevent the out-settlers from being robbed and plundered, and to restore the natives to a friendly intercourse. With these views (founded on the opinions of the principal officers coinciding with mine), I gave orders for every person doing their utmost to bring Pemulwye in either dead or alive
official.who: Governor Philip Gidley King to Lord Hobart, Secretary of State for the Colonies, despatch reporting Pemulwuy's death, as quoted by the National Museum of Australia

today.text: However, conflict was inevitable because of fundamentally opposed viewpoints. The Eora had a complex system of laws that governed social relations, behaviour and resource use. The European invaders had no appreciation of this and believed the Eora people to be savages. An outbreak of smallpox in 1789, introduced by the European invaders, had a significant impact on the local people.
today.who: National Museum of Australia (an Australian Government agency), Defining Moments: Pemulwuy

stories.warn: Every Eora voice here except Bennelong's letter comes through the colonists who wrote it down, in their English and their words ('natives', 'Indians', 'savage', 'tribe'), which are quoted, not endorsed. Bennelong's letter was dictated to a scribe and survives only in a copy. Names are spelt many ways in the sources: Bennelong/Baneelon/Bennillong, Pemulwuy/Pimelwi/Pe-mul-wy/Pemulwye, Colbee/Cole-be, Bidjigal/Bideegal, McIntyre/McEntire/McIntire. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers should be aware that this card names people who have died and describes the taking of heads. The Rose Hill men's and Boladeree's words are Tench's paraphrases.
disputed: Where the 1789 epidemic came from. Tench at the time could only ask whether it was native to the country, brought by La Pérouse's French ships, by Cook, or by the First Fleet itself, and Collins noted that the Eora already had a name for it (gal-gal-la), which some historians take as a sign it had visited before. Among historians who accept it was smallpox, one theory holds that it came overland from Macassan trepang fishers in the north; another that it came with European ships; the independent scholar Christopher Warren argues it was probably released deliberately by the British, a view some Aboriginal scholars share, while the historians Henry Reynolds, Peter Dowling and Cassandra Pybus regard deliberate release as unproven. A 2026 modelling study by Corey Bradshaw and colleagues in Nature Human Behaviour found that its results 'strongly suggest' the disease came from the British outpost (which held variola matter for inoculation, whether it escaped by accident or was released), that there was 'no plausible pathway' for it to arrive from the north in time, and that the epidemic may have spread thousands of kilometres, 'killing as many as 220,000 Aboriginal people'.

Smallpox or chickenpox. Most historians call the 1789 disease smallpox, and the virologist Frank Fenner thought the scanty data favoured it; the medical writers Ford and Carmody argue that its failure to infect any British colonist rules smallpox out and point to chickenpox.

Unprovoked or retribution. McIntyre swore on his deathbed that he had given no offence and had fired on an Aboriginal man only once, and Phillip called the spearing unprovoked; but Tench records that 'most people doubted' his confession, and the Australian Dictionary of Biography, cited by the National Museum, suggests the spearing punished his violence towards Aboriginal people. Spearings of convicts and settlers were real and repeated (Phillip counted 17 killed or wounded by December 1790), as were the colonists' killings in reprisal.

Who shot Pemulwuy. Following Keith Vincent Smith it has generally been assumed the killer was Henry Hacking; Doug Kohlhoff argues settlers from Parramatta, Toongabbie and Prospect Hill were more likely.
stories.blind: Almost everything known about the Eora in these years was written by the colonists: Tench, Collins, Phillip, King. The Eora speak in their journals only when it suited the writer to record them, through interpreters and in English, and the single text in an Aboriginal voice, Bennelong's letter, was dictated to a scribe and survives in a German printed copy. Pemulwuy left no words at all; the women, the Bidjigal fighters and the people who died in the rock shelters in 1789 are seen only from outside, and the Eora's own record lives in oral tradition and Country, not in these books.
reading: Watkin Tench, A Complete Account of the Settlement at Port Jackson (1793), Project Gutenberg
David Collins, An Account of the English Colony in New South Wales, vol. I (1798), Project Gutenberg
National Museum of Australia, Defining Moments: Pemulwuy
National Library of Australia, Letter from Bennelong to Mr Phillips (manuscript copy)

stories.title: The Rhineland massacres of 1096
stories.where: Mainz, Germany (also Speyer, Worms and Cologne; approximate)
facts: Peter the Hermit's preaching in Germany inspired bands of Crusaders who never reached Jerusalem; one of them, led by Count Emicho, carried out a series of pogroms against the Jews of Rhineland towns in 1096, first in Speyer and then with increasing ferocity in Worms, Mainz and Cologne.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Crusades/The-First-Crusade-and-the-establishment-of-the-Latin-states

On 3 May 1096 (8 Iyyar) Crusaders surrounded the synagogue of Speyer and, unable to break in, killed eleven Jews they found outside it; on 18 May they attacked Worms, killing first those who had stayed in their houses and, eight days later, those who had sought refuge in the bishop's castle, about 800 victims in all.
https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-crusades

In Mainz the Jews paid the bishop 400 pieces of silver for protection; when Emicho's Crusaders arrived on 27 May the burghers opened the gates, the Jews took up arms under Kalonymus ben Meshullam, the bishop fled, and more than 1,000 Jews died, at the enemy's hands or their own.
https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-crusades

Offered only baptism or death, many chose to be killed or to take their own lives rather than abandon their faith, and only a few survived by accepting conversion; this freely accepted martyrdom, Kiddush ha-Shem ('for the glory of God'), became the defining Jewish answer to the Crusaders.
https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-crusades

In Cologne, attacked on 30 May, the bishop dispersed the Jews to nearby villages, but the Crusaders found them there; Emicho's army was later crushed by the Hungarians, and the Encyclopaedia Judaica counts more than 5,000 victims in all that year, a total that also covers Trier, Regensburg, Metz, Prague and Bohemia.
https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-crusades

In 1097 Emperor Henry IV allowed Jews baptized under duress to return openly to Judaism, which the antipope Clement III strongly condemned, and in 1098 he ordered an inquiry into what had become of the murdered Mainz Jews' property.
https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-crusades

voices.text: Alle Gemeinden haben ein Fasten angeordnet, wir thun das unsrige, Gott möge uns und euch befreien aus jeder Noth und Bedrängniss, denn wir sind euretwegen in grosser Furcht. Was uns selbst betrifft, so brauchen wir uns nicht zu ängstigen; wir haben derartiges nicht einmal gerüchtsweise vernommen, von einer Gefahr, dass das Schwert über unserm Leben schwebe, haben wir nichts gehört.
voices.who: The leaders of the Jewish community of Mainz, answering a warning letter from the Jews of France, as recorded in the anonymous Hebrew chronicle known as the Mainz Anonymous (German tr. S. Baer, 1892). In plain English: 'All the communities have proclaimed a fast; we are doing our part. May God deliver us and you from every distress and trouble, for we are in great fear for your sake. As for ourselves, we need not be afraid; we have not heard so much as a rumour of such things, nothing of any danger of the sword hanging over our lives.'
voices.doc: Anonymer Bericht der Darmstädter Handschrift (Mainz Anonymous), in Neubauer & Stern, Hebräische Berichte über die Judenverfolgungen während der Kreuzzüge (Berlin, 1892), p. 170 (OCR corrected)

voices.text: Als der Bischof Johann das erfuhr, kam er mit vieler Mannschaft, um der Gemeinde aufrichtig beizustehen, er liess sie in seine Gemächer bringen und rettete sie aus den Händen der Feinde. Einige der Städter liess er ergreifen und ihnen die Hände abhauen, denn er war ein Frommer unter den Völkern, darum liess Gott durch ihn uns Heil und Rettung entstehen.
voices.who: The Jews of Speyer on their bishop, John, as recorded in the Mainz Anonymous (German tr. S. Baer, 1892). In plain English: 'When Bishop John learned of it, he came with many men to help the community in good faith; he had them brought into his chambers and saved them from the hands of the enemy. He had some of the townsmen seized and their hands cut off, for he was a righteous man among the nations; therefore God brought us help and rescue through him.'
voices.doc: Anonymer Bericht der Darmstädter Handschrift (Mainz Anonymous), in Neubauer & Stern, Hebräische Berichte (Berlin, 1892), p. 171

voices.text: Ewiger, Gott Israels, willst du denn ein Ende machen dem Ueberreste Israels? Wo sind all deine furchtbaren Wunderthaten, von denen unsere Väter uns erzählten? Hast du uns nicht aus Egypten und Babel heraufgeführt und so oft uns gerettet?
voices.who: The Jews of Mainz, crying out on hearing of the killings in Speyer and Worms, as preserved in the Hebrew chronicle of Solomon bar Samson (German tr. S. Baer, 1892). In plain English: 'Lord, God of Israel, will you make an end of the remnant of Israel? Where are all your awesome wonders that our fathers told us of? Did you not bring us up out of Egypt and Babylon and save us so many times?'
voices.doc: Bericht des Salomo bar Simeon, in Neubauer & Stern, Hebräische Berichte (Berlin, 1892), p. 86 (OCR corrected)

voices.text: Denn darum streueten wir unser Geld aus und gaben dem Bischof und seinen Oberen und Dienern und den Städtern gegen 400 Mark Silber und dem Bösewicht Emicho sieben Pfund Gold, damit sie uns beistehen sollten. Aber es nützte uns nicht das Geringste, bis jetzt fand unsere Wunde keine Heilung.
voices.who: The Jews of Mainz, in a first-person passage that Solomon bar Samson took over from an earlier account (German tr. S. Baer, 1892). In plain English: 'That is why we scattered our money and gave the bishop, his officers and servants and the townspeople some 400 marks of silver, and the wicked Emicho seven pounds of gold, so that they would stand by us. But it did not help us in the least; to this day our wound has found no healing.'
voices.doc: Bericht des Salomo bar Simeon, in Neubauer & Stern, Hebräische Berichte (Berlin, 1892), p. 93 (OCR corrected)

voices.text: Israels Männer umgürteten sich ein Jeder mit seinen Waffen im inneren Hofe des Bischofs und näherten sich alle dem Thore, um mit den Irrenden und den Städtern zu kämpfen, und sie kämpften gegen einander bis in die Mitte des Thores. Aber unsere Sünden verursachten, dass die Feinde siegten und die Thore einnahmen. […] Auch die Leute des Bischofs, welche sie doch ihres Beistandes versichert hatten, flohen zuerst, und überlieferten sie so der Hand der Feinde
voices.who: The Jews of Mainz on the defence of the archbishop's courtyard, as preserved by Solomon bar Samson (German tr. S. Baer, 1892; 'die Irrenden', 'those who go astray', is the chronicle's name for the Crusaders). In plain English: 'The men of Israel each girded on his weapons in the inner courtyard of the bishop, and all of them went towards the gate to fight the Crusaders and the townsmen, and they fought each other up to the middle of the gateway. But our sins caused the enemy to prevail and take the gates. […] The bishop's men too, who had assured them of their help, were the first to flee, and so delivered them into the hands of the enemy.'
voices.doc: Bericht des Salomo bar Simeon, in Neubauer & Stern, Hebräische Berichte (Berlin, 1892), p. 95 (OCR corrected)

voices.text: Jammere ob der einzigen Gemeinde, die ihren Schöpfer als Einzigen verherrlichte durch zehn heilige Märtyrer. […] Die heilige Vereinigung — im Glanzmonat ward sie der Herrlichkeit zugesellt und in den Verband der Seligen aufgenommen.
voices.who: Eliezer bar Nathan of Mainz, a rabbi and liturgical poet born about 1090, a child at the time, in a short lament for the martyrs of Speyer set into his chronicle (German tr. S. Baer, 1892, who notes that he could not render these elegies word for word). In plain English: 'Lament for the singular community that glorified its Creator as the One through ten holy martyrs. […] The holy fellowship, in the month of splendour, was joined to glory and received into the company of the blessed.'
voices.doc: Bericht des Elieser bar Nathan, in Neubauer & Stern, Hebräische Berichte (Berlin, 1892), pp. 154–155

witness.text: An einem Orte waren vereinigt: Thora, Grösse, Reichthum, Ehre, Weisheit, Demuth und Wohlthätigkeit, Zaun um Zaun zur Umzäunung ihrer Worte. Und jetzt ist ihre Weisheit vernichtet; sie sind aufgerieben worden wie Jerusalems Söhne bei dessen Zerstörung.
witness.who: Solomon bar Samson's own lament, written about 1140, for the community of Mainz (German tr. S. Baer, 1892). In plain English: 'In one place were united Torah, greatness, wealth, honour, wisdom, humility and charity, fence upon fence to guard their words. And now their wisdom is destroyed; they have been worn away like the sons of Jerusalem at its destruction.'
witness.doc: Bericht des Salomo bar Simeon, in Neubauer & Stern, Hebräische Berichte (Berlin, 1892), p. 94 (OCR corrected)

witness.text: The Jews of this city, knowing of the slaughter of their brethren, and that they themselves could not escape the hands of so many, fled in hope of safety to Bishop Rothard. They put an infinite treasure in his guard and trust, having much faith in his protection, because he was Bishop of the city. Then that excellent Bishop of the city cautiously set aside the incredible amount of money received from them. He placed the Jews in the very spacious hall of his own house, away from the sight of Count Emico and his followers, that they might remain safe and sound in a very secure and strong place.
witness.who: Albert of Aachen, canon of Aachen, who never went east but wrote his history of the First Crusade from the accounts of returning crusaders (tr. August C. Krey, 1921)

witness.text: This slaughter of Jews was done first by citizens of Cologne. These suddenly fell upon a small band of Jews and severely wounded and killed many; they destroyed the houses and synagogues of the Jews and divided among themselves a very large amount of money.
witness.who: Albert of Aachen on the townspeople of Cologne (tr. August C. Krey, 1921)

witness.text: So the hand of the Lord is believed to have been against the pilgrims, who had sinned by excessive impurity and fornication, and who had slaughtered the exiled Jews through greed of money, rather than for the sake of God's justice, although the Jews were opposed to Christ. The Lord is a just judge and orders no one unwillingly, or under compulsion, to come under the yoke of the Catholic faith.
witness.who: Albert of Aachen, explaining the rout of Emicho's army in Hungary (tr. August C. Krey, 1921)

witness.text: Im Jahre 900 habe ich Salomo bar Simon diese Begebenheit abgeschrieben in Mainz. Dort habe ich von den Alten das Ereigniss erfragt und nach ihren Aussagen jede Sache gehörig geordnet; sie haben mir diese Heiligung erzählt.
witness.who: Solomon bar Samson, the Mainz chronicler, on how he compiled his account (German tr. S. Baer, 1892; the Hebrew year 900 of the fifth millennium is 1140). In plain English: 'In the year 900 I, Solomon bar Simson, copied out this account ('abgeschrieben', literally 'copied') in Mainz. There I asked the elders about what happened and set everything in order according to their testimony; they told me of this sanctification.'

official.text: Just at that time, there appeared a certain soldier, Emico, Count of the lands around the Rhine, a man long of very ill repute on account of his tyrannical mode of life. Called by divine revelation, like another Saul, as he maintained, to the practice of religion of this kind, he usurped to himself the command of almost twelve thousand cross bearers. As they were led through the cities of the Rhine and the Main and also the Danube, they either utterly destroyed the execrable race of the Jews wherever they found them (being even in this matter zealously devoted to the Christian religion) or forced them into the bosom of the Church.
official.who: Ekkehard of Aura, German Benedictine monk and chronicler, later abbot of Aura, who went on the Crusade of 1101 and gives the account of the crusading Church; he condemns Emicho, but describes the attacks on Jews as zeal for the Christian religion (tr. August C. Krey, 1921)

official.text: Sehet, wir ziehen nach einem fernen Lande, ziehen dahin, um mit den Königen des Landes Krieg zu führen, wir wagen unser Leben, um alle jene Nationen, die nicht an den Gekreuzigten glauben, zu töten und zu zertrümmern — um wie viel mehr verdienen es die Juden, die ihn umgebracht und gehängt haben!
official.who: The Crusaders' reasoning, as recorded by their victims in the Mainz Anonymous (German tr. S. Baer, 1892). In plain English: 'Look, we are going to a distant land to make war on its kings; we risk our lives to kill and crush all the nations that do not believe in the Crucified. How much more do the Jews deserve it, who killed and hanged him!'

official.text: Da entbrannte der Zorn des Königs und er schickte in alle Provinzen seines Reiches, an die Fürsten, Bischöfe, Grafen, auch an den Herzog Gottfried Briefe, Worte des Friedens, dass sie die Juden beschützen sollen, damit keiner sie anrühre, ihnen Böses zu thun, dass sie vielmehr ihnen beistehen und Zuflucht gewähren sollen.
official.who: Emperor Henry IV's order to protect the Jews, after Kalonymus of Mainz sent him word in Italy, as recorded by Solomon bar Samson; the letters themselves do not survive (German tr. S. Baer, 1892). In plain English: 'Then the king's anger was kindled, and he sent letters, words of peace, to all the provinces of his realm, to the princes, bishops and counts and to Duke Godfrey too, that they should protect the Jews, so that no one should touch them to do them harm, but rather stand by them and give them refuge.'

today.text: Die SchUM-Stätten zeigen aber auch von die dunklen Seiten dieser Geschichte. Jüdinnen und Juden wurden in Speyer, Mainz und Worms immer wieder verfolgt, ihre Wohnviertel verwüstet, ihre Gemeinden zerstört.
today.who: Frank-Walter Steinmeier, President of Germany, presenting the UNESCO World Heritage certificate for the ShUM sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, inscribed in 2021 (German, as published by the Federal Government). He speaks of the persecutions over the centuries in general, not of 1096 alone. In plain English: 'But the ShUM sites also show the dark sides of this history. Jews in Speyer, Mainz and Worms were persecuted again and again, their quarters devastated, their communities destroyed.'

stories.warn: The Hebrew chronicles are quoted in Seligmann Baer's 1892 German translation, with the site's own plain-English glosses. Baer softened or left out the chronicles' insults against Christianity and marked those places with an asterisk, and he says the short elegies could not be rendered word for word. The chronicles are religious memorials written a generation or more later; they call the Crusaders 'those who go astray' and curse Emicho. Albert of Aachen and Ekkehard are Christian clerics writing from reports, in August C. Krey's 1921 English.
disputed: How many died. The Hebrew chronicles count eleven dead at Speyer (Solomon bar Samson and the Mainz Anonymous) or ten (Eliezer bar Nathan), about 800 at Worms, and 1,100 at Mainz on a single day; Albert of Aachen puts the Mainz dead in the bishop's hall at about 700. The Encyclopaedia Judaica gives more than 1,000 for Mainz and more than 5,000 victims in all (including Trier, Regensburg, Metz and Bohemia); Wikipedia's summary gives 2,000 Jews.

Faith or money? The chronicles give the attackers a religious motive: revenge for the Crucifixion before fighting Muslims, and the Mainz Anonymous reports a proclamation that whoever killed a Jew would have all his sins forgiven. Albert of Aachen, a Christian, says they killed 'through greed of money', and the townspeople of Cologne and Worms shared in the attacks and the plunder; historians also point to crusaders' need for money and their debts. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, nothing in Pope Urban II's call seemed to threaten the Jews; bishops and the emperor tried, with mixed results, to protect them.

Did the bishops protect or betray? The Mainz Anonymous calls Bishop John of Speyer a righteous man who saved his Jews without a bribe. At Mainz, Solomon bar Samson writes that the archbishop's officers advised the Jews to hand over their money only to get them and their wealth into their power, while his editor notes that the chronicle treats the archbishop himself as sincere at first; Albert of Aachen calls Ruthard 'that excellent Bishop'. Ruthard fled; Solomon says the crowd wanted to kill him too for speaking for Israel.

When and by whom the chronicles were written. Solomon bar Samson says he wrote in Mainz in 1140 from what the elders told him, but parts of his text are in the first person, which his 1892 editor took as a sign of an eyewitness or contemporary source; the editor also found episodes placed out of order. Albert of Aachen has the killing begin in Cologne, while the Hebrew chronicles start with Speyer. Modern historians debate whether the chronicles show the victims' own views (Israel Yuval) or those of the survivors' descendants writing in the 12th century (Jeremy Cohen).
stories.blind: The dead left no words of their own. What survives on the Jewish side is three Hebrew chronicles put together in the 12th century by survivors and their descendants as memorials of martyrdom, shaped by liturgy and scripture, plus later laments and memorial books. The Christian side is told by clerics such as Albert of Aachen and Ekkehard, who wrote from reports and judged the attackers by their own faith. Emicho, his followers and the townspeople who joined them left no account of their own, and the forced converts who later returned to Judaism appear only in a line or two.
reading: A. Neubauer and M. Stern (eds.), tr. S. Baer, Hebräische Berichte über die Judenverfolgungen während der Kreuzzüge (Berlin, 1892), full text
August C. Krey, The First Crusade: The Accounts of Eye-Witnesses and Participants (1921), full text
ShUM Sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz (UNESCO World Heritage Centre)

stories.title: The Japanese invasions of Korea (the Imjin War)
stories.where: Korean peninsula (pin: Seoul, South Korea)
facts: Having unified Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi launched invasions of Korea in 1592 and 1597 with the ultimate, though unrealistic, goal of conquering China and beyond; the campaigns failed, the Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin won lasting fame for repelling the Japanese fleets, and Hideyoshi died in 1598.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Toyotomi-Hideyoshi

Japan quickly occupied large parts of Korea in 1592, but Ming Chinese reinforcements and the Joseon navy's attacks on Japanese supply fleets forced a withdrawal from the north; Korean civilian militias then fought a guerrilla war, a truce followed in 1596, and after a second invasion in 1597 the Japanese withdrew in 1598.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War

At Dongnae, in the first days of the war, the commander Konishi Yukinaga ordered that no prisoners be taken after the Korean commander refused to let his army pass; Wikipedia says the twelve-hour siege killed 3,000 and the Japanese killed everyone, civilians included.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War

Korea suffered the most of the three countries: its arable land fell to 66% of the prewar total, 90% of the cultivated land in Gyeongsang Province alone was destroyed, famine, disease and rebellion followed, and the palaces of Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung were burned.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War

The violence did not run one way only: Wikipedia, in part citing Stephen Turnbull, says the Ming forces were often no better than the Japanese in the destruction and crimes they committed, that Korean armies also seized food from civilians and Korean bandits robbed other Koreans, and that Korean women were assaulted by Japanese, Chinese and Korean soldiers alike; the baekjeong, an outcast group, set fire to government offices holding the census ledgers.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War

In the second invasion, Japanese soldiers brought back noses instead of whole heads as proof of their kills, civilians' as well as soldiers'; Hideyoshi had them entombed on the grounds of the Hōkōji temple in Kyoto, in a mound first called the Nose Mound and later the Ear Mound (Mimizuka), dedicated on 28 September 1597.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimizuka

voices.text: 於是城中吏民作亂。挺刃橫路縱擊之。墜廟社主路中。指從行宰臣大罵曰。汝等平日。偸食國祿。今乃誤國欺民乃爾耶。[…] 路上見婦女幼稚。皆怒髮上指。相與號呼曰。旣欲棄城。何故紿我輩入城。獨使魚肉於賊手耶。
voices.who: The clerks, townspeople, women and children of P'yŏngyang, when the king's court prepared to abandon the city, as recorded by Yu Sŏng-nyong, the king's chief state councillor, who was there (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'Then the clerks and people of the city rose up, blocked the road with blades and struck out, and knocked the royal ancestral tablets onto the road. Pointing at the ministers they cursed: "All your days you have fed on the state's stipends, and now you ruin the country and deceive the people like this!" [...] On the road I saw women and children, hair standing on end with rage, crying out together: "If you meant to abandon the city, why did you trick us into coming inside, only to leave us alone as fish and meat for the bandits?"'
voices.date: 1592, 6th lunar month (July by the Western calendar)
voices.doc: Yu Sŏng-nyong, Chingbirok (懲毖錄), book 1, as transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 有人在田間。望之痛哭曰。國家棄我去。我輩何恃而生也。
voices.who: A man in the fields, watching the king flee Seoul for the north, as recorded by Yu Sŏng-nyong, who rode in the king's party (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'There was a man in the fields who watched us and wept bitterly: "The state has abandoned us and gone. What are we to live on now?"'
voices.date: 1592, 30th day of the 4th lunar month (June by the Western calendar), the day the king left Seoul
voices.doc: Yu Sŏng-nyong, Chingbirok (懲毖錄), book 1, as transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 余隨入城見城中遺民百不一存其存者皆飢羸疲困面色如鬼時日氣烘熱人死及馬死者處處暴露臭穢滿城行者揜鼻方過公私廬舍一空
voices.who: Yu Sŏng-nyong, chief state councillor of the defeated Korean court, entering Seoul after the Japanese left it (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'I followed them into the city. Of the people left in it, not one in a hundred survived, and those who did were all starved, wasted and exhausted, their faces like ghosts. The weather was hot; dead people and dead horses lay exposed everywhere, the stench filled the city, and passers-by had to cover their noses. Public and private houses alike were empty.'
voices.date: 1593, 20th day of the 4th lunar month (May by the Western calendar)
voices.doc: Yu Sŏng-nyong, Chingbirok (懲毖錄), book 2, as transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 中外飢甚且困於饋運老弱顚溝壑壯者爲盜賊重以癘疫死亡殆盡至父子夫婦相食暴骨如莾
voices.who: Yu Sŏng-nyong, chief state councillor, on the country while Ming troops were stationed in the south during the truce (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'Throughout the land the hunger was extreme, made worse by the burden of carrying supplies; the old and weak fell into the ditches, the able-bodied became bandits, and on top of this came epidemics, until almost all were dead; fathers and sons, husbands and wives ate one another, and bones lay exposed like weeds.'
voices.doc: Yu Sŏng-nyong, Chingbirok (懲毖錄), book 2, as transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 賊兵退時賊蹂躪三道所過皆焚燒廬舍殺戮人民凡得我國人悉割其鼻以示威
voices.who: Yu Sŏng-nyong, chief state councillor, on the second invasion (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'When the enemy's troops withdrew, they trampled three provinces; wherever they passed they burned the houses and slaughtered the people, and of every one of our people they caught they cut off the nose, to strike terror.'
voices.doc: Yu Sŏng-nyong, Chingbirok (懲毖錄), book 2, as transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 余見璘軍人歐辱守令無忌以繩繫察訪李尙規頸曳之流血滿面
voices.who: Yu Sŏng-nyong, chief state councillor, on the Ming admiral Chen Lin's soldiers, Korea's allies (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'I saw Chen Lin's soldiers beat and humiliate district magistrates without restraint; they tied a rope round the neck of the post-station inspector Yi Sang-gyu and dragged him along, his face covered in blood.' Yu adds that Yi Sun-sin later made Chen Lin's men and his own obey the same rule, and anyone who took so much as a thread from the people was seized and beaten.
voices.doc: Yu Sŏng-nyong, Chingbirok (懲毖錄), book 2, as transcribed on Chinese Wikisource

voices.text: 蛇渡僉使來言。豆峙度賊事虛傳。而光陽之人。變着倭服。自相作亂云。不勝痛憤。昏。吳壽成自光陽來告曰。光陽賊事。皆晉州避亂人及縣人出此凶計。官庫一空。閭里寂然。
voices.who: Yi Sun-sin, commander of the Korean navy, in his war diary (Nanjung ilgi), on a raid he had been told was Japanese (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'The commander of Sado came and said the report of enemies crossing at Tuch'i was false: people of Kwangyang had put on Japanese clothes and were rioting among themselves. I could not bear my pain and anger. In the evening O Su-sŏng came from Kwangyang and reported that the "enemy" affair at Kwangyang was all the evil scheme of refugees from Chinju and people of the county; the government storehouses were emptied and the villages lay silent.'
voices.date: 1593, 11th day of the 7th lunar month (August by the Western calendar)
voices.doc: Yi Sun-sin, war diary, year Kyesa, in Yi Ch'ungmugong chŏnsŏ (李忠武公全書, 1795), book 5, as transcribed on Korean Wikisource

witness.text: As a mark of his spiteful spirit, Hideyoshi ordered that in this second invasion the noses and ears of all Koreans killed or captured should be cut off and sent to Japan. And so from time to time these half-savage soldiers sent loads of Korean noses and ears, pickled in salt, and they were buried in the monastery of Ta-bul-sa in the city of Kyoto, there to remain to all ages a disgusting memento of the most unprovoked and wanton cruelty that ever disgraced the annals of a great people. Many of the Koreans who lost their noses or ears at that time survived many years
witness.who: Homer B. Hulbert, American missionary and teacher in Korea, writing from Korean records with the help of a Korean scholar (The History of Korea, vol. 2, 1905); a strongly pro-Korean writer

witness.text: the Kagoshima samurai rose to the demands of the occasion, and repulsed the allies with terrific slaughter, pursuing them hotly for miles and taking as many as 38,700 heads. These were buried under a tumulus; but the ears and noses had previously been cut off, packed in barrels, and sent to Japan, where they were subsequently deposited near the Temple of Dai-butsu in the capital, and that Mimi-dzuka, or “Ear-mound,” raised over them which is still shown to travellers as one of the sights of Kyoto by Japanese ciceroni.
witness.who: James Murdoch, Scottish historian of Japan, on the Satsuma victory over the Ming and Korean armies at Sach'ŏn (A History of Japan, vol. 2, 1903, p. 358)

official.text: 夫人生于世也，雖歷長生，古來不满百年焉。欝欝久居此乎，不屑國家之隔，山海之遠，一超直入大明國；易吾朝風俗於四百餘州，施帝都政化於億萬斯年者，在方寸中。貴國先驅而入朝，依有遠慮，無近憂者乎？
official.who: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, ruler of Japan (kampaku), in his letter to the King of Korea, as preserved in the Japanese collection Zoku zenrin kokuhōki (classical Chinese). Gloss: 'A man's life, however long, has never reached a hundred years. Why should I stay pent up here? Heedless of the distance of seas and mountains, I will leap straight into the great Ming, change its four hundred provinces to the customs of my country, and spread the rule of my imperial capital for ten thousand years: this is in my heart. If your country goes ahead as vanguard and comes to court, will you not, having thought far ahead, be spared nearby troubles?' The Korean envoys read it as a demand that Korea lead the attack on China.

official.text: 按史征韓後役我軍連捷諸将有所斬獲截敵鼻献功其数幾万公喜其勝賞其功而愍彼士為国致命埋其獲於京都大仏之前為築墳塋立大卒塔婆名曰鼻塚
official.who: Inscription of 1898 beside the mound in Kyoto, signed by the abbot Murata Jakujun (Kyoto City notes the text was drafted for him by Yumoto Fumihiko) for the 300th anniversary of Hideyoshi's death, which praises his 'compassion' (classical Chinese, as transcribed by Kyoto City; parts worn away were restored from an 1898 newspaper). Gloss: 'According to the histories, in the later campaign against Korea our armies won victory after victory; the generals took heads and cut off the enemies' noses to present as proof of merit, in their tens of thousands. His Highness rejoiced in the victory and rewarded their merit, but, pitying those soldiers who had given their lives for their country, he buried the trophies before the Great Buddha in Kyoto, raised a grave mound with a great stupa, and named it the Nose Mound.'

today.text: この侵略を韓国では壬辰丁酉倭乱といい，朝鮮は膨大な損害を被った。日本軍は朝鮮の軍民の鼻を切り取り戦功の証明とした。
today.who: Kyoto City, in its official register of the city's historical monuments (Japanese). Gloss: 'In Korea this invasion is called the Imjin and Chŏngyu Japanese war, and Korea suffered enormous damage. The Japanese army cut off the noses of Korean soldiers and civilians as proof of military merit.'

stories.note: Research in progress: no Japanese eyewitness who condemned the killing is quoted yet. The army chaplain Keinen's diary (Chōsen nichinichi ki) was not found in a public-domain transcription, and Luís Fróis's Portuguese history of Japan was not found in a pre-1931 printed copy of the Korean chapters. The words of ordinary Koreans survive only as Yu Sŏng-nyong recorded them.
stories.warn: The Korean, Chinese and Japanese texts are quoted in their original classical Chinese and Japanese from Wikisource and Kyoto City transcriptions, with the site's own plain-English glosses, not published translations. Yu Sŏng-nyong was the chief minister who ran the war and wrote partly to defend his record; Hulbert (1905) writes as a partisan of Korea in the language of his time. The texts describe mass killing, mutilation and cannibalism in famine.
disputed: How many died?
