Wikipedia's summary gives more than 1,000,000 Korean civilian and military deaths, more than 30,000 Ming dead and more than 100,000 Japanese killed, captured or missing, and flags the Japanese figure as resting on a possibly unreliable source. Old Korean counts are not always trusted: Hulbert (1905) reports the Korean accounts' 'almost incredible' figure of 70,000 Koreans killed at Chinju in 1593, with an equal number of Japanese, and says the Japanese figure must be an exaggeration.

How many noses lie in the mound? Wikipedia says at least 38,000 Koreans and over 30,000 Chinese, and elsewhere cites a count of 185,738 Korean and 29,014 Chinese heads taken in all (214,752), noting that some were probably discarded; Murdoch (1903) gives 38,700 heads taken by the Satsuma men at Sach'ŏn alone in October 1598, a year after the mound was dedicated, and says their noses went to Kyoto too; the 1898 Kyoto inscription says 'tens of thousands'; and the Korean monk Pak Sam-jung, campaigning in 1996 to bring them home, spoke of 126,000 people. Japanese collectors, Wikipedia notes, took noses from civilians as well as soldiers.

Captives and potters. Wikipedia says 50,000 to 60,000 captives were taken to Japan, that only 7,500 were returned by diplomacy, and that many of the rest were sold to Portuguese traders; Hulbert says an envoy brought back about 3,000 in 1606. Korean potters were set to work in kilns founded by Japanese lords, but Wikipedia also says the Arita porcelain makers of 1616 had been 'enticed to relocate' after the war, so not every potter in Japan was a captive in the same sense.

Did the Ming save Korea? Wikipedia says Ming reinforcements, with the Korean navy, forced the Japanese out of the north. Murdoch (1903) agrees with Hulbert that before China raised a hand the invasion had virtually collapsed, and says that in a way the Chinese counter-invasion was a calamity for Korea; Yu Sŏng-nyong's own record shows Ming soldiers abusing Korean officials, and Turnbull (as Wikipedia reports him) says Ming forces were often no better than the Japanese.
stories.blind: The Korean side of this war is told almost entirely by its ruling class: the chief minister Yu Sŏng-nyong and the admiral Yi Sun-sin, both writing to the court and to posterity. Ordinary Koreans speak only in the lines Yu chose to record, and the tens of thousands carried off to Japan and sold abroad, the women assaulted by every army, and the outcasts who burned the census registers left no words of their own. Japanese foot soldiers and the Chinese conscripts who died in Korea are just as silent, while Hideyoshi's letters and the monuments to his 'compassion' survive in full.
reading: Yu Sŏng-nyong, Chingbirok 懲毖錄 (Chinese Wikisource)
Yi Sun-sin, war diary, in Yi Ch'ungmugong chŏnsŏ, books 5–7 (Korean Wikisource)
H. B. Hulbert, The History of Korea, vol. 2 (1905, Project Gutenberg)
J. Murdoch, A History of Japan, vol. 2 (1903, archive.org)
Kyoto City: Mimizuka repair memorial stone (in Japanese)

stories.title: The Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands
stories.where: Lonthor (Banda Besar), Banda Islands, Indonesia (approximate)
facts: Nutmeg is native to the volcanic Banda Islands; today their inhabitants are mostly descendants of Javanese, Makassarese and people from neighbouring islands brought in as labourers to work the Dutch nutmeg plantations.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Banda-Islands

The Dutch East India Company (VOC) wanted the Bandanese to sell their spices to it alone, while the Bandanese preferred free trade; in May 1609 Bandanese chiefs lured the Dutch commander Pieter Verhoeff and two other commanders into an ambush and killed them, 46 Dutchmen died in all, and the Dutch retaliated by plundering villages before a peace in August put the islands under Dutch authority.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_conquest_of_the_Banda_Islands

The Bandanese went on selling to the English and to Asian traders in breach of their treaties, and by 1614 the VOC directors had concluded that the whole archipelago must be conquered even if it meant destroying the native population; in 1616, when the Dutch took the island of Ai, about 400 people, many of them women and children, drowned trying to flee to English-held Run.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_conquest_of_the_Banda_Islands

In 1621 Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen brought a fleet with Dutch soldiers and Japanese mercenaries, took Lonthor, the main island, on 11 March, and accepted the surrender of the orang kaya (the island elders); after confessions of a conspiracy were extracted by torture, Wikipedia says, condemned orang kaya were beheaded by Japanese mercenaries.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_conquest_of_the_Banda_Islands

Coen reported to the directors in May 1621 that he was sending 789 people to Jacatra (Batavia) on the ship Dragon, 287 men, 256 women and 246 children, and that some 150 of the people who had fled into the mountains had already died of dysentery.
https://archive.org/stream/janpieterszcoenb01coen/janpieterszcoenb01coen_djvu.txt

The Dutch repopulated the islands mainly with enslaved people from the East Indies, India and China working for Dutch planters (perkeniers); surviving Bandanese were enslaved too, and Wikipedia says the native Bandanese population had dropped to 100 by 1681.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_conquest_of_the_Banda_Islands

voices.text: soo de gouverneur een nieuw accoort ende eewige vrede met haer wilde maecken, sy waeren bereyt en daertoe wel genegen, mits dat daervan op haer landt souden handelen; soo niet, souden na de compst van den generael vertoeven.
voices.who: The Bandanese of Lonthor and the rest of Banda, answering the Dutch governor's offer of peace, as recorded by Jan Pieterszoon Coen in his report to the VOC directors (Dutch, in reported speech). Gloss: 'if the governor wished to make a new agreement and eternal peace with them, they were ready and well inclined to it, provided it was negotiated on their own land; if not, they would wait for the coming of the governor-general.'
voices.doc: Coen to the Heeren XVII, 31 July 1620, in H. T. Colenbrander (ed.), Jan Pietersz. Coen: Bescheiden omtrent zijn bedrijf in Indië, vol. 1 (The Hague, 1919), p. 569 (OCR corrected)

voices.text: presenteerende een eewich accoort met ons te maecken, alle andre natie van den handel van Banda 't excluderen ende alle de noten ende foelie aen ons alleen te leveren.
voices.who: Envoys of the Bandanese, coming to the Dutch while Coen's fleet prepared to attack, as recorded by Coen (Dutch, reported speech). Gloss: 'offering to make an eternal agreement with us, to exclude every other nation from the trade of Banda and to deliver all the nutmeg and mace to us alone.' Coen answered that they had long promised and sworn this and not kept it, and demanded a fort in their chief places; the Bandanese would not agree, and the talks ended.
voices.doc: Coen and Martinus Sonck to the Heeren XVII, 6 May 1621, in Colenbrander (ed.), Coen: Bescheiden, vol. 1 (1919), p. 626

voices.text: Whereupon the said Inhabitants asked us if we could and would defend them, but perceiving we were not able to defend our selves, much lesse to secure them : they were forced to yeeld themselves and the Iland into his hands. [...] which they at the first refused to doe, alleaging that they had formerly given and surrendred the Land to the King of England, and in respect they had lived so long with the English, they would not now offer us any injurie or violence.
voices.who: The people of the island of Run, when a Dutch force came to take it and ordered them to throw down the English guns, as recorded by the English East India Company's factors on Run in a letter to the Company (rivals of the Dutch)
voices.doc: 'A Letter written to the East India Company in England, from their Factours', in Samuel Purchas, Hakluytus Posthumus or Purchas his Pilgrimes (1625), reprinted Glasgow 1905, vol. 5, pp. 139–140

witness.text: Which when the Bandanezes perceived (doubting that he meant to make them all slaves and to carrie them to some other places) they agreed together to retyre themselves into the highest and strongest places of the Land, and there did fortifie themselves, whereupon the Dutch slue of them and tooke twelve hundred persons Prisoners, most of them being women and children, which they have since carryed to Jacatra and other places.
witness.who: The English East India Company's factors in Banda, in a letter to the Company in London, printed by Samuel Purchas; the English were the Dutch company's rivals for the islands and had lost Run to them

witness.text: considering they have lately at Banda hanged 40 of the principal of those people and carried 800 persons along with General Coen to inhabit Jacatra, “breeds such fear and doubt in these people, as they remain in ecstasy ;” many of them fled
witness.who: William Nicolls, English East India Company agent in the Moluccas, writing to the English merchants in Japan about the effect of the news on the islanders there, as abstracted by the British government's Calendar of State Papers (1870), no. 1050

witness.text: desirous to revenge the wrongs and cruelties offered unto them by the Hollanders, did dissemble their intents, entertayning Van Hoofe with vaine hopes, promising him to come to some agreement ; by which meanes they drew Van Hoofe with threescore or more of his Commanders and Souldiours, unto a place in which the Bandaneses had advantage. Now instead of agreement, in warlike manner they set upon Van Hoofe, and slew him and almost his Companie.
witness.who: The English East India Company's printed answer to the Dutch declaration, describing how the Bandanese killed the Dutch admiral Verhoeff ('Van Hoofe') in 1609; written to defend the English case, it still records the killing plainly

official.text: Aldus hebben wy door Goodts genade de moetwillige, trotse Bandanesen (die soo lange voor de haentiens van Indien vernaempt zijn geweest) sonder bloetstortinge, tegen opinie van veele, overwonnen.
official.who: Jan Pieterszoon Coen, governor-general of the VOC, with Martinus Sonck, reporting to the directors (Dutch). Gloss: 'Thus by God's grace, against the opinion of many, we have conquered without bloodshed the wilful, proud Bandanese, who have so long been famed as the fighting cocks of the Indies.'

official.text: By den raedt hierop gelet wesende, zijn alle de gevangen orangkays ter doot verwesen ende 44 met den swaerde gerecht. Twee hebben haer selven in torture verstiet, ende een isser over boort gesprongen ende verdroncken.
official.who: Coen and his council (signed Coen, Pieter de Carpentier, Jan Dircksz. Lam and Willem van Antsen) to the directors, after reporting that the 45 captive orang kaya had 'confessed' to plotting to retake the forts and murder Coen (Dutch). Gloss: 'The council having considered this, all the captured orang kaya were condemned to death and 44 executed with the sword. Two killed themselves under torture, and one jumped overboard and drowned.'

official.text: Ontrent 2500 sijnder soo van honger ende ellende als met den swaerde vergaen. Alsnoch hebben niet gehoort, datter van gants Banda meer dan ontrent 300 Bandanesen ontcomen zijn. Het schijnt dat de hartneckicheyt in dese lieden soo groot geweest is, dat liever al te zamen in miserie hebben willen vergaen, dan aen d' onse overgeven.
official.who: Coen and his council to the directors, on the end of the campaign in the mountains (Dutch). Gloss: 'About 2,500 have perished, from hunger and misery as well as by the sword. So far we have not heard that more than about 300 Bandanese from all of Banda escaped. It seems their stubbornness was so great that they would rather all perish in misery than give themselves up to us.' The letter goes on to blame their leaders' pride.

official.text: This that is formerly declared, is the true state and proceedings of that, which hath beene done now lately, and before in the Iland of Banda, wherein nothing hath beene done, but that which (according to the Law of Nations, and the aforesaid Contract, made, and promised to bee holden, and without any wrong done to the Liberties of the English Companie, agreed upon with the Companie of the Netherland) might and ought to have beene done.
official.who: The Dutch East India Company's public declaration on Banda, printed at Amsterdam in 1622, in the English translation printed by Purchas; it accuses the Bandanese of breaking their contracts of 1609, 1616 and 1617, robbing the Company's warehouses and murdering its servants

stories.note: Research in progress: no Bandanese account in their own words has yet been found in a public-domain printing. The Hikayat Lonthoir (oral tradition of the Bandanese exiles in the Kei Islands) was not found in a pre-1931 edition, and the 1616 letter of the Bandanese to the King of England quoted by Wikipedia was not found in a checked public-domain copy. No Dutch or Indonesian government statement on the conquest was found to quote.
stories.warn: Every Bandanese word here comes through their enemies or rivals: Coen's own reports in 17th-century Dutch (quoted from the 1919 printed edition, with the site's plain-English glosses and corrections of scanning errors), and English East India Company men who were fighting the Dutch for the same islands. The Dutch account speaks of conquest 'without bloodshed' and of confessions obtained under torture. The texts describe mass death, executions and the deportation of families.
disputed: How many Bandanese were there, and how many died? Wikipedia reports that Vincent Loth and Charles Corn put the whole population before the conquest at about 15,000, of whom only about 1,000 survived; Peter Lape estimated that 90% were killed, enslaved or deported; Hans Straver put Lonthor alone at 4,500–5,000, with about 1,700 enslaved and 2,500 dead of famine and disease. Coen wrote in May that about 1,200 people had been taken in all, and his council in November counted about 2,500 dead and only about 300 escaped; the English factors spoke of 1,200 prisoners, mostly women and children. Wikipedia's article on the conquest gives 2,800 Bandanese killed and 1,700 enslaved.

The killing of the orang kaya. Coen's council wrote that 45 were seized, 44 executed 'with the sword', two died under torture and one drowned; Wikipedia says 24 were beheaded by Japanese mercenaries on 8 May; the English agent Nicolls heard that 40 'of the principal' had been hanged. The charge of a conspiracy rests on confessions the Dutch themselves say were taken under torture. Coen's council's own letter says only that the orang kaya were executed 'with the sword' and does not name who carried it out.

Who broke faith? The VOC's declaration says the Bandanese broke contracts made in 1609, 1616 and 1617, robbed its warehouses and murdered its servants, encouraged by the English. The English answer replied that the Dutch never had any agreement in Banda but what was gotten by force, while conceding that the Bandanese killed Verhoeff and his men in 1609 by a feigned negotiation; Wikipedia agrees that the chiefs lured him into an ambush.

Hero or 'Butcher of Banda'? Wikipedia says Coen was long considered a Dutch national hero, but his legacy has been controversial since the 19th century; the conquest is now widely called a genocide, and in 2012, after a citizens' initiative, the city council of Hoorn, his birthplace, added a text to his statue's pedestal explaining the controversy and some of his atrocities.
stories.blind: The Bandanese who lived through the conquest left no writing that survives in a printed edition: what they said reaches us only as Coen chose to report it to his directors, or as English traders, who wanted the nutmeg for themselves, reported it home. The thousands who starved in the mountains, the families shipped to Batavia and sold, the orang kaya condemned on confessions taken under torture, and the Japanese mercenaries who carried out the executions all go unheard. The exiles' own memory, carried to the Kei Islands, survives in oral tradition rather than in these archives.
reading: Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands (Wikipedia)
H. T. Colenbrander (ed.), Jan Pietersz. Coen: Bescheiden omtrent zijn bedrijf in Indië, vol. 1 (1919, archive.org)
Purchas his Pilgrimes, vol. 5 (1625; Glasgow reprint 1905, archive.org): Courthope's and Hayes's journals, the factors' letter, the Dutch declaration and the English answer
Calendar of State Papers, Colonial Series, East Indies, China and Japan, 1617–1621 (1870, archive.org)

stories.title: The Khoikhoi and the Dutch at the Cape: 'the natural owner, or the foreign invader?'
stories.where: Table Bay and the Cape Peninsula, Western Cape, South Africa
facts: Jan van Riebeeck landed at the Cape on 6 April 1652 to set up a refreshment station for Dutch East India Company (VOC) ships; in 1657 the Company released some employees from their contracts and gave them freehold land along the Liesbeeck Valley, and in 1659 Khoikhoi men led by Doman, angered by the spreading farms and the loss of prime grazing land, seized seven of the Company's draught oxen, opening the first Khoikhoi–Dutch war (1659–60).
https://www.sahistory.org.za/article/establishment-cape-and-its-impact-khoikhoi-and-dutch

Doman attacked on rainy days, when the Dutch muskets would not fire, and was wounded on 19 July 1659; the war ended when the Dutch made peace with the Goringhaiqua and the Goarchoqua around April and May 1660, after which the Khoikhoi lost more land, by 1676 they were barred from living near the castle, and in 1713 a smallpox epidemic further weakened them.
https://www.sahistory.org.za/article/establishment-cape-and-its-impact-khoikhoi-and-dutch

To close the settlement's eastern boundary van Riebeeck built a wooden fence with watch towers from the Salt River towards Kirstenbosch and, in 1660, planted a hedge of indigenous wild almond (Brabejum stellatifolium) and thorny shrubs, meant also to stop Khoikhoi raids on the colonists' livestock; a remnant of the hedge still grows in Kirstenbosch.
https://www.sanbi.org/gardens/kirstenboch/history/kirstenbosch-nbg-van-riebeecks-hedge/

The Company's own record shows violence on both sides: in October 1653 its interpreter Autshumato (Herry) left the fort with his people on the day 42 Company cattle were driven off and a Dutch herd boy was found murdered; in July 1658 the Council ordered all Herry's cattle at the Salt River seized and held him prisoner, and in December 1659 he escaped from Robben Island.
https://archive.org/stream/recordorseriesof00mood/recordorseriesof00mood_djvu.txt

In July 1673 men of the Cochoqua chief Gonnema, coming as if to barter sheep, killed a corporal, a soldier and two free men at the Company's Saldanha Bay post; a Dutch and burger force returned on 25 July with about 800 cattle and 900 sheep, and on 26 June 1677 Gonnema's envoys accepted a peace that bound the Cochoqua to deliver 30 horned cattle a year as tribute.
https://archive.org/stream/recordorseriesof00mood/recordorseriesof00mood_djvu.txt

Krotoa (Eva), niece of Autshumato, was taken into van Riebeeck's household at about 10 or 11 and became the Company's interpreter; she married Pieter van Meerhof on 2 June 1664, was banished to Robben Island in March 1669, and died there on 29 July 1674.
https://www.sahistory.org.za/people/krotoa-eva

voices.text: They also asked, whether, if they were to come into Holland, they would be permitted to act in a similar manner, saying, “what would it signify if you remained here at the Fort, but you come quite into the interior, selecting the best for yourselves, and never once asking whether we like it, or whether it will put us to any inconvenience.”
voices.who: The Goringhaiqua ('Caepmans') leaders, among them the chief Gogosoa and Autshumato (Herry), about 40 in all, making peace at the fort after the first war, as recorded in Jan van Riebeeck's journal
voices.doc: Journal of Commander Van Riebeeck, 6 April 1660, in D. Moodie (ed. and trans.), The Record: or a Series of Official Papers relative to the Condition and Treatment of the Native Tribes of South Africa, Part I (Cape Town, 1838), p. 205
voices.lic: Public domain (Moodie's English translation, published Cape Town 1838)

voices.text: have we then no cause to prevent you from procuring any cattle? for, if you get many cattle, you come and occupy our pasture with them, and then say the land is not wide enough for us both! who then can be required, with the greatest degree of justice, to give way, the natural owner, or the foreign invader?
voices.who: The same Goringhaiqua leaders, answering the Dutch objection that there was not grass enough for both peoples' cattle, as recorded in van Riebeeck's journal
voices.doc: Journal of Commander Van Riebeeck, 6 April 1660, in D. Moodie (ed. and trans.), The Record: or a Series of Official Papers relative to the Condition and Treatment of the Native Tribes of South Africa, Part I (Cape Town, 1838), p. 205
voices.lic: Public domain (Moodie's English translation, published Cape Town 1838)

voices.text: being asked why they did us this injury, declared that it was for no other reason than because they saw that we were breaking up the best land and grass, where their cattle were accustomed to graze, trying to establish ourselves every where, with houses and farms, as if we were never more to remove, but designed to take, for our permanent occupation, more and more of this Cape country, which had belonged to them from time immemorial.
voices.who: A wounded Goringhaiqua ('Caepman') fighter taken prisoner in July 1659, who 'spoke tolerable Dutch', as reported by van Riebeeck and his Council to Batavia
voices.doc: Despatch from Commander Van Riebeeck and Council to the Governor General and Council, Batavia, 29 July 1659, in D. Moodie (ed. and trans.), The Record: or a Series of Official Papers relative to the Condition and Treatment of the Native Tribes of South Africa, Part I (Cape Town, 1838), p. 186

stories.note: Research in progress: all quotations come from Moodie's 1838 English translation, checked against the archive.org scan; they have not yet been compared with the Dutch original (Dagverhaal van Jan van Riebeeck) or with Leibbrandt's Precis.
stories.warn: Every Khoikhoi word here was spoken through interpreters (Krotoa, Doman, Autshumato), written down in Dutch by the Company's clerks and translated into English by Donald Moodie in 1838. The record calls the Khoikhoi 'Hottentoos' or 'Hottentots', a term now considered offensive; it is kept only inside quotations. OCR errors in the scan (e.g. 'Kerry' for 'Herry') were corrected against the page images.
disputed: Cause of the first war. Van Riebeeck's journal calls the Khoikhoi raids cattle stolen 'wrongfully and without cause' and the land 'justly won by the sword in defensive warfare'; the Khoikhoi speakers it records put the cause in the loss of their grazing land, as does SAHO today. Wikipedia notes that the Khoisan's loss of influence is 'often seen' as their trading it away for livestock, against the view that their resistance was a response to dispossession.

Bought or taken? The 1672 agreements record the Cape district and Hottentots Holland as sold for goods 'estimated' at 4000 reals each and delivered 'to his satisfaction'; Governor Goske's own despatch of 1673 values the goods at ƒ33 : 17 and ƒ81 : 16 prime cost. Moodie notes that the directors' 1660 suggestion of purchase was not carried out until about ten years later, and SAHO states that after the second war the VOC claimed the land by conquest.

Krotoa: go-between or collaborator? Doman called her 'the Hollander's advocate'; SAHO describes her as a staunch friend of the Dutch who was torn between them and her own people whose land was being taken; the South African government in 2016 honoured her as instrumental in working out the terms that ended the first war.
stories.blind: The Khoikhoi left no writing of their own: their arguments survive only as the VOC's clerks chose to record them, through interpreters whose own loyalties were questioned on both sides, and then in a 19th-century English translation. The man Willem Willems shot, the herd boy killed in 1653 (named only as David) and most Khoikhoi casualties are unnamed or uncounted; the Cochoqua side of the second war is almost silent, apart from envoys' names and their cry of 'Sam, Sam' (peace) when the 1677 terms were read to them.

stories.title: The 1860 civil war in Mount Lebanon and the Damascus massacre
stories.where: Mount Lebanon and Damascus (pin: Deir al-Qamar, Lebanon, approximate)
facts: In 1858 Tanyus Shahin, a Maronite peasant leader in Kasrawan, demanded that the feudal class of Mount Lebanon give up its privileges; when this was refused, the poor peasants revolted against the shaykhs, pillaging their land and burning their homes.
https://countrystudies.us/lebanon/18.htm

In the spring of 1860 tit-for-tat killings spread through the mixed Christian–Druze districts; on 29 May Maronites from Keserwan raided mixed villages and forced out their Druze residents, and by 31 May Druze fighters controlled the Metn, where between 35 and 40 Maronite-majority villages were set alight and some 600 Maronites slain.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_civil_conflict_in_Mount_Lebanon_and_Damascus

At Hasbaya, where Christians had taken refuge in the government house on the Ottoman commander's advice and surrendered around 500 guns, Druze fighters killed about 1,000 Christian males, men and boys, while sparing the women; Christian deaths at Hasbaya and Rashaya together were roughly 1,800, and between 1,200 and 2,200 Christians were killed at Deir al-Qamar.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_civil_conflict_in_Mount_Lebanon_and_Damascus

In July 1860 a crowd of Druzes, Bedouins, Muslim city commoners and Kurdish auxiliary forces attacked Bab Tuma, the Christian quarter of Damascus, and some Ottoman soldiers joined or led the rioters; the Algerian exile Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri had earlier persuaded the French consul to fund arms for about 1,000 of his men, mostly Algerians, to defend the Christians, and the violence tapered off completely by 17 July.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_civil_conflict_in_Mount_Lebanon_and_Damascus

The Ottoman envoy Fuad Pasha oversaw a court-martial alongside an international tribunal; Druze notables such as Sa'id Jumblatt were sentenced to death for rebellion, Ottoman and European sources record roughly 357 executions in Damascus, and a French expeditionary corps of 6,000 soldiers landed in Beirut on 16 August 1860.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_civil_conflict_in_Mount_Lebanon_and_Damascus

An international commission of France, Britain, Austria, Prussia and the Ottoman Empire, meeting from 5 October 1860, blamed the 1842 partition of Mount Lebanon for the massacre; under the Statute of 1861 Mount Lebanon was separated from Syria and placed under a non-Lebanese Christian governor (mutasarrif) appointed by the sultan with the powers' approval, assisted by a council of twelve members from the different religious communities.
https://countrystudies.us/lebanon/18.htm

voices.text: Their acts of violence towards us in killing our co-religionists, both secretly and openly, have become well known to all; their wish is evidently to compass our ruin and entire extermination. [...] so that we have now been reduced to the necessity of defending ourselves, and to seek, by all means in our power, for relief from the oppression and distress surrounding us from these foes, who seemed determined to exterminate us. We believe that we are justified in resorting to these extremes by all laws, natural, judicial, and administrative.
voices.who: The Christians of the Mixed Districts of Mount Lebanon, in a memorial to Khurshid Pasha, the Ottoman governor at Beirut, ten days before the war broke out; it also shows that the Christians were arming
voices.doc: Memorial from the Christians of the Mixed Districts in Mount Lebanon to Khorsheed Pasha, as reprinted from the British consular correspondence in J. Lewis Farley, The Massacres in Syria (London, 1861), pp. 131–133 (OCR corrected)

voices.text: The woman in question at last turned round to the cadi in indignation and disgust, and said, "You have forgot to ask me one important question, whether my husband went to heaven or to hell!"
voices.who: A Christian widow at the Ottoman special tribunal at Mukhtara, after producing two witnesses to her husband's killing by a Druze and being questioned about the gun, the wound and how he fell, as recorded by Colonel Charles Churchill
voices.doc: Charles Churchill, The Druzes and the Maronites under the Turkish Rule from 1840 to 1860 (London, 1862), pp. 244–245

voices.text: These notables remitted, some days afterwards, to his Excellency, a list of the names of four thousand six hundred Druses, Mussulmans, and Metuâlis, inhabiting the Lebanon, the Anti-Lebanon, and the Haurân, and taken from among thirty thousand combatants, and not solely from among eight thousand Druses, as it is pretended [...] the undersigned bishops declare that they have never signed any such paper, and therefore that it would be impossible to produce it.
voices.who: The bishops of Beirut, Acre, Zahle and Baalbek (Tobia Aoun, Butros Boustani, Basil Chahiat, Malathios), answering Lord John Russell's statement in Parliament that they had demanded 4,600 executions, in a letter to the European commissioners
voices.doc: Letter of the bishops of Lebanon to the European commissioners at Beirut, in J. Lewis Farley, The Massacres in Syria (London, 1861), pp. 138–142 (OCR corrected)

witness.text: But many of the Moslemin scorned to disown the Christians and provided them with excellent eatables and sent to them plenty of money for their expenses [to cover the expenses for their sustenance]. And in [the suburb of] al-Maydan were [lived] Saleh Agha al-Muhayiny and Sa'yd Agha an-Nury, companions of manliness and religion [doughty and righteous men], who forbade the Moslemin of al-Maydan to interfere with [undertake anything against] the followers of Jesus [Christians].
witness.who: Iskander ibn Ya'qub Abkarius, a Christian man of letters of Beirut, in his Arabic chronicle of the 1860 massacres, written at the time; English by J. F. Scheltema (the square brackets are the translator's) (a Beirut writer describing Damascus, so placed with the outside witnesses)
witness.doc: Abkarius, Book of the Marvels of the Time concerning the Massacres in the Arab Country, tr. J. F. Scheltema, The Lebanon in Turmoil: Syria and the Powers in 1860 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1920), p. 134 (OCR corrected)

witness.text: The Turkish soldiers came to assist them, under the pretence of putting an end to the disturbance, but making common cause with the rioters, and killing, robbing, and plundering with them. A few old Mussulmans made efforts to stop the business, but the Turkish officers had no wish for peace [...] Seeing matters were so desperate, I lost no time in taking under my protection these unfortunate Christians. I sallied forth, taking my Algerines with me, and we were able to save the lives of men, women, and children, and bring them home with us.
witness.who: The Emir Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri, the exiled Algerian resistance leader living in Damascus, in a letter to the managers of a silk works, as printed in English translation in New York in 1860

witness.text: With the exception of the very lowest class, the settled Mussulman population of Damascus took no part in the slaughter of the Christians. On the contrary, ulemas, mollahs, and sheikhs of the different religious orders of Islamism, and many of the notables of the place, were active in saving Christian lives, wherever an opportunity of so doing offered itself.
witness.who: The Constantinople correspondent of the London Times, as reprinted in The Massacres in Syria (New York, 1860)

witness.text: I went to distribute clothing yesterday to one room; there were six women, all new made widows, with no male child or friend to comfort or care for them. Another room had five such widows. A friend of mine has taken nine women into his family, all widows, made such in the slaughter at Deir el Komr.
witness.who: William M. Thomson, American missionary at Beirut, in a letter printed in The Missionary Herald

witness.text: Several hundred Christians followed in the track of the French expedition, and committed some excesses. Wound up to a pitch of exasperation which knew no control at the complete impunity which had hitherto attended the cold-blooded barbarities of the Druzes, they slew, it is said, upwards of one hundred of them, including a few women.
witness.who: Charles Churchill, a British officer long resident in Lebanon, whose book is strongly hostile to the Ottoman authorities and the Druze chiefs, on Christian reprisals

official.text: "Tell the Ambassador," said Fuad Pasha to the chief dragoman of the French Embassy, "that at the peril of my life, I shall wipe out the stain which rests upon the honour of the army, and that the troops will do their duty."
official.who: Fuad Pasha, Ottoman foreign minister and the Sultan's extraordinary commissioner for Syria, before sailing for Beirut, as recorded by the British writer J. Lewis Farley

official.text: The plenipotentiary of the Sublime Porte takes note of this declaration of the representatives of the high contracting powers, and undertakes to transmit it to his court — pointing out — that the Sublime Porte has employed, and continues to employ, her efforts in the sense of the wish expressed above.
official.who: The Ottoman plenipotentiary's reply in the Paris protocol, after the five European powers declared they sought no territorial advantage or exclusive influence and called for better conditions for the Sultan's Christian subjects, as quoted by Churchill

official.text: The Maronites were armed, and the Druses, therefore, expected that they should be attacked. The Maronites, on the other hand, were apprehensive of being themselves attacked, and, being mutually animated by the most violent animosity, those massacres took place which we have all so much to lament. As an instance of the fierceness of the different races, I may mention that, according to the report of Lord Dufferin, Fuad Pasha having asked the Bishops of the different Christian sects how many of the 8,000 adult males in that part of the country ought, in their opinion, to be put to death in expiation of the massacres which had taken place, the Bishops, by their signatures to a paper, required that no less than 4,600 of the 8,000 should be executed
official.who: Lord John Russell, British Foreign Secretary, in the House of Commons (Hansard); the bishops denied signing any such paper (see voices)

official.text: I have never interfered in any way whatever in the war. I have always done all I possibly could for the Christians. My constant endeavours have been to pacify and keep down the Druzes; but they wont listen to me. I have no power over my people. The commonest man among them disobeys my orders and laughs at my authority. I know all sorts of absurd reports have been spread about my being an influential person amongst the Druzes, and all the blame of what is happening has been laid most unjustly at my door.
official.who: Sa'id Bey Jumblatt, the leading Druze chief, to an English envoy who brought the consuls' demand for peace, as recorded 'in nearly the following terms' by Charles Churchill, who did not believe him; Jumblatt was later sentenced to death by the Ottoman tribunal (the Druze leader's words as a hostile witness reported them, so placed with the official account)
official.doc: Charles Churchill, The Druzes and the Maronites under the Turkish Rule (London, 1862), pp. 202–203 (OCR corrected)

stories.note: Research in progress: the British Parliamentary Papers ('Correspondence relating to the Affairs of Syria, 1860–61') could not be opened in a checkable full-text copy (HathiTrust showed a bot check), so consular despatches are quoted only as reprinted by Farley (1861) and Churchill (1862). Mikhail Mishaqa's own English narrative of his escape, dated Damascus, August 1860, is printed in The Massacres in Syria (New York, 1860), but the scan's text is too garbled to verify word for word; his memoir in English (1988) is in copyright. No text of the Règlement Organique and no current government statement was quoted.
stories.warn: Abd al-Qadir's letter and Abkarius's chronicle are English translations from Arabic (1860 and 1920). Churchill and Farley were partisan British writers of the time: Churchill blames the Turks and the Druze chiefs, Farley defends the Maronites. Sa'id Jumblatt's words reach us only through Churchill, who says he gives them in 'nearly' his terms and disbelieved them. The texts describe massacres and the plight of widows; scanning errors have been corrected.
disputed: Death tolls. The Library of Congress study speaks of about 10,000 Christians killed by the Druzes; Wikipedia says most sources put those killed in and around Mount Lebanon between 7,000 and 11,000, some over 20,000, and its summary gives 12,000 for Damascus. Churchill counted 11,000 Christians massacred and 4,000 dead of destitution. For Damascus, Abd al-Qadir's letter gave an estimate of 3,300, the Times correspondent reported consular figures of 6,000 to 8,000 against a private letter's 2,000, the missionary Thomson wrote of more than 5,000, and Abkarius put the dead at about 5,000.

Ottoman complicity. Churchill wrote that the Turks connived at, instigated, ordered and shared in the Damascus massacre, and Abd al-Qadir wrote that Turkish soldiers made common cause with the rioters; the Times correspondent believed the governor Ahmed Pasha sincere but utterly incapable. Wikipedia reports that some Ottoman soldiers joined or led the rioters and that Ottoman troops aided Druze and Muslim forces by direct support or by disarming Christians, while Fuad Pasha's executions of officials and rioters were praised even by his harshest European critics.

Who started the war? Farley argued from the consuls' reports that the Maronites were not the aggressors; Russell told Parliament that both sides were armed and each feared attack. Churchill himself describes the Maronite peasant revolt against their own sheikhs and Christian reprisals in September 1860, and Wikipedia quotes the historian Ussama Makdisi that whether the Maronite mobilization was a response to Druze provocations or the cause of Druze aggression 'is not, and probably will never be, known'.

Punishment and the 4,600 names. Russell, citing Lord Dufferin, said the bishops had signed a demand that 4,600 of 8,000 Druze men be executed; the bishops replied that lay notables had given Fuad Pasha a list of 4,600 accused on his own request, never a death list, and Churchill writes that after the Christian deputies withdrew, 500 Druze prisoners were released and about 240 exiled to Tripoli in Africa. In Parliament Sir James Fergusson said the Beirut trial of the Druze chiefs was 'perhaps, the grossest perversion of justice which history recorded'.

European motives. In the Paris protocol of 3 August 1860 the powers declared they sought no territorial advantage or exclusive influence; Wikipedia says France sent 6,000 soldiers to protect the Syrian Christians and to increase its own power in the region, and Churchill blamed British and Turkish jealousy for keeping the French from acting. Wikipedia also notes that Makdisi criticises European writers, Churchill among them, for presenting 1860 as 'age-old' sectarian hatred.
stories.blind: The record is dominated by Christian sufferers, their bishops and their British, American and French sympathisers, and by the Ottoman and British officials who argued over punishment. The Druze peasants who fought, burned and were killed, and the Druze families who fled or were later attacked in reprisal, have no voice here except their chief, Sa'id Jumblatt, whose words reach us through a hostile Englishman. The Muslim townspeople of Damascus, both those who rioted and those who hid Christians, speak only through others; so do the hundreds hanged or shot on Fuad Pasha's orders. The women of Hasbaya, Deir al-Qamar and Damascus appear as widows counted by missionaries, and only one is heard, through Churchill.

stories.title: The Indian rebellion of 1857
stories.where: Northern and central India (pin: Delhi, India; also Meerut, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi)
facts: The rebellion of 1857–59 against British rule began in Meerut with an uprising of Indian troops (sepoys) in the service of the British East India Company and spread to Delhi, Agra, Kanpur and Lucknow; Western historians long called it the 'Indian Mutiny' or 'Sepoy Mutiny', and in India it is also called the 'First War of Independence'.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Indian-Rebellion-of-1857

The pretext was the new Enfield rifle, whose cartridges were rumoured to be greased with pig and cow fat, an insult to both Muslims and Hindus; Britannica says there is no conclusive evidence that either was actually used, but the rumour fed a larger suspicion, sharpened by the annexation of Oudh (Awadh) in 1856, that the British were undermining Indian society.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Indian-Rebellion-of-1857

On 10 May 1857 the Meerut troopers shot their British officers and marched to Delhi, where by nightfall the pensioned Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II had been nominally restored to power; apart from the emperor and his sons and Nana Sahib, none of the important Indian princes joined the rebels.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Indian-Rebellion-of-1857

The rebels commonly shot their British officers on rising and carried out massacres at Delhi, Kanpur and elsewhere; at Cawnpore (Kanpur), after the British garrison surrendered, Nana Sahib offered it safe passage, but his forces then killed about 400 British women and children.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Indian-Rebellion-of-1857

Some British officers began severe measures before any such murders were known, and in the end, Britannica says, the reprisals far outweighed the original excesses: hundreds of sepoys were bayoneted or fired from cannons in a frenzy of British vengeance, though some British officers did protest the bloodshed.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Indian-Rebellion-of-1857

When Delhi was retaken after a week of street fighting in September 1857, the troops of the besieging force looted and pillaged the city, and a large number of its citizens were killed in retaliation for the British and Indian civilians who had been killed by the rebels; the British arrested Bahadur Shah, and Major William Hodson had his sons Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan and his grandson Mirza Abu Bakr shot under his own authority.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857

voices.text: It is well known to all, that in this age the people of Hindostan, both Hindoos and Mohammedans, are being ruined under the tyranny and oppression of the infidel and treacherous English. […] It is evident that the Europeans, by the introduction of English articles into India, have thrown the weavers, the cotton-dressers, the carpenters, the blacksmiths, and the shoemakers, &c., out of employ, and have engrossed their occupations, so that every description of native artisan has been reduced to beggary.
voices.who: A rebel proclamation (ishtahar) issued in the name of a grandson of the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah, as translated in the Delhi Gazette and reprinted by the British historian Charles Ball, who calls it a manifesto of the king
voices.doc: Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 2, pp. 630–632
voices.lic: Public domain (Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, London Printing and Publishing Co., 1858–59)

voices.text: It is not a secret thing, that under the British government, natives employed in the civil and military services, have little respect, low pay, and no manner of influence; and all the posts of dignity and emolument in both the departments, are exclusively bestowed on Englishmen […] Lastly, be it known to all, that whoever, out of the above-named classes, shall, after the circulation of this Ishtahar, still cling to the British government, all his estates shall be confiscated, and his property plundered, and he himself, with his whole family, shall be imprisoned, and ultimately put to death.
voices.who: The same rebel proclamation, on Indians in the Company's service and on those who stayed loyal to the British, as translated in the Delhi Gazette and reprinted by Charles Ball
voices.doc: Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 2, pp. 631–632
voices.lic: Public domain (Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, London Printing and Publishing Co., 1858–59)

voices.text: To eat pigs and drink wine — to bite greased cartridges, and to mix pig's fat with flour and sweetmeats — to destroy Hindoo and Mussulman temples on pretence of making roads — to build churches — to send clergymen into the streets and alleys to preach the Christian religion — to institute English schools, and to pay a monthly stipend for learning the English sciences, while the places of worship of Hindoos and Mussulmans are to this day entirely neglected; with all this, how can the people believe that religion will not be interfered with?
voices.who: Begum Hazrat Mahal of Oudh (Awadh), regent for her young son Birjis Qadir and leader of the rebel government of Oudh, in her counter-proclamation answering Queen Victoria's proclamation; English 'Translation by Order' (made for the British authorities), reprinted by Charles Ball
voices.date: late 1858 (after the Queen's proclamation of 1 November 1858)
voices.doc: Proclamation by the Begum of Oude, in Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 2, pp. 542–543
voices.lic: Public domain (Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, London Printing and Publishing Co., 1858–59)

voices.text: If our people were discontented with our royal predecessor, Wajid Ali Shah, how comes it they are content with us? And no ruler ever experienced such loyalty and devotion of life and goods as we have done. What, then, is wanting that they do not restore our country? Further, it is written in the proclamation, that they want no increase of territory, but yet they cannot refrain from annexation. If the Queen has assumed the government, why does her majesty not restore our country to us when our people wish it? […] No one has ever seen in a dream that the English forgave an offence.
voices.who: Begum Hazrat Mahal of Oudh, ruler of the rebel government, in the same counter-proclamation (English 'Translation by Order', reprinted by Charles Ball)
voices.doc: Proclamation by the Begum of Oude, in Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 2, p. 543
voices.lic: Public domain (Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, London Printing and Publishing Co., 1858–59)

voices.text: All that has been done, was done by that rebellious army. I was in their power, what could I do? They came suddenly, and made me a prisoner. I was helpless, and constrained by my fears, I did whatever they required, otherwise they would immediately have killed me. This is universally known. I found myself in such a predicament that I was weary of my life, while my officials had no hopes of theirs being spared. In this state of things, I resolved to accept poverty, and adopted the garb, colored with red earth, of a religious mendicant
voices.who: Bahadur Shah II, the last Mughal emperor, in his written defence at his trial by a British military commission (the official English translation read in court)
voices.doc: Translation of the written defence put in by Bahadur Shah, Ex-King of Delhi, in Proceedings on the Trial of Muhammad Bahadur Shah (Government of India printing, Calcutta, 1895), p. 133ff.
voices.lic: Public domain (Government of India record of 1858; printed by the Superintendent of Government Printing, Calcutta, 1895)

voices.text: In the city no one's life was safe. All able-bodied men who were seen were taken for rebels and shot. […] Many other well-known men of the city were killed, being mistaken for rebels. In this way God showed His anger: the green as well as the dry trees were consumed; the guiltless shared the same fate as the guilty. As innocent Christians fell victims on the 11th of May, so the same evil fate befel Mahommedans on the 20th September, 1857. The gallows slew those who had escaped the sword.
voices.who: Mainodin Hassan Khan, a Delhi police officer (in charge of the Paharganj police station) who threw in his lot with the rebels and later fled, on the British recapture of Delhi; his narrative as translated by Charles Theophilus Metcalfe
voices.doc: Two Native Narratives of the Mutiny in Delhi, trans. C. T. Metcalfe (1898), pp. 71–73

voices.text: I replied: “Hakimjee, your judgment is not good. The massacre of innocent women and children is not a good work in the eyes of the Most High God. When this insurrection is suppressed, and the English power re-established, the saving of these lives will stand you in good stead.
voices.who: Mainodin Hassan Khan, Delhi police officer, recalling how he pleaded with the emperor's physician Hakim Ahsanullah to stop the killing of Europeans on the day the rebels entered Delhi (his narrative as translated by C. T. Metcalfe)
voices.doc: Two Native Narratives of the Mutiny in Delhi, trans. C. T. Metcalfe (1898), pp. 50–51

witness.text: In fact, the peculiar aggravation of the Cawnpore massacres was this, that the deed was done by a subject race — by black men who dared to shed the blood of their masters, and that of poor helpless ladies and children. Here we had not only a servile war and a sort of Jacquerie combined, but we had a war of religion, a war of race, and a war of revenge, of hope, of some national promptings to shake off the yoke of a stranger, and to re-establish the full power of native chiefs, and the full sway of native religions.
witness.who: William Howard Russell, war correspondent of The Times, in India 1858–59 (My Diary in India, vol. 1, 1860, p. 164)

witness.text: an officer who was attached to Renaud's column, when it moved out from Allahabad in advance of Havelock's force (Neill being at Allahabad), told me that the executions of natives in the line of march were indiscriminate to the last degree. The officer in command was emulous of Neill, and thought he could show equal vigour. In two days forty-two men were hanged on the road-side, and a batch of twelve men were executed because their faces were "turned the wrong way" when they were met on the march. All the villages in his front were burned when he halted.
witness.who: William Howard Russell, The Times correspondent, reporting what a British officer told him about a column marching on Cawnpore in June–July 1857 (My Diary in India, vol. 2, 1860, p. 402)

witness.text: On their part, the Oudians were unquestionably in the position of men struggling for the independence of their country and the defence of their homes. On our side, it was undeniable that we were fiercely striving to tighten the grasp of recent aggression; while we eased our consciences by endeavouring to believe that the men who resisted us were rebels; the fact being, that they owed us no allegiance
witness.who: Charles Ball, British historian of the rising, writing in London (The History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 2, pp. 632–633)

official.text: We deeply lament the evils and misery which have been brought upon India by the acts of ambitious men, who have deceived their countrymen by false reports, and led them into open rebellion. Our power has been shown by the suppression of that rebellion in the field; we desire to show our mercy by pardoning the offences of those who have been thus misled, but who desire to return to the path of duty. […] Our clemency will be extended to all offenders, save and except those who have been, or shall be, convicted of having directly taken part in the murder of British subjects. With regard to such the demands of justice forbid the exercise of mercy. […] Firmly relying ourselves on the truth of Christianity, and acknowledging with gratitude the solace of religion, we disclaim alike the right and desire to impose our convictions on any of our subjects.
official.who: Queen Victoria, Proclamation by the Queen in Council to the princes, chiefs, and people of India, which took over the government of India from the East India Company

official.text: Whenever a rebel is caught he is immediately tried; and, unless he can prove a defence, he is sentenced to be hanged at once: but the chief rebels, or ringleaders, I make first clean up a certain portion of the pool of blood, still two inches deep, in the shed where the fearful murder and mutilation of women and children took place. To touch blood is most abhorrent to the high-caste natives; they think, by doing so, they doom their souls to perdition. Let them think so. My object is to inflict a fearful punishment for a revolting, cowardly, barbarous deed, and to strike terror into these rebels.
official.who: Brigadier-General James Neill, British commander at Cawnpore after its recapture, in a letter quoted by Charles Ball (The History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 1, pp. 389–390)

official.text: The entire defence indeed is a mere tissue of denials of guilt; assertion of his not having been a free-agent; and an endeavour to put the onus of his misconduct upon others.
official.who: Major F. J. Harriott, Deputy Judge Advocate General and government prosecutor, replying to Bahadur Shah's defence before the military commission at Delhi

today.text: On this day in 1857 began the historic First War of Independence, which ignited a spirit of patriotism among our fellow citizens and contributed to the weakening of colonial rule.
today.who: Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India, in a post on Twitter (now X) republished by the Government of India's Press Information Bureau

stories.note: Research in progress: the first proclamation is often called the 'Azamgarh Proclamation' (issued in August 1857 by the Mughal prince Firoz Shah); Ball's printing does not give that name, date or author beyond 'the grandson of Bahadur Shah', and no encyclopaedia page confirming them was checked, so the card does not use the name. No words of an ordinary sepoy, peasant or villager are quoted yet; the Persian and Urdu writings of the Delhi poet Ghalib on the sack of Delhi (Dastanbuy, 1858; letters) were not found in a checkable public-domain transcription.
stories.warn: The Indian proclamations and Bahadur Shah's defence survive here only in English translations made by or for the British (the Begum's is marked 'Translation by Order'); Bahadur Shah wrote his defence to save his life, and Mainodin Hassan Khan wrote his narrative afterwards for a British patron, Metcalfe, having himself been accused of joining the rebels. Russell and Neill write in the racial language of their time. The texts describe mass killing and executions.
disputed: Mutiny or war of independence? Britannica says the rising was long called the 'Indian Mutiny' or 'Sepoy Mutiny' by Western historians and is also called the 'First War of Independence' in India, and that treating it merely as a sepoy mutiny underestimates its political and social causes; Wikipedia notes that the 'First War of Independence' label also has critics in India, and that the name of the revolt remains contested.

How many died? Wikipedia says approximately 6,000 of the 40,000 British living in India were killed, and that, on a rough comparison of dubious pre-1857 demographic data with the 1871 census, probably 800,000 Indians were killed, and very likely more, in the rebellion itself and in the famines and epidemics it caused; for Oudh alone it cites estimates of 150,000 Indians killed, 100,000 of them civilians. No exact count exists on either side.

Was Bahadur Shah a leader or a prisoner of the rebels? In his defence he said the soldiers made him a prisoner and used his seal without his knowledge; the prosecutor called the defence 'a mere tissue of denials of guilt', and on 9 March 1858 the commission found him guilty of all the charges of rebellion, treason and murder; he was sent into exile at Rangoon, arriving on 9 December 1858 (Ball). Britannica describes him as 'nominally restored to power by a tumultuous soldiery', while Wikipedia says that on 16 May up to 50 British prisoners were killed by some of the emperor's servants outside the palace.

Atrocity stories. Reports that British women had been 'dishonoured' at the Bibighar and elsewhere inflamed British opinion, but Wikipedia says the consensus of the detailed inquiries, one ordered by Lord Canning, was that there was no convincing evidence of such crimes, although British women and children had been killed outright.
stories.blind: The rising is told here by those with power to write: an emperor pleading for his life, a queen-regent and a Mughal prince issuing proclamations, a Delhi police officer writing for a British patron, and British commanders, correspondents and historians. Every Indian text reached print through British translators. The tens of thousands of sepoys who rose, the villagers hanged along the roads or killed in famine and disease, and the British women, children and Indian servants killed at Delhi and Cawnpore left almost no words of their own.
reading: Charles Ball, The History of the Indian Mutiny, vol. 2 (1858–59, archive.org)
Proceedings on the Trial of Muhammad Bahadur Shah (Government of India, 1895, archive.org)
Two Native Narratives of the Mutiny in Delhi, trans. C. T. Metcalfe (1898, archive.org)
W. H. Russell, My Diary in India, vols. 1–2 (1860, archive.org)

stories.title: The 1971 killings in East Pakistan (Bangladesh)
stories.where: East Pakistan, now Bangladesh (pin: Dhaka)
facts: In the 1970 elections the Awami League, led by Mujibur Rahman, won 167 of the 169 seats allotted to East Pakistan and with them a majority in Pakistan's National Assembly; on 3 March 1971 President Yahya Khan, under pressure from West Pakistani leaders, particularly Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, prevented it from taking power, prompting widespread protests and calls for independence.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Bangladesh-Liberation-War

On 25 March 1971 Pakistan launched Operation Searchlight, a massive military intervention intended to quash the independence movement by targeting intellectuals, activists and the Hindu minority; many students were among those killed, and Mujibur Rahman declared independence on 26 March shortly before he was arrested and taken to West Pakistan.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Bangladesh-Liberation-War

From May to October 1971 the army and its local allies systematically destroyed villages, collectively punishing civilians for the guerrilla insurgency of the Mukti Bahini; Britannica estimates that 200,000 to 400,000 women were sexually assaulted, and that as many as 15 million refugees crossed into India.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Bangladesh-Liberation-War

The violence ran both ways: in early March 1971, before the army struck, Bengali mobs killed non-Bengalis, 300 Biharis in rioting in Chittagong alone according to Wikipedia, and the Pakistani government used this 'Bihari massacre' to justify its crackdown; during the war some Biharis joined pro-army militias, and Wikipedia gives between 1,000 and 150,000 Biharis killed in reprisal attacks by Bengali militias and mobs.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Bangladesh_genocide

India, which gave the rebels training and military support, went to war with Pakistan on 3 December 1971, and Pakistani forces in East Pakistan surrendered on 16 December, securing Bangladesh's independence; afterwards many Bihari muhajirs were persecuted as alleged collaborators, many were killed and hundreds of thousands were placed in camps.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Bangladesh-Liberation-War

The United States under President Nixon kept supporting Pakistan for Cold War reasons, although the American diplomat Archer Blood in Dhaka warned of a 'reign of terror' by Pakistani troops; Britannica says the US went on sending weapons to Yahya Khan's government despite restrictions by Congress.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Bangladesh-Liberation-War

voices.text: I have come before you today with a heart laden with sadness. You are aware of everything and know all. We have tried with our lives. And yet the sadness remains that today, in Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna, Rajshahi and Rangpur the streets are soaked in the blood of my brothers. […] The weapons we have bought with our money to defend the country against foreign aggression are being used against the poor and downtrodden of my country today. It is their hearts the bullets pierce today.
voices.who: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, leader of the Awami League, which had won the 1970 election in East Pakistan, speaking to a mass rally in Dhaka (official English translation, Government of Bangladesh)
voices.doc: Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Fifth Schedule (speech of 7 March 1971, 'Translated'), Ministry of Law, bdlaws.minlaw.gov.bd
voices.lic: Government of Bangladesh legal text (Constitution, Fifth Schedule, official translation, added 2011); government edict, brief credited quotation

voices.text: Bear in mind that the enemy has infiltrated our ranks to cause confusion and sow discord among us. In our Bengal, everyone, be he Hindu or Muslim, Bangalee or non-Bangalee, is our brother. It is our responsibility to ensure their security. Our good name must not be sullied.
voices.who: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, Awami League leader, in the same speech, as attacks on non-Bengalis were already taking place (official English translation, Government of Bangladesh)
voices.doc: Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Fifth Schedule
voices.lic: Government of Bangladesh legal text (Constitution, Fifth Schedule, official translation, added 2011); government edict, brief credited quotation

voices.text: Why did they shoot innocent people-women, children, beggars in the street-firing at random into houses? If they were angry with the Awami League, why did they not punish the leaders instead of taking vengeance on anyone within range of their guns?
voices.who: A middle-aged refugee in a camp in India, unnamed, as recorded by the field team of the US Senate subcommittee on refugees
voices.doc: Edward M. Kennedy, Crisis in South Asia, report to the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Refugees (US Government Printing Office, 1971), section 'The night of March 25th and after'
voices.lic: Public domain (US government work: report to the US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Refugees, 1971)

voices.text: It is so senseless. You do not know who might shoot you. It might be a soldier who decides you were an Awami League supporter. It might be a young Mukti Bahini fighter who sees you are middle-aged and therefore assumes you are unwilling to oppose the army. Or it might simply be a miscreant who wants to loot your home or shop. We had to flee this madness.
voices.who: A well-educated middle-aged Bengali man in a refugee camp, unnamed, as recorded by the US Senate subcommittee's field team
voices.doc: Edward M. Kennedy, Crisis in South Asia, report to the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Refugees (US Government Printing Office, 1971)
voices.lic: Public domain (US government work: report to the US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Refugees, 1971)

voices.text: I do not know why they shot me-I don't belong to any political party-I was just a railway clerk.
voices.who: A 55-year-old railway employee, unnamed, wounded in the head when the Pakistani army attacked his railway station at noon, speaking in an Indian border hospital, as recorded by the US Senate subcommittee's field team
voices.doc: Edward M. Kennedy, Crisis in South Asia, report to the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Refugees (US Government Printing Office, 1971), section 'Civilian war casualties'
voices.lic: Public domain (US government work: report to the US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Refugees, 1971)

witness.text: Here in Dacca we are mute and horrified witnesses to a reign of terror by the Pak military. Evidence continues to mount that the MLA authorities have a list of Awami League supporters whom they are systematically eliminating by seeking them out in their homes and shooting them down. […] Moreover, with support of Pak military, non-Bengali Muslims are systematically attacking poor people’s quarters and murdering Bengalis and Hindus.
witness.who: Archer K. Blood, US Consul General in Dacca, in a cable to the State Department headed 'Selective Genocide' (Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969–1976, vol. E–7, doc. 125)

witness.text: Our government has failed to denounce the suppression of democracy. Our government has failed to denounce atrocities. Our government has failed to take forceful measures to protect its citizens while at the same time bending over backwards to placate the West Pak dominated government […] But we have chosen not to intervene, even morally, on the grounds that the Awami conflict, in which unfortunately the overworked term genocide is applicable, is purely internal matter of a sovereign state.
witness.who: Officers of the US Consulate General, USAID and USIS in Dacca, in the dissent cable sent with Consul General Archer Blood's endorsement (the 'Blood Telegram', FRUS 1969–1976, vol. XI, doc. 19)

witness.text: The same is true for the number of Bengalis or Bihari Muslims or West Pakistanis who were slaughtered during the holocaust of March-which preceded the outbreak of civil war-when Bengalis attacked Biharis in sporadic fits of terrorism. Certainly tens of thousands died during March--and since the outbreak of civil war on March 25, when the Pakistan army unleashed its massive power and began to implement a policy of indiscriminate terror, death estimates run in the hundreds of thousands.
witness.who: Senator Edward M. Kennedy, chairman of the US Senate subcommittee on refugees, in his report after visiting the refugee areas in India (Crisis in South Asia, 1971)

witness.text: Nothing is more clear, or more easily documented, than the systematic campaign of terror-and its genocidal consequences-launched by the Pakistan army on the night of March 25th. […] Hardest hit have been members of the Hindu community who have been robbed of their lands and shops, systematically slaughtered, and, in some places, painted with yellow patches marked "H".
witness.who: Senator Edward M. Kennedy, in the conclusions of the same report (Crisis in South Asia, 1971)

official.text: Meanwhile murder, arson and widespread disorder in defiance of governmental authority were let loose in the province. […] Eventually a point was reached where the Awami League put forward final proposals which virtually amounted to dismemberment of the country. Since they had no such mandate from the people and as unity of the country was at stake, firm action had to be taken to assert governmentʼs authority and to safeguard the integrity of Pakistan. There was no option but to take that decision. The situation in East Pakistan is well under control and normal life is being restored. Accounts to the contrary circulated by some outside sources especially from news media, do not reflect the correct position and are designed to mislead world public opinion.
official.who: General Agha Mohammad Yahya Khan, President of Pakistan and chief martial law administrator, in a message to President Nixon delivered by the Pakistani ambassador (FRUS 1969–1976, vol. XI, doc. 16)

today.text: WHEREAS in the conduct of a ruthless and savage war the Pakistani authorities committed and are still continuously committing numerous acts of genocide and unprecedented tortures, amongst others on the civilian and unarmed people of Bangladesh,
today.who: The Proclamation of Independence issued at Mujibnagar by the elected representatives of Bangladesh on 10 April 1971, which since the Fifteenth Amendment (2011) forms the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of Bangladesh, as published on the Government of Bangladesh's laws site (checked November 2026). Pakistan's official position differs: see 'disputed'.

stories.note: Research in progress: no words of a Bihari / Urdu-speaking survivor of the killings of March or December 1971 were found in a public-domain or government source; Yahya Khan's radio broadcast of 26 March 1971 and the Hamoodur Rahman Commission report were not found in a checkable government copy, so the commission's figure is given only as Britannica reports it. Refugees are quoted only as recorded, unnamed, in the US Senate report. The 26 March declaration attributed to Mujibur Rahman (Sixth Schedule of the Constitution) is not quoted because its exact wording is debated.
stories.warn: Mujibur Rahman's speech is quoted from the Government of Bangladesh's official English translation; the refugees' words were recorded in English by a US Senate team, and Kennedy and the Dhaka consulate were openly critical of US policy. Yahya Khan's message is his government's justification at the time. The texts refer to mass killing, and the war involved mass sexual violence.
disputed: How many died? Britannica puts the deaths from the liberation war and the India-Pakistan war together at between 300,000 and 3,000,000, and notes that Pakistan's Hamoodur Rahman Commission estimated close to 26,000 while Bangladesh has claimed about 3,000,000. Wikipedia adds that the CIA and State Department, midway through, conservatively estimated 200,000 killed, that independent researchers estimate around 300,000 to 500,000, that the 3 million estimate 'has come under strict scrutiny', and that Sarmila Bose's 50,000–100,000 figure has been strongly criticised.

Was it genocide? Bangladesh's founding proclamation speaks of 'acts of genocide', the US consulate in Dacca used the word in 1971, and Senator Kennedy wrote of 'genocidal consequences'. Wikipedia's article describes the killings as genocide in its opening sentence, but also states that allegations of genocide were rejected by most UN member states at the time and rarely appear in textbooks and academic sources on genocide studies, and that the political scientists Richard Sisson and Leo E. Rose deny that a genocide occurred; Britannica's article does not use the word. Because the scholarly classification is still debated, this card does not apply the 'Genocide' theme.

Who struck first, and who suffered most? Pakistan justified the crackdown by Bengali attacks on Biharis in early March. Wikipedia reports that, according to Sarmila Bose and the Pakistani journalist Anthony Mascarenhas, the army showed great restraint until 25 March, while Mascarenhas judged the army's actions from then on far worse and on a larger scale than the violence by Bengalis. Senator Kennedy's report also records the Bengali killings of Biharis in March.

Pakistan's position. Wikipedia says Pakistan 'deeply regretted any crimes that may have been committed' in 1974, President Musharraf expressed regret for the 'excesses' in 2002, and in 2015 the Foreign Ministry rejected any 'insinuation of complicity in committing crimes or war atrocities'; Britannica notes that Pakistan has not officially taken accountability for the war crimes of 1971.
stories.blind: The record of 1971 in English is dominated by outsiders: American diplomats, a US senator, and the Pakistani government justifying itself. Bengali villagers, Hindus driven out, and the women assaulted speak here only in a few unnamed lines taken down by a Senate team, and the Bihari and other Urdu-speaking civilians killed by Bengali mobs and fighters left almost nothing in public-domain sources. Both the Pakistani army's internal record (the Hamoodur Rahman Commission) and many Bangladeshi accounts were shaped by the politics of the two states that emerged from the war.
reading: FRUS 1969–1976, vol. XI, South Asia Crisis, 1971 (Office of the Historian)
FRUS 1969–1976, vol. E–7, Documents on South Asia, 1969–1972 (Office of the Historian)
E. M. Kennedy, Crisis in South Asia (1971, Google Books full view)
Constitution of Bangladesh, Schedules (Ministry of Law, PDF)

stories.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
stories.where: Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco, now central Mexico City, Mexico
facts: Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, was founded about 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco and joined to the mainland by causeways; its population in 1519 has been estimated at about 400,000, the largest residential concentration in Mesoamerican history, and it was destroyed by the Spanish conquistadores under Hernán Cortés in 1521.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Tenochtitlan

Aztec rule rested on tribute and war: its provinces paid tribute according to what each region produced, human sacrifice was commonly practised, war was ideologically a religious duty that supplied prisoners for sacrifice, and, as their power grew, the Aztecs ritually killed prisoners from all parts of what is now Mexico.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Aztec

Many subject peoples bitterly resented paying tribute to the Aztecs, and Cortés eventually gained more than 200,000 Indigenous allies; Tlaxcala, in chronic war with Montezuma II, first resisted Cortés and then became his most faithful ally, and in 1520 his captain Pedro de Alvarado massacred many leading Aztec chiefs during a festival in the city.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hernan-Cortes

After the Spaniards were driven out of the city in 1520, a smallpox epidemic struck the Valley of Mexico, including Tenochtitlan, and killed much of the Indigenous leadership, while the Spaniards, among whom smallpox had long been endemic, were affected relatively little; Cuauhtémoc was made ruler in February 1521.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Tenochtitlan

The siege lasted from 26 May to 13 August 1521; during the fighting the defenders sacrificed Spanish prisoners at the altar of Huitzilopochtli, and after the surrender, when Cortés demanded the gold lost in 1520, Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba were tortured.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Tenochtitlan
Cortés later took Cuauhtémoc with him on his expedition to Honduras and, hearing of a plot against the Spaniards, ordered him hanged.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cuauhtemoc
