Gloss: 'And they took and picked out the women, the fair ones, the ones with light-coloured bodies. And some of the women, to slip past them, smeared their faces with mud and dressed in rags, rags for skirts and tatters for blouses; they put nothing but rags on themselves.'
voices.doc: Florentine Codex, Book XII, ch. 40, fol. 82v (Nahuatl column), transcription by James Lockhart, Early Nahuatl Library
voices.lic: Public domain (Nahuatl text of the Florentine Codex, c. 1575–77); checked against James Lockhart's transcription on the Early Nahuatl Library (site © Early Nahuatl Library; only the 16th-century Nahuatl words are reproduced, not Lockhart's translation or notes)

voices.text: Then Guatemoc said to Cortés "Señor Malinche, I have surely done my duty in defence of my City, and I can do no more and I come by force and a prisoner into your presence and into your power, take that dagger that you have in your belt and kill me at once with it"! and when he said this he wept tears and sobbed and other great Lords whom he had brought with him also wept.
voices.who: Cuauhtémoc, the last Mexica ruler, at his surrender, as recorded decades later by the conquistador Bernal Díaz del Castillo (A. P. Maudslay's English translation); Cortés's own letter of 1522 reports the same request, in indirect speech
voices.doc: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, trans. A. P. Maudslay, vol. 4 (Hakluyt Society, 1912), p. 182 (OCR corrected)

witness.text: Los Españoles y sus amigos pusiéronse en todos los caminos, y robaron á los que pasaban, tomándolos el oro que llevaban, y escudriñándolos todos sus hatos, y todas sus vestiduras, y ninguna otra cosa tomaban sino el oro, y las mugeres mozas hermosas, y algunas de las mugeres por escaparse disfrazábanse poniendo lodo en la cara, y vistiéndose de andrajos: también tomaban mancebos y hombres recios para esclavos, pusieron los nombres de tlamacazque, y á muchos de ellos herraron en la cara.
witness.who: Fray Bernardino de Sahagún, Franciscan missionary who compiled Book XII with Nahua informants, in his own Spanish version of their account, as printed by Carlos María de Bustamante (Historia de la conquista de México, Mexico, 1829, pp. 56–57). Gloss: 'The Spaniards and their allies posted themselves on all the roads and robbed those who passed, taking the gold they carried and searching all their bundles and clothes; they took nothing else but the gold, and the young, beautiful women; and some of the women, to escape, disguised themselves by putting mud on their faces and dressing in rags. They also took young men and strong men as slaves, called them tlamacazque, and branded many of them on the face.'
witness.date: written down decades later, on August 1521

witness.text: and his forebodings were realised, when, a few days later, upon his protesting that there was no treasure left in the city, Cortes consented to his torture to force him to speak. Bernal Diaz seeks to excuse Cortes's part in this unworthy proceeding.
witness.who: Francis Augustus MacNutt, American historian and translator of Cortés's letters, in an editor's note on Cuauhtémoc (Letters of Cortes, vol. 2, 1908, p. 127)

official.text: Our friends accompanied us, armed with swords and shields, and such was the slaughter done that day on water and on land, that with prisoners taken they numbered in all more than forty thousand men; and such were the shrieks and the weeping of the women and children that there was none whose heart did not break; and we had more trouble in preventing our allies from killing and inflicting tortures than we had in fighting with the Indians, for no such inhuman cruelty as the natives of these parts practice was ever seen amongst any people.
official.who: Hernán Cortés, commander of the Spanish and allied forces, in his third letter of relation to the Emperor Charles V, in F. A. MacNutt's translation (Letters of Cortes, vol. 2, 1908, pp. 123–124)

official.text: It appears they had perished to the number of more than fifty thousand, from the salt water which they drank, or from starvation, and pestilence. […] As the people of the city came towards us, I ordered Spaniards to be stationed in all the streets, to prevent our allies from killing those unhappy creatures, who were beyond number; and I also ordered the captains of our allies not to allow in any way those fugitives to be killed, but, as they were so many, it was not possible to prevent it that day, so more than fifteen thousand persons were massacred.
official.who: Hernán Cortés, third letter to Charles V, on the last day of the siege (MacNutt's translation, 1908, p. 126)

official.text: I assert that during three days and nights they never ceased streaming out and all three causeways were crowded with men, women and children, so thin, yellow, dirty and stinking, that it was pitiful to see them.
official.who: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, conquistador who fought in the siege, in his True History written decades later (Maudslay's translation, vol. 4, 1912, p. 187)

official.text: When proclamation was made that they were to be taken to a certain house to be branded, most of us soldiers took those slaves that we possessed to be marked with the brand of His Majesty, which was a G. which was meant to signify Guerra (war),
official.who: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, on the branding of Indigenous captives as war slaves at Texcoco during the campaign (Maudslay's translation, vol. 4, 1912, p. 54)

today.text: Canal 22, institución de la Secretaría de Cultura, dedica una programación especial en el marco de la conmemoración de los 500 años de resistencia indígena, 1521 toma de México-Tenochtitlán
today.who: Mexico's federal Secretaría de Cultura, press release (Spanish). Gloss: 'Canal 22, an institution of the Ministry of Culture, is dedicating special programming to the commemoration of 500 years of Indigenous resistance, 1521, the taking of Mexico-Tenochtitlan.' The Mexican government marked the 500th anniversary in 2021 as '500 years of Indigenous resistance'.

stories.note: Research in progress: the Nahuatl lament of the Anales de Tlatelolco (the 'broken spears' passage) was not found in a public-domain printing and is not quoted; the modern English translations of it and of Book XII (Anderson and Dibble; León-Portilla, The Broken Spears; Lockhart, We People Here) are in copyright and are only described. No Tlaxcalan account (for example the Lienzo de Tlaxcala) has been added yet.
stories.warn: The Nahuatl is quoted from James Lockhart's transcription of the Florentine Codex manuscript (spelling and word division as on that page, including run-together words), with the site's own plain-English glosses, not a published translation; Sahagún's Spanish is quoted from the 1829 printing. The Florentine Codex was written down decades after 1521 from elderly informants, and Díaz wrote his True History decades later; Cortés wrote to the emperor about his own campaign. The texts describe epidemic, famine, mass killing, enslavement and branding.
disputed: How many died? Wikipedia's summary gives estimates of 100,000 to 240,000 killed in the campaign overall, warriors and civilians, and at least 40,000 Aztec civilians killed and captured; Cortés himself wrote that more than 40,000 were killed or taken on one day, that more than 50,000 had perished from salt water, starvation and pestilence, and that more than 15,000 were massacred by his allies on the last day. Britannica puts the city's population in 1519 at about 400,000.

Did Moctezuma think Cortés was a god? Britannica says historians long held that the Aztecs expected the return of Quetzalcóatl and that Cortés used this fear, but that some 21st-century historians questioned whether the Aztecs thought Cortés was a god at all, and suggested the well-known story was a Spanish creation later incorporated into Aztec lore; Wikipedia's article likewise calls it now believed to be a myth of the conquerors.

Who conquered Tenochtitlan? Britannica credits Cortés with more than 200,000 Indigenous allies, and Wikipedia says it is well accepted that these allies were indispensable to his success; Cortés's own letter blames the allies for the worst killing, while saying they were 'reproved and punished by us'. The Mexican government's 2021 commemoration framed the year as '500 years of Indigenous resistance'.

How far is the Nahua account a single 'Aztec' voice? Wikipedia describes Book XII as the conquest told from the point of view of the conquered of Tenochtitlan-Tlatelolco, and reports Lockhart's view that Sahagún collected statements from people of relatively advanced age and high status, written down in Nahuatl by aides he had trained; the friar's project ran from 1545 until his death in 1590.
stories.blind: The Mexica side survives mainly through elders of Tlatelolco and Tenochtitlan who spoke decades later to a Franciscan friar's trained assistants, so the view is that of a surviving nobility in one twin city. The tens of thousands who died of smallpox and hunger, the women taken on the roads, and the men branded as slaves appear only as numbers or in a line or two. The Tlaxcalan and other Indigenous allies who made up the great majority of Cortés's forces and were indispensable to his victory are barely heard in this card, while Cortés's own letters to the emperor and Díaz's memoir survive in full.
reading: Florentine Codex, Book XII, Nahuatl and Spanish transcription (Early Nahuatl Library)
Sahagún, Historia de la conquista de México, ed. Bustamante (1829, archive.org)
Letters of Cortes, trans. F. A. MacNutt, vol. 2 (1908, archive.org)
Bernal Díaz del Castillo, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, trans. A. P. Maudslay, vol. 4 (1912, archive.org)

stories.title: The Russian conquest of Khiva and the Yomud Turkmen
stories.where: Yomud Turkmen lands west of Khiva, between Hazavat (Uzbekistan) and Ilyali (Yylanly, Turkmenistan); pin: Khiva, Uzbekistan (approximate)
facts: The khanate of Khiva, on the Amu Darya (Oxus) northwest of Bukhara, had repelled Russian invasions in 1717 and 1839, but in 1873 it was conquered and made a Russian protectorate.
https://www.britannica.com/place/khanate-of-Khiva

The conquest was led by Konstantin Kaufmann, the first governor-general of Russian Turkistan, who had made Bukhara a Russian protectorate in 1868; in 1873 he occupied Khiva, and Russia gained all of the khanate's territory north of the Amu Darya.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Konstantin-Petrovich-Kaufmann

Russian columns crossed the deserts in the spring of 1873; on the way the Orenburg column burned the village of Mangit, where, Wikipedia says, the inhabitants were slaughtered because of some firing from the village; the Khan surrendered in June, and the treaty of August 1873 abolished the Khivan slave trade and slavery, opened the khanate to Russian merchants, and laid an indemnity of 2,200,000 rubles on Khiva, payable in instalments until 1893.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khivan_campaign_of_1873

Khiva was a slave market: the American reporter J. A. MacGahan, who rode with the Russians, wrote that Turkmen raiders caught Persians on the Persian frontier and sold them in Khiva and Bukhara, and that from all he could gather about 27,000 of the 30,000 Persians in Khiva were slaves, though the Khan's minister Mat-Murad put the number at only 3,000 or 4,000.
https://archive.org/stream/cu31924028413486/cu31924028413486_djvu.txt

After the city fell, Kaufmann demanded 300,000 rubles from the Yomud Turkmen at short notice; according to the American diplomat Eugene Schuyler, who read the official orders, he kept twelve of the seventeen elders who came to Khiva as hostages and on 18 July ordered General Golovachev to march on the Yomud settlements if they were not collecting the money.
https://archive.org/stream/cu31924100211451/cu31924100211451_djvu.txt

From 21 July Cossacks burned the Yomud farms, houses and grain along the march, and cavalry charges overtook families fleeing into the desert; by MacGahan's estimate the column ravaged nearly 100 square miles, and afterwards much of the indemnity laid on the Turkmen tribes was paid with the women's silver ornaments.
https://archive.org/stream/cu31924028413486/cu31924028413486_djvu.txt

voices.text: When asked what they wanted, they replied, that they wished to know why the Russians were invading their country. They had never made war on the Russians; why were the Russians making war on them? […] "We are," they said, "many thousands, and if the Russians overrun our country, severe shall be their punishment." And they were, they said, determined to fight.
voices.who: Yomud Turkmen horsemen who stopped to parley with the Russian advance guard while their families fled, as recorded by J. A. MacGahan, the American correspondent riding with the column
voices.doc: J. A. MacGahan, Campaigning on the Oxus, and the Fall of Khiva (London, 1874), pp. 359–360 (OCR corrected)

witness.text: "We have sworn friendship with you, and consider ourselves your allies. Now the other tribe of Russians from Turkistan are making war upon us, and we think you ought to help us against them just as we would help you against your enemies."
witness.who: Yomud Turkmen who came to the officers of the Russian Orenburg column, which had passed through their country on friendly terms, as told to MacGahan afterwards by the Russian officer Count Shuvalov and recorded by MacGahan (reported second-hand: Yomuds to officers of the Orenburg column, then Count Shuvalov to MacGahan, who calls the request naive)

witness.text: They rarely dismounted, but simply rode up to the houses, applied their blazing torches to the projecting eaves of thatch, and the stacks of unthreshed grain, and then galloped on. Five minutes afterwards, sheets of seething flame and darkling smoke showed how well they had done their work. The entire country was on fire. […] This was war such as I had never before seen, and such as is rarely seen in modern days.
witness.who: J. A. MacGahan, American war correspondent of the New York Herald, riding with General Golovachev's column (Campaigning on the Oxus, 1874, p. 359)

witness.text: In the marsh are twenty or thirty women and children, up to their necks in water, trying to hide among the weeds and grass, begging for their lives, and screaming in the most pitiful manner. […] As we withdrew, I looked in vain for the women and children I had seen in the water. They had all disappeared; and as I saw them nowhere in the vicinity, I am afraid that, frightened by the rockets, they threw themselves into the water, and were drowned.
witness.who: J. A. MacGahan, riding with the Cossacks who pursued the fleeing Yomud families (Campaigning on the Oxus, 1874, pp. 364–365)

witness.text: The power of the Yomud Turcomans was broken; their ruin complete. The greater part of their live stock had been captured. All of their wheat, grain, and forage, upon which they depended for subsistence during the winter, had been burned, and their dwellings laid in ashes.
witness.who: J. A. MacGahan (Campaigning on the Oxus, 1874, p. 409)

witness.text: When we had gone about twenty-five miles from Khiva, General Golovatchef said before a large number of officers in my presence: "I have received an order from the Commander-in-Chief - I hope you will remember it and give it to your soldiers. This expedition does not spare either sex or age. Kill all of them." After this the officers delivered this command to their several detachments.
witness.who: An unnamed eyewitness who marched with the Russian column, 'taken down from his own lips' by Eugene Schuyler, American diplomat in Russia (Turkistan, vol. 2, 1876, p. 359); Schuyler does not name him, and the words he reports from General Golovachev are not in any published order

witness.text: To help in raising this sum the Turkoman women had to strip themselves of all their ornaments, and bring them into the Russian camp for sale at whatever prices could be obtained. Every necklace and bracelet thus given up will leave a long legacy of hatred.
witness.who: Eugene Schuyler, American diplomat, on the 310,000 rubles Kaufmann demanded from the Turkmen tribes on 2 August 1873, after the campaign (Turkistan, vol. 2, 1876, p. 359)

official.text: To follow more closely the payment of the contribution by the Yomuds, I ask your Excellency to start with your detachment for Hazavat on July 7 (19), and to encamp in a suitable place. If your Excellency sees that the Yomuds are not occupying themselves with getting together money, but are assembling for the purpose of opposing our troops, or perhaps even for leaving the country, I order you immediately to move upon the settlements of the Yomuds which are placed along the Hazavat canal and its branches, and to give over the settlements of the Yomuds and their families to complete destruction, and their herds and property to confiscation.
official.who: General Konstantin Kaufmann, governor-general of Turkistan and commander of the expedition, written order No. 1167 to General Golovachev, in Eugene Schuyler's English translation (Turkistan, vol. 2, 1876, p. 357)

official.text: If the Yomuds become submissive, stop ravaging them, but keep watch of what is being done among them, and at the least attempt to migrate, carry out my order for the final extermination of the disobedient tribe.
official.who: General Kaufmann, order No. 1217 to General Golovachev, which also approved his conduct and advised him to keep the grain rather than burn it, in Schuyler's translation (Turkistan, vol. 2, 1876, p. 358)

official.text: With these views General Kaufmann decided that, profiting by the presence of the Russian troops in the Khanate, it was necessary in some degree to change the order of things regarding the Turkomans, materially and morally, by subduing their pride and their license.
official.who: The Russian official report of the campaign (Military Journal, December 1873), as quoted by Schuyler (Turkistan, vol. 2, 1876, p. 356); the report argued that the Turkmen had never obeyed the Khan and that peace was impossible unless they felt Russian power

official.text: 18. A war indemnity of 2,200,000 rubles is levied upon Khiva, to pay the expenses of the campaign, which was solely caused by the government and people of Khiva.
official.who: Treaty of peace between Russia and the Khan of Khiva, article 18, in the English text printed by MacGahan (Campaigning on the Oxus, 1874, p. 419); article 17 confirms the emancipation of the slaves and the ban on slavery 'in all future time'

stories.note: Research in progress: no Turkmen or Khivan account in their own languages has been found in a public-domain transcription. The Khivan court chronicles of the period (in Chagatai) and Turkmen oral tradition about the 1873 war were not found in a quotable copy, and no freed Persian or Russian slave's own words survived in the sources checked. Every Turkmen voice on this card was written down by a foreign reporter.
stories.warn: The Turkmen words survive only in English, as remembered and written down by J. A. MacGahan (1874), one of them passed on to him by a Russian officer. MacGahan admired the Turkmen and wrote vividly; Wikipedia's article notes that some of his writing seems fictionalized. Schuyler's eyewitness is anonymous. The sources use the period's spellings (Turcoman, Turkoman, Golovatchoff, Golovatchef) and the language of their time about Central Asian peoples. The texts describe the burning of homes and the killing of fleeing families.
disputed: Were women and children killed? MacGahan, who rode with the Cossacks on 21 July, wrote that apart from one case he stopped there was no violence offered to women and children, and that General Golovachev seemed to want the Yomuds to escape; Schuyler's unnamed eyewitness says Golovachev passed on an order to spare neither sex nor age and that nearly everyone the troops met was killed, children included. Wikipedia's article notes that MacGahan seems to be its only source and that some of his writing seems fictionalized.

Why attack the Yomuds? The Russian official report says the Turkmen had to be subdued, materially and morally, because they had never obeyed the Khan and could turn him against Russia. Schuyler answers that the Yomud elders had already offered submission and been promised they would be left alone, calls the holding of hostages an evident breach of faith, and reports that officers wanted a real battle to earn the Cross of St George; MacGahan thought Kaufmann wrong but believed he acted on his own judgment, not as the Khan's tool.

Were the Yomuds slave raiders? MacGahan wrote that capturing Persians for sale had been one of the Turkmen's principal resources, but that the Turkmen of Khiva owned fewer slaves than the Uzbeks and were not implicated in slave-dealing at all, which he blamed on the Tekke Turkmen near the Caspian. The violence also went both ways: MacGahan found a Persian left for dead in the sands by Yomuds, and Schuyler's eyewitness describes Turkmen killing a Russian picket of eight men during the campaign.

How many died? Wikipedia's summary gives 33 Russians killed and 124 wounded for the campaign against Khiva and more than 5,000 killed on the Khivan side, without separating out the Yomud campaign; for the Yomud fighting of 28 July Schuyler's eyewitness speaks of several hundred bodies left on the ground. No count of Yomud civilians who died has been found.
stories.blind: The Yomud Turkmen left no written account of the burning of their country that has been found; they speak here only in two short speeches recorded by an American reporter, one of them second-hand. The women whose silver paid the indemnity, the families who fled into the desert, and the tens of thousands of Persian captives freed on paper in 1873 are described by Russian officers and foreign travellers but not heard, while Kaufmann's orders, the official report and the treaty survive in full.
reading: J. A. MacGahan, Campaigning on the Oxus, and the Fall of Khiva (1874, archive.org)
Eugene Schuyler, Turkistan, vol. 2 (1876; 1877 printing, archive.org)

stories.title: The Circassian expulsion
stories.where: Black Sea coast and mountains of the North-West Caucasus between Anapa and Sochi, Russia; refugee camps at Trebizond (Trabzon) and Samsun, Turkey; pin: Sochi (approximate)
facts: Russia claimed Circassia under the Treaty of Adrianople, by which Turkey had ceded it, while Britain told Russia in 1856 that it had never recognised that right, the Circassians being independent tribes who did not acknowledge the Sultan.
https://archive.org/stream/accountspapers0075grea_j6k1/accountspapers0075grea_j6k1_djvu.txt

In early 1864 Russian columns under Count Evdokimov crossed the main Caucasus ridge; the official Journal de St-Pétersbourg reported that the Abadzekh had left their villages for assigned points on the Kuban plain or for Turkey, that the Ubykh were defeated in mid-March, that the troops reached the mouth of the Sochi on 25 March, and that on 2 April (dates as given in the report) Grand Duke Michael received the elders' submission and ordered them to the coast.
https://archive.org/stream/accountspapersof0063grea_f5p4/accountspapersof0063grea_f5p4_djvu.txt

The same report said that 30,000 people had left from the mouth of the Tuapse in March and about 50,000 more were waiting at Anapa, Novorossiisk, the Dzhubga and the Tuapse, with at least as many to come from the Ubykh and Jiget lands; the British consul at Trebizond reported in May that Russia insisted on their leaving by the end of May (old style).
https://archive.org/stream/accountspapersof0063grea_f5p4/accountspapersof0063grea_f5p4_djvu.txt

At Trebizond the British consul counted more than 3,500 deaths from December 1863 to mid-February 1864, 3,000 of them emigrants, as typhus spread; by May the mortality in the camps averaged 120 to 150 a day, and 500 deaths had occurred at Samsun in forty-eight hours.
https://archive.org/stream/accountspapersof0063grea_f5p4/accountspapersof0063grea_f5p4_djvu.txt

Britannica states that Russia in 1860 began a campaign to forcibly resettle the Circassians in the valley of the Kuban, and that by 1864 almost the entire Circassian population, some 400,000 people, had instead emigrated to the Ottoman Empire, many thousands dying of starvation and disease on the way.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Circassian

A slave trade ran from the Circassian coast to Turkey before the conquest: Russia said that suppressing it had been the principal object of its coastal forts, and Britain said it had pressed the Porte to prevent slaves being carried from Circassia to Turkey.
https://archive.org/stream/accountspapers0075grea_j6k1/accountspapers0075grea_j6k1_djvu.txt

voices.text: It is now more than eighty years since the Russian Government is unlawfully striving to subdue and annex to its dominions Circassia, which since the creation of the world has been our home and our country. It slaughters like sheep the children, helpless women, and old men that fall into its hands. […] But during the last year or two it has taken advantage of a famine caused by a drought with which the Almighty visited us, as well as by its own ravages, and it has occasioned us great distress by its severe attacks by sea and land. Many are the lives which have been lost in battle, from hunger in the mountains, from destitution on the sea-coast, and from want of skill at sea.
voices.who: Petition 'signed by the people of Circassia' to Queen Victoria, sent to the British ambassador at Constantinople, in the English translation printed by the British government
voices.doc: Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants in Turkey (presented to the House of Commons, 1864), in Accounts and Papers 1864, vol. LXIII, Inclosure in No. 3, pp. 2–3
voices.lic: Public domain (UK government publication, 1864; also reprinted in Burnaby, 1877)

voices.text: But if it is not possible to afford this help for the preservation of our country and race, then we pray to be afforded facilities for removing to a place of safety our helpless and miserable children and women that are perishing by the brutal attacks of the enemy as well as by the effects of famine; and if neither of these two requests are taken into consideration, and if in our helpless condition we are utterly annihilated notwithstanding our appeals to the mercy and grace of the Governments, then we shall not cease to invoke our right in the presence of the Lord of the Universe […]
voices.who: The same petition of the people of Circassia, after asking Britain to stop the Russian attacks
voices.doc: Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants in Turkey (presented to the House of Commons, 1864), in Accounts and Papers 1864, vol. LXIII, Inclosure in No. 3, p. 3

voices.text: The Circassians are a very small and weak people; they have no money, they pay no taxes, they have no government, they have no newspapers, they are ignorant; but this they do know, that many years Russia has been fighting against them […] From Europe or from England no help has come to us. We have heard that if there was justice to be found it was in England; we came then to England, weak and poor, expecting to find justice from you.
voices.who: Hadji Hayden Hassan and Kustar Ogli Ismael, deputies sent by the Circassian tribes to plead their case in Britain, in their statement to the British public (English text as reprinted by Frederick Burnaby)
voices.date: 1862–63 (undated; the statement says the Crimean War ended 'seven years ago')
voices.doc: Statement of the Circassian Deputies in reference to the Crimean War, in F. Burnaby, On Horseback through Asia Minor, vol. 2 (London, 1877), Appendix X, pp. 354–360

witness.text: A Russian detachment having captured the village of Toobeh on the Soobashi River, inhabited by about 100 Abadzekh, and after these had surrendered themselves prisoners, they were all massacred by the Russian troops. […] As the Russian troops gain ground on the coast, the natives are not allowed to remain there on any terms, but are compelled either to transfer themselves to the plains of the Kouban or emigrate to Turkey.
witness.who: Consul Dickson, British consul at Soukoum-Kalé (Sukhumi), reporting a deed that 'has come to my knowledge' (not seen himself), to Earl Russell (Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants in Turkey (presented to the House of Commons, 1864), in Accounts and Papers 1864, vol. LXIII, No. 4, p. 3)

witness.text: The probable immediate result of the present cruel war cannot be better illustrated than by a local saying, that "even a woman might now-a-days travel from Soudjouk-Kalé to Anapa without fear of meeting a single human being."
witness.who: Consul Dickson at Soukoum-Kalé, to Earl Russell (Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants, 1864, No. 2, p. 2)

witness.text: Amongst those who have reached, hundreds are labouring under disease, superinduced by famine and misery which they suffered previous to embarkation. […] From the best information obtainable, the mortality must have exceeded 3,500 between December and this date, of which, emigrants 3,000, Turks 470, Greeks 36, Armenians 17, Catholics 9, and Europeans 6.
witness.who: Consul Stevens, British consul at Trebizond, to Earl Russell (Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants, 1864, No. 1, p. 1)

witness.text: The mortality amongst them averages from 120 to 150 per diem: 35,000 to 40,000 have been landed at Samsoon, and have infected that place to an alarming extent; as many as 500 deaths have recently occurred there in forty-eight hours. […] As many as 200,000 more are reported ready to quit their country, and Russia insists upon their leaving by the end of May, old style.
witness.who: Consul Stevens at Trebizond, to Earl Russell (Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants, 1864, No. 15, p. 11); the same despatch blames the emigrants' own habits for the spread of disease

witness.text: The continued advances of the Russians in Circassia, and the ill-treatment experienced by the natives from the Russian troops, have led to an almost complete emigration from the country: 25,000 have already reached Trebizond, and others are endeavouring to escape in small boats at every risk. […] the loss of life which is occasioned by their hazardous attempts to escape from their conquerors is shocking to humanity.
witness.who: Sir Henry Bulwer, British ambassador at Constantinople, to Earl Russell, forwarding the Circassian petition (Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants, 1864, No. 3, p. 2)

witness.text: It is apparent that the Russian Government have long taken an absolute resolution at any risk to remove the whole of the mountaineers still in arms from their native places. […] The policy of Russia, though unrelenting, has not been deliberately sanguinary. There was no desire to exterminate the people; the object was to remove them.
witness.who: Lord Napier, British ambassador at St Petersburg, giving his own view to Earl Russell, largely from Russian official information (Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants, 1864, No. 13, p. 9)

official.text: The Vice-Chancellor replied that the tribes had insisted on leaving the country; that the Imperial Government regretted it; that it was absolutely necessary to remove these people from their mountain fastnesses, where their predatory and martial habits would be incurable; but that a fair offer had been made to all to settle on lands in the plain, which they had rejected.
official.who: Prince Gorchakov, Russian foreign minister (Vice-Chancellor), as reported by the British ambassador Lord Napier to Earl Russell (Papers respecting the Settlement of Circassian Emigrants, 1864, No. 10, p. 6)

official.text: tous les versants septentrionaux de la chaîne, depuis la Laba jusqu'à la mer, et les versants méridionaux, depuis l'embouchure du Kouban jusqu'à l'ancien fort Véliaminow, étaient nettoyés des populations hostiles. […] Quoique l'on ne puisse pas affirmer que la guerre du Caucase soit complètement terminée avant que nos soldats aient parcouru tous les défilés des montagnes et en aient expulsé les derniers habitants, il est à espérer du moins que nous ne rencontrerons plus de résistance opiniâtre nulle part […]
official.who: The Russian official Journal de St-Pétersbourg, reporting the spring campaign (in French; in plain English: by early spring all the northern slopes of the range from the Laba to the sea, and the southern slopes from the mouth of the Kuban to the old fort Veliaminov, 'were cleared of hostile populations'; and although the Caucasian war could not be called completely over until the soldiers had gone through every mountain pass and 'expelled the last inhabitants', it was hoped there would be no more stubborn resistance anywhere). Printed as Inclosure in No. 12 (pp. 7–9) of the British Papers

official.text: L'autorité supérieure du Caucase propose spontanément aux montagnards qui se soumettent, de deux choses l'une; ou de s'établir sur les points qui leur sont assignés sur les bords du Kouban, ou bien émigrer en Turquie, alternative dans laquelle elle leur laisse une entière liberté de choix.
official.who: Official correction ('rectification communiquée') published in the Messager d'Odessa and reprinted in the Journal de St-Pétersbourg (in French; in plain English: the supreme authority of the Caucasus freely offers the mountaineers who submit one of two things, to settle at the points assigned to them on the banks of the Kuban or to emigrate to Turkey, leaving them entire freedom of choice). Inclosure in No. 14, p. 10

stories.note: Research in progress: Russia's present official position and the 21 May diaspora commemoration have not yet been checked against an official page. The Grand Duke Michael's order of the day ending the war was found only in an 1864 magazine article (Once a Week) whose archive.org copy carries an uploader's CC BY-NC-ND label, so it was not used. No text of the 1861 Circassian Mejlis declarations was found in a public-domain printing.
stories.warn: The Circassian words survive only in English translations made or printed by the British (translator not named), and the deputies' statement was written for a British audience. The French quotations are the Russian government's own published wording. Consular reports include hearsay (Dickson's Toobeh report) and the prejudices of the time (Stevens calls the emigrants indolent and blames them for the disease). The texts describe massacre, epidemic and death on a large scale. The 'today' quotation is in Georgian with a plain-English gloss.
disputed: How many left and how many died? In May 1864 the Russian Minister of War spoke of 100,000 emigrants and foreign newspapers of 300,000; Lord Napier thought it might exceed 150,000; Consul Stevens reported 200,000 more ready to leave. Britannica today gives some 400,000 emigrants, with many thousands dying of starvation and disease on the way. The Grand Duke Michael, as Napier reported, said the distress on the Russian side had been exaggerated and that no epidemic prevailed there, the suffering coming on the voyage and at Trebizond. The Ottoman government had already spent £200,000 on the refugees, the British ambassador reported.

Choice, expulsion or extermination? Russian official statements say the mountaineers who submitted were given entire freedom to choose between the Kuban plain and Turkey, and Gorchakov said the tribes insisted on leaving; Consul Dickson reported that on the coast they were not allowed to remain on any terms, and the petition speaks of slaughter. Lord Napier judged that Russia had resolved to remove all the mountaineers still in arms but did not wish to exterminate them. In 2011 the Parliament of Georgia recognised the mass destruction and expulsion as genocide. Whether the term applies is not settled here and the Genocide theme is left off.

Who bears the blame for the deaths? Bulwer blamed Russian ill-treatment; Napier reported that the Turks had greatly encouraged the emigration and then asked Russia to slow it, and that the Grand Duke blamed Turkish mismanagement at Trebizond; Stevens blamed the emigrants' own habits; Dickson pointed also to famine, cattle plague and the blood feuds that kept the tribes divided.
stories.blind: The Circassians speak here only through a petition and a deputies' statement translated into English for British readers; no account by the refugees in the Trebizond and Samsun camps, by the women and children sold there, or by the Ubykh, whose language later died out, was found in a public-domain copy. The Russian government's version survives in its own official newspaper, and British consuls and ambassadors wrote the rest.

Correspondence respecting trade with the eastern coast of the Black Sea, in Accounts and Papers vol. LXXV (1863, archive.org)

stories.title: The Pequot War
stories.where: Pequot country between the Connecticut and Pawcatuck rivers; pin: the Pequot fort at Mystic (Mistick), Connecticut, USA (approximate)
facts: The Pequot War was fought in 1636–37 by the Pequot against English settlers from the Massachusetts Bay, Connecticut and Saybrook colonies and their Native allies, including the Narragansett and Mohegan, and it eliminated the Pequot as an impediment to English colonization of southern New England.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pequot-War

The Pequot had themselves subjugated dozens of other tribes in the 1620s and early 1630s in an attempt to control the region's fur and wampum trade, and by 1635 they controlled modern-day Connecticut and eastern Long Island; resentment among those tribes led them to seek alliance with the newly arrived English.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pequot-War

The Pequot killed the trader John Stone and his crew in early 1634, giving explanations that suggested they saw the killing as justified; after another trader, John Oldham, was found murdered off Block Island in July 1636, a killing assumed to be the work of Manisses Indians, Massachusetts Bay sent about 90 soldiers under John Endecott, who burned villages and cornfields on Block Island and in Pequot territory, and the Pequot answered by besieging the English fort at Saybrook.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pequot-War

Connecticut declared war on 1 May 1637 after a Pequot attack on Wethersfield, the first time women and children were killed in the war; during the Mistick campaign of 10–26 May 1637 an English force of 77 Connecticut soldiers with as many as 250 Native allies attacked and burned the fortified Pequot village at Mistick, where some 400 Pequot, including an estimated 175 women and children, were killed in less than an hour, half of them burned to death.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pequot-War
In the following months the English pursued the fleeing Pequot communities, executing leaders and fighting men and enslaving women and children, until the Swamp Fight at Fairfield ended the war.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pequot-War

Under the treaty made at Hartford in 1638 between Connecticut, the Narragansett and the Mohegan, the surviving Pequots were divided between the Narragansett and Mohegan sachems, were not to live in their ancient country nor be called by their ancient name, and their land was to be the property of the English of Connecticut.
https://archive.org/stream/historyofindians00defo/historyofindians00defo_djvu.txt

voices.text: Could ye blame us for revenging so cruel a murder? for we distinguish not between the Dutch and English, but took them to be one nation, and therefore we do not conceive that we wronged you, for they slew our king; and thinking these captains to be of the same nation and people as those that slew him, made us set upon this course of revenge. […] We know no difference between the Dutch and the English; they are both strangers to us, we took them to be all one; therefore we crave pardon; we have not wilfully wronged the English.
voices.who: A Pequot ambassador, 'a grave senior', sent aboard Endecott's ships to explain the killing of Captain Stone (the Pequot said Dutch traders had killed their sachem after taking his ransom), as recorded by Captain John Underhill, an officer of the English force; a marginal note in Underhill's book calls the story a 'devised excuse'
voices.doc: John Underhill, Newes from America (London, 1638), reprinted in C. Orr (ed.), History of the Pequot War (Cleveland, 1897), pp. 57–58

voices.text: Then they said, Have you fought enough? We said we knew not yet. Then they asked if we did use to kill women and children? We said they should see that hereafter. So they were silent a small space, and then they said, We are Pequits, and have killed Englishmen, and can kill them as mosquetoes, and we will go to Conectecott and kill men, women, and children, and we will take away the horses, cows and hogs.
voices.who: Pequot warriors parleying outside the besieged English fort at Saybrook, as recorded by its commander, Lieutenant Lion Gardener, through the interpreter Thomas Stanton ('we' is Gardener and Stanton)
voices.date: early 1637, during the siege of Saybrook fort
voices.doc: Lion Gardener, Relation of the Pequot Warres (written 1660), in Orr (ed.), History of the Pequot War (1897), pp. 131–132

witness.text: Our Indians came to us, and much rejoiced at our victories, and greatly admired the manner of Englishmen's fight, but cried Mach it, mach it; that is, It is naught, it is naught, because it is too furious, and slays too many men.
witness.who: The Native allies of the English (Narragansett and Mohegan warriors; Underhill calls them 'our Indians') after the burning of the Mystic fort, as recorded by Captain John Underhill (Newes from America, 1638; Orr ed. 1897, p. 84)

witness.text: 5. That the assault would be in the night, when they are commonly more secure and at home, by which advantage the English, being armed, may enter the houses and do what execution they please. 6. That before the assault be given, an ambush be laid behind them, between them and the swamp, to prevent their flight, &c. […] 8. That it would be pleasing to all natives, that women and children be spared, &c.
witness.who: Advice of the Narragansett to the English (their sachem Miantonomo had lately held council at Williams's house) before the Mystic attack, as gathered and written down by Roger Williams, the Providence minister who mediated with them, in a letter to Governor John Winthrop (Letters of Roger Williams, Narragansett Club, 1874, pp. 18–19; the long s of that printing is transcribed as s)
witness.date: May 1637 (the 1874 editor dates the letter to about 22 May)

witness.text: for so are we all Indians as the English are, and say brother to one another; so must we be one as they are, otherwise we shall be all gone shortly, for you know our fathers had plenty of deer and skins, our plains were full of deer, as also our woods, and of turkies, and our coves full of fish and fowl. But these English having gotten our land, they with scythes cut down the grass, and with axes fell the trees; their cows and horses eat the grass, and their hogs spoil our clam banks, and we shall all be starved
witness.who: Miantonomo, Narragansett sachem and former English ally, urging the Montauk of Long Island to join a general rising against the English; spoken to the Montauk elders while their sachem Wyandanch was away, passed on to Wyandanch and by him to Lion Gardener, who wrote it down and opposed the rising (Relation, written 1660; Orr ed. 1897, pp. 142–143); the speech continues with a call to attack the English

official.text: But God was above them, who laughed his Enemies and the Enemies of his People to Scorn, making them as a fiery Oven: Thus were the Stout Hearted spoiled, having slept their last Sleep, and none of their Men could find their Hands: Thus did the Lord judge among the Heathen, filling the Place with dead Bodies!
official.who: Captain John Mason, commander of the Connecticut force at Mystic, A Brief History of the Pequot War (written about 1670, first printed 1736; Orr ed. 1897, p. 30)

official.text: It may be demanded, Why should you be so furious? (as some have said). Should not Christians have more mercy and compassion? But I would refer you to David's war. When a people is grown to such a height of blood, and sin against God and man, and all confederates in the action, there he hath no respect to persons, but harrows them, and saws them, and puts them to the sword, and the most terriblest death that may be. Sometimes the Scripture declareth women and children must perish with their parents. Sometimes the case alters; but we will not dispute it now. We had sufficient light from the word of God for our proceedings.
official.who: Captain John Underhill, commander of the Massachusetts Bay men at Mystic, answering critics of the killing (Newes from America, 1638; Orr ed. 1897, pp. 81–82)

official.text: It was a fearfull sight to see them thus frying in the fyer, and the streams of blood quenching the same, and horrible was the stinck and sente ther of; but the victory seemed a sweete sacrifice, and they gave the prays therof to God, who had wrought so wonderfuly for them, thus to inclose their enimise in their hands, and give them so speedy a victory over so proud and insulting an enimie.
official.who: William Bradford, governor of Plymouth Colony, Of Plymouth Plantation, in W. T. Davis's edition (1908), pp. 339–340

stories.note: Research in progress: no Connecticut or US government acknowledgement was found. The 1638 Treaty of Hartford is summarised from De Forest (1851); its original text was not found in a public-domain printing.
stories.warn: Every Native word on this card was written down by English colonists, two of them commanders who fought the Pequot, and some came through an interpreter; Underhill's own margin dismisses the Pequot ambassador's account. The texts keep 17th-century spelling (Pequits, Conectecott, fyer) and the colonists' religious language, and they describe people burned to death.
disputed: How many died at Mystic? Mason wrote six or seven hundred, 'as some of themselves confessed', with seven captured and about seven escaped; Underhill wrote that by the Pequots' own report about four hundred were in the fort and not above five escaped; Bradford wrote about 400. Britannica gives some 400, including an estimated 175 women and children.

Massacre or just war? Mason and Underhill presented the burning as God's judgment and Underhill cited Scripture for killing women and children; the Narragansett allies, by Underhill's own account, cried that it was too furious and slew too many, and their leaders had asked through Roger Williams that women and children be spared. Britannica calls it the Mistick Massacre.

Who started it? Britannica says the immediate cause is often given as the killing of English traders, but that those deaths were the culmination of decades of conflict between Native peoples made worse by the Dutch and English; the Pequot explained Stone's death as revenge for a Dutch killing of their sachem, while Underhill called that a devised excuse. Allies were not only victims: the Narragansett advised a night assault and an ambush to cut off flight, and Bradford says they stood aloof and stopped any who broke away.
stories.blind: No Pequot account of the war in their own hand survives in these sources; Pequot words reach us only as written by the men who besieged and burned them, Underhill and Gardener, and Narragansett counsel only through Roger Williams and Gardener. The women and children killed at Mystic and those enslaved afterwards are counted, not heard, while the English commanders and Plymouth's governor wrote full narratives and the 1638 treaty even forbade the survivors their name.
reading: Charles Orr (ed.), History of the Pequot War: the contemporary accounts of Mason, Underhill, Vincent and Gardener (1897, archive.org)
William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation, ed. W. T. Davis (1908, archive.org)
Letters of Roger Williams, 1632–1682 (Narragansett Club, 1874, archive.org)
J. W. De Forest, History of the Indians of Connecticut (1851, archive.org)

today.text: Framed against the sky, the lone tree on a knoll represents Mashantucket, the “much wooded land” where the Pequots hunted and kept alive their identity as an independent people. Displayed on the knoll is the signature of Robin Cassasinnamon, the Pequots’ first leader following the 1637 massacre at Mystick Fort.
today.who: Mashantucket Pequot Museum and Research Center (tribally owned), describing the seal of the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation

stories.title: The Potosí mita
stories.where: Potosí and the Cerro Rico silver mountain, Bolivia (with the Huancavelica mercury mines, Peru)
facts: Silver was discovered at Potosí in 1545 and the city quickly became famous for its wealth: within three decades its population passed 150,000, making it the largest city in the New World, and it peaked at 160,000 about 1650.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Potosi-Bolivia

Viceroy Francisco de Toledo (1569–81) made Indigenous chieftains responsible for collecting tribute and providing forced labour, and the Huancavelica mines, opened in 1563, produced the mercury essential to processing Potosí's silver efficiently.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Peru/Discovery-and-exploration-by-Europeans

Under the Inca, most people performed their mit'a (labour turn) in or near their home communities, often in agriculture, and service in mines was extremely rare; under Toledo, communities had to provide one seventh of their male labour force at any one time for public works, mines and agriculture.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mita_(Inca)

Toledo turned the mita into an annual forced migration to Potosí: in 1578 it was decided that more than 14,000 natives and their families would be required to work in the mines for a wage set below the market rate, and the families' earnings went mostly to pay the men's tribute.

https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-review-of-social-history/article/free-and-unfree-labour-in-the-colonial-andes-in-the-sixteenth-and-seventeenth-centuries/B00B9D39F97F968E9F6655462D8FB723

Mitayos were never the whole workforce: a description of 1603 counts around 58,800 Indians working in Potosí, of whom 5,100 were mitayos, 10,500 contracted workers (mingas) and 43,200 free wage earners, but the mitayos had to do tasks others did not want, such as carrying ore up ladders, for a lower wage; by the end of the colonial period nearly half the labourers were mitayos.

https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-review-of-social-history/article/free-and-unfree-labour-in-the-colonial-andes-in-the-sixteenth-and-seventeenth-centuries/B00B9D39F97F968E9F6655462D8FB723

The economist Melissa Dell describes the mita as an extensive forced mining labour system in effect in Peru and Bolivia between 1573 and 1812, and her study finds that districts once subjected to it have lower household consumption and more stunted growth in children today.
https://www.econometricsociety.org/publications/econometrica/2010/11/01/persistent-effects-perus-mining

voices.text: En las dichas minas de Guancabilca de azogue es adonde tiene tanto castigo los yndios pobres y rreciuen tormentos y mucho muerte de yndios. Adonde se acaua y pasa tormentos los caciques prencipales deste rreyno, acimismo en todas las demás minas de Potocí de plata y de Chocllo Cocha de plata y de Carauaya de oro y minas de otras partes destos rreynos.
voices.who: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, an Andean (Indigenous) nobleman, in his chronicle addressed to King Philip III. Plain gloss: in the mercury mines of Huancavelica the poor Indians are punished, tormented and many die; there the principal chiefs of this kingdom are worn down and tormented, and so too in the silver mines of Potosí and Choclococha, the gold mines of Carabaya and the other mines of these kingdoms
voices.doc: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (autograph manuscript, Royal Library of Denmark, GKS 2232 4º), 'Capítulo de los mineros', p. 526 [530]
voices.lic: Public domain (autograph manuscript, about 1615, Royal Library of Denmark). Wording checked against the manuscript page image (https://poma.kb.dk/permalink/2006/poma/530/es/image/); spelling is Guaman Poma's, while expanded abbreviations (yñs = yndios), word division and punctuation follow the library's online transcription

voices.text: Y otros se huyen de las dichas minas, otros de los caminos por no llegar a las dichas minas y por no murir muerte supitania. Antes quieren yr a murir que a biuir y dizen que le acauen una ues porque, en cogiendo el mal de azogado, se seca como palo y tiene asma y no puede de día ni de noche beuir. Y dura un año o dos desta manera y se muere.
voices.who: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Andean nobleman and chronicler, on why people flee the mine draft. Plain gloss: others run away from the mines, or from the road, so as not to reach the mines and die a sudden death; they say they would rather it finished them at once, because whoever catches the mercury sickness dries up like a stick, has asthma and cannot live by day or night; it lasts a year or two and he dies
voices.doc: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (autograph manuscript, Royal Library of Denmark, GKS 2232 4º), 'Mineros', p. 527 [531]
voices.lic: Public domain (autograph manuscript, about 1615, Royal Library of Denmark). Wording checked against the manuscript page image (https://poma.kb.dk/permalink/2006/poma/531/es/image/); spelling is Guaman Poma's, while expanded abbreviations (dhas = dichas, q = que), word division and punctuation follow the library's online transcription

witness.text: They labour in these mines in continuall darknes and obscuritie, without knowledge of day or night. And forasmuch as those places are never visited with the Sunne, there is not onely a continual darkness, but also an extreme colde, with so grosse an aire contrary to the disposition of man, so as such as newly enter are sicke as they at sea. […] A man carries ordinarily the weight of two arrobas of mettall vpon his shoulders, tied together in a cloth in maner of a skippe, and so mount they three and three. He that goes before carries a candle tied to his thumb, for, as it is said, they have no light from heaven, and so go they vp the ladder holding it with both their handes
witness.who: José de Acosta, a Spanish Jesuit who lived in Peru and went down one of the Potosí mines himself, Natural and Moral History of the Indies (Seville, 1590), book IV, chapter 8, in Edward Grimston's English translation of 1604 (Hakluyt Society edition, 1880, pp. 207–208; an arroba is about 25 lb)

official.text: De los indios que van á labrar las minas de Potosí, la orden que se tuvo en repartirlos y la que se dio en su manera de servicio y trabajo, acrecentamiento de doctrinas, pagos de sus jornales y como y en que moneda se los habian de pagar y que cantidad cada dia y ante que justicia para que no pudiesen ser maltratados ni dejados de pagar, está dada al real Consejo una muy larga relación […] y que antes reciban los naturales provecho en lo espiritual y temporal que no daño
official.who: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, who organised the Potosí mita, in the memorial he gave King Philip II on the state in which he left Peru (Relaciones de los vireyes y audiencias que han gobernado el Perú, vol. 1, Lima 1867, section XXIII, p. 24). Plain gloss: the order for assigning the Indians who go to work the Potosí mines, their service and work, more religious teaching, the payment of their day-wages, in what coin and how much a day and before which judge, so that they could not be ill-treated or left unpaid, has been sent to the Royal Council in a long report; [in the omitted words Toledo asks the king to have it reviewed and not to let more Indians be added to the Potosí draft, though some press for it,] so that the natives receive benefit, spiritual and material, rather than harm
official.date: about 1582 (written after his 13 years as viceroy from 1569)

official.text: Quedan abolidas las mitas, ó mandamientos, ó repartimientos de Indios, y todo servicio personal, que bajo de aquellos ú otros nombres presten á los particulares, sin que por motivo ó pretexto alguno puedan los Jueces ó Gobernadores destinar ó compeler á aquellos naturales al expresado servicio.
official.who: The Spanish Cortes (parliament) at Cádiz, Decree CCVII 'Abolición de las mitas', article I (Colección de los decretos y órdenes ... de las Cortes, vol. 3, Madrid 1820). Plain gloss: the mitas, mandamientos or repartimientos of Indians and all personal service rendered to private persons under those or other names are abolished, and no judge or governor may assign or force the natives into that service for any reason

today.text: By the 17th century there were 160,000 colonists living in Potosí along with 13,500 Indians who were forced to work in the mines under the system of mita (mandatory labour).
today.who: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'City of Potosí', site description (inscribed 1987; on the List of World Heritage in Danger since 2014). © UNESCO; description licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/igo/)

stories.note: Research in progress: no petition or complaint by mitayos or their kurakas (chiefs) was found in a public-domain printing within the time allowed; Guaman Poma is the only Andean voice here. The Dominican friar Domingo de Santo Tomás's letter of 1 July 1550, which called Potosí a 'boca del infierno' (mouth of hell) before the mita began, is printed only in J. M. Vargas (Quito, 1937) and in a 2018 draft English translation by Kris Lane on Tulane's Friends of Potosí site (no licence stated), so it is linked in reading, not quoted. Both Guaman Poma passages were checked word for word against the manuscript page images on the Royal Library's site (GKS 2232 4º, pp. 526 [530] and 527 [531]); only the editors' expansions of abbreviations, word division and punctuation come from the library's transcription.
stories.warn: The Spanish quotations keep their original spelling (Guaman Poma writes rreyno, yndios, trauajo, azogue = mercury; the 1812 decree uses ó and ú). The glosses in 'who' are the site's plain summaries, not translations. Acosta's English is Grimston's of 1604. Toledo's memorial is his own defence of his government, written for the king.
disputed: How many died? Wikipedia's Cerro Rico article reports the belief that around eight million miners died in total; it adds that other sources estimate 'hundreds of thousands', and that eight million was the total number of deaths in the whole Viceroyalty of Peru, not just the Potosí mines, and that historians such as Peter Bakewell, Noble David Cook, Enrique Tandeter and Raquel Gil Montero give completely different estimates. Gil Montero gives no death toll, though she lists 'a significant increase in mortality rates' among the main facts affecting the native population; Carpio and Guerrero (2021), using surname data, argue that the mita 'caused the decimation of the native-born male population'.

Did people flee the mita? Guaman Poma wrote that people abandoned their towns and ran away on the road to escape it, and Gil Montero notes that this was the traditional explanation for the growing number of migrants (forasteros); she writes that recent research shows many migrants were working in other mines and paying tribute and the cost of their replacement under the mita, and that during the seventeenth century people migrated chiefly because of colonial obligations.

Does the mita still shape the region? Dell (2010) finds lower household consumption and more child stunting today in districts once subject to the mita; Abad and Maurer (2025), using data on 500 Indigenous settlements, find that forced labour severely harmed the communities but that the effects nearly disappeared by the end of the colonial period, with no significant later 'reversal of fortune'.
stories.blind: The viceroy who built the system, the Cortes that ended it, Jesuit and Dominican clerics and UNESCO all speak in this record; the only Andean voice found in print is Guaman Poma, a nobleman writing to the king, not a mitayo. The men who climbed the ladders, and the wives and children who travelled with them to Potosí, appear as counts (14,000, 13,500, 5,100), not in their own words; petitions by their kurakas survive mainly in Spanish archives, unpublished or in modern copyrighted editions.
reading: Guaman Poma, Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (Royal Library of Denmark, facsimile and transcription)
Raquel Gil Montero, 'Free and Unfree Labour in the Colonial Andes in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries' (International Review of Social History, 2011)
