stories.title: The Stolen Generations
stories.where: Australia, every state and territory; pin: the Cootamundra Training Home for Aboriginal girls, New South Wales (approximate)
facts: Western Australia's Aborigines Act 1905 made the Chief Protector of Aborigines the legal guardian of every Aboriginal child to the age of 16 and permitted authorities to 'send and detain' Aboriginal children in institutions and in 'service' (work); it governed Aboriginal lives in the state for nearly 60 years, until it was repealed in 1964.
https://www.findandconnect.gov.au/entity/aborigines-act-1905/

In New South Wales the Aborigines Protection Board had sought the power to remove children, but the 1909 Act gave it only the powers that applied to neglected white children; the 1915 amendments gave it the power to remove any Indigenous child at any time and for any reason, and led to thousands of children being taken from their parents on the basis of race alone.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/aborigines-protection-act

Babies were sent to the United Aborigines Mission Home at Bomaderry, girls to the Cootamundra Girls Home and boys to the Kinchela Aboriginal Boys Training Home; the Board said the children received care and education, but oral histories from the children show the homes to be harsh and desolate places, the children were brought up to reject their Aboriginal heritage, and abuse was widespread.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/aborigines-protection-act

Because of poor record keeping no one knows how many children were removed: the historian Peter Read has suggested that up to 50,000 'would not be unreasonable', and the 1997 Bringing Them Home report suggested that at most one in three and at least one in ten Indigenous children were removed.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/aborigines-protection-act

Aboriginal people organised against the removals: in early 1925 Fred Maynard and others helped Aboriginal families at Nambucca Heads rescue their own children from the Board's custody on Stuart Island, and the Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association he launched demanded that children no longer be separated from their families or indentured as domestics and menial labourers.
https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/maynard-charles-frederick-fred-11095

The NSW Aborigines Protection Act was repealed in 1969; a main recommendation of the 1997 Bringing Them Home report was a national apology to the Stolen Generations, which the Australian Government made on 13 February 2008.
https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/aborigines-protection-act

voices.text: As it is the proud boast of Australia that every person born beneath the Southern Cross is born free, irrespective of origin, race, color, creed, religion or any other impediment we, the representatives of the original people, in conference assembled, demand that we shall be accorded, the same full right, and privileges of citizenship as are enjoyed by all other sections of the community.
voices.who: Resolution of the Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association, read by 'the president' (the report does not make clear whether this was the chairman, Kempsey branch president Eugene Miranda, or the association's president Fred Maynard, who had just spoken) and carried unanimously at its Kempsey conference, attended, the paper says, by about 200 Aboriginal people. Printed in the Macleay Chronicle (Kempsey), 7 October 1925, pp. 4 and 8, in an unsigned contributed report
voices.doc: 'Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association', The Macleay Chronicle, 7 October 1925, p. 8 (Trove)

witness.text: He declared that on the North Coast of New South Wales he had found 60 native men, women, and children suffering from starvation. The public did not hear of these conditions because there was a "hush" policy. He said that help from the police was not sought, as it was feared that the children would be taken from their parents. That was considered crueller than starvation.
witness.who: The chief spokesman (not named in the report) of a deputation of seven Aboriginal members of the Australian Aborigines Progressive Association, two of them women, meeting the Bishop Coadjutor of Sydney and the chairman of the Australian Board of Missions; his words are given in indirect speech by the Sydney correspondent of the Christchurch Press (Press, 7 December 1927, Papers Past; a shorter cable in the Hawke's Bay Tribune, 16 November 1927, calls the spokesman the association's president). Published 1927, public domain

official.text: The Board may assume full control and custody of the child of any aborigine, if after due inquiry it is satisfied that such a course is in the interest of the moral or physical welfare of such child. The Board may thereupon remove such child to such control and care as it thinks best. The parents of any such child so removed may appeal against any such action on the part of the Board to a Court as defined in the Neglected Children and Juvenile Offenders Act, 1905, in a manner to be prescribed by regulations.
official.who: Parliament of New South Wales, Aborigines Protection Amending Act 1915 (Act No. 2, 1915, assented to 15 February 1915), section 4, inserting section 13A into the Aborigines Protection Act 1909 (Government Printer's official print, p. 122, archived copy of the NSW Government's PDF; New South Wales Crown copyright in a work published in 1915 has expired). The National Museum of Australia's reproduction prints 'moral and physical'; the official print reads 'moral or physical'

official.text: The object of the Board is to rescue these children from the environment of camp life, where they have little chance of reaching 15 or 16 years of age without getting into trouble, and to afford them an opportunity to earn their own living and reach years of discretion in good surroundings and under helpful influences before they are thrown on their own responsibility. Some criticism of this system has found expression, it being contended that the separation of the sexes will only tend to expedite the passing of the Aboriginal race. The Board, however, takes a very different view. Its object is to save the children from certain moral degradation on the Reserves and Camps, and give them a chance to reach maturity, after which they are given every facility to return either on holiday or permanently, according to their wish, to their own districts, where they are expected to take up suitable employment.
official.who: New South Wales Board for Protection of Aborigines, annual report for the year ended 30 June 1925 (dated 11 December 1925; NSW Legislative Assembly paper, printed 14 January 1926), section 'Cootamundra Home', p. 2 (National Library of Australia digitised copy; NSW Crown copyright in a paper published in 1926 has expired, though the library lists its copyright as undetermined)

today.text: We apologise for the laws and policies of successive Parliaments and governments that have inflicted profound grief, suffering and loss on these our fellow Australians. We apologise especially for the removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families, their communities and their country. For the pain, suffering and hurt of these Stolen Generations, their descendants and for their families left behind, we say sorry.
today.who: Prime Minister Kevin Rudd, 'Apology to Australia's Indigenous Peoples', motion moved in the House of Representatives, Canberra (PM Transcripts, transcript 15758; licensed from the Commonwealth of Australia under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Licence)

stories.note: Research in progress: no words of a removed child or of a parent written or printed before 1931 were found; the survivors' testimonies collected for the 1997 Bringing Them Home report are not quoted because the report is excluded from the Australian Human Rights Commission's Creative Commons licence and carries an 'all rights reserved' notice (it is described in facts and linked in reading). Living survivors are not named. Australian Hansard (CC BY-NC-ND) is not quoted; the 2008 apology comes from PM Transcripts (CC BY 4.0). Section 13A is quoted from the official 1915 print (NSW Government PDF, Wayback capture of 31 January 2020); it reads 'moral or physical welfare', and the National Museum of Australia's reproduction ('moral and physical') differs on that word.
stories.warn: The documents use the racial language of their time ('aborigine', 'half-caste', 'camp life', 'the passing of the Aboriginal race'). The 1927 spokesman's words are a correspondent's indirect report, not his own text. This story concerns the removal of children from their families; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that linked sources may contain names and images of people who have died.
disputed: How many children? Bringing Them Home estimated between one in three and one in ten Indigenous children; Peter Read has suggested up to 50,000; Robert Manne has said the lower figure of one in ten is more likely, estimating 20,000 to 25,000 children over six decades; in April 2000 the federal minister John Herron tabled a report saying that, as 'only 10%' had been removed, they did not constitute a whole 'generation'. Manne defended the term as a metaphor for a collective experience.

Rescue or removal? The Board wrote in 1925 that its object was to rescue children from camp life, and the historian Keith Windschuttle has argued that the removals were done for the children's good and that the abuses have been exaggerated; many historians, including Read and Manne, reject this, and the National Museum notes oral histories describing the homes as harsh and desolate and abuse as widespread. The anthropologist Ron Brunton criticised the 1997 inquiry because testimony was not cross-examined; the inquiry's Sir Ronald Wilson replied that state governments themselves had acknowledged a lot of cruelty in applying the laws.

Was it genocide? Bringing Them Home found that the removals amounted to genocide under international law as well as systematic racial discrimination; in Kruger v Commonwealth the High Court rejected the plaintiffs' claim that the 1918 Northern Territory Aboriginals Ordinance authorised genocide as defined by the Convention; others dispute that the policies were intended to destroy Indigenous people, and Manne writes that the report's genocide argument has since been 'generally acknowledged' to be wrong in law, because cultural assimilation is not legally genocide, while comparing A. O. Neville's 'breeding out the colour' aims to Nazi racial views. The Genocide theme is left off this card because the question is in live dispute.

What have courts and governments decided? In Kruger v Commonwealth (1997) the High Court majority found the Northern Territory's 1918 Aboriginals Ordinance beneficial in intent and without the purpose of genocide; in Williams (NSW Court of Appeal, 2000) a claimant placed under the Board's control at the Bomaderry children's home lost a negligence claim because the court found no duty of care, and a Federal Court claim, Cubillo v Commonwealth (2000), was also heard; in 2007 Bruce Trevorrow, removed from his parents as a baby, became the first member of the Stolen Generations to be awarded compensation by a court (A$525,000; South Australia lost its appeal in 2010). New South Wales ran a compensation scheme from 2017 to 2022 (A$75,000 per survivor), and in 2021 the federal government announced a A$378 million fund offering A$75,000 payments to survivors from the Northern Territory, the Australian Capital Territory and Jervis Bay Territory.
stories.blind: The Protection Boards and Protectors wrote annual reports year after year, and governments, a royal commission and the 1997 inquiry produced the paper trail; the removed children themselves left almost nothing in print before 1931, and their later testimony (the heart of Bringing Them Home) cannot be quoted here for licence reasons. Aboriginal adults appear in the 1920s press mainly through the Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association, often summarised by white reporters; many records of individual removals were never made or were destroyed.
reading: Aborigines Protection Act: 1915, NSW Government gains power to remove Aboriginal children (National Museum of Australia, Defining Moments)

Bringing Them Home: Report of the National Inquiry into the Separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children from Their Families, 1997 (Australian Human Rights Commission; read online, not licensed for reuse)
Apology to Australia's Indigenous Peoples, 13 February 2008 (PM Transcripts)
Charles Frederick (Fred) Maynard, by Heather Goodall and John Maynard (Australian Dictionary of Biography)
Aborigines Act 1905, Western Australia (Find and Connect)
Reports of the NSW Aborigines Protection Board, 1894–1938 (National Library of Australia)

stories.title: The First Jewish Revolt and the destruction of Jerusalem
stories.where: Roman Judaea, Galilee and the cities of Syria; pin: the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, where the Second Temple was burned in 70. The last fortress, Masada, stands above the Dead Sea to the south
facts: The First Jewish Revolt (66–70 CE; the last fortress, Masada, held out until April 73) was a Jewish rebellion against Roman rule in Judaea. In the autumn of 66 the Jews drove the Romans out of Jerusalem and defeated a punitive force under Gallus, the imperial legate in Syria, in the pass of Beth-Horon, and a revolutionary government was set up. The emperor Nero sent Vespasian, later joined by his son Titus; the Romans took Galilee, where the historian Josephus commanded the Jewish forces, and Josephus surrendered after the fall of Jotapata.
https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Jewish-Revolt

The killing ran in both directions from the start. According to Josephus, the Roman garrison in Jerusalem surrendered its arms on a sworn promise of safety and was then cut down by Eleazar's men, with only the commander Metilius spared; on the same day the people of Caesarea killed more than 20,000 of their Jewish neighbours, Jewish bands then raided and burned Syrian villages and cities, and the Syrian cities killed Jews living among them, more than 13,000 at Scythopolis alone.
https://lexundria.com/j_bj/2.449-2.480/wst

Inside Jerusalem the rebel factions killed other Jews. Josephus writes that after the Idumaeans joined the Zealots, 8,500 dead lay in the Temple courts after one night, that the Idumaeans killed the high priests Ananus and Jesus, and that Zealots and Idumaeans together then put to death about 12,000 of the nobility.
https://penelope.uchicago.edu/josephus/war-4.html

Josephus writes that the Sicarii who held Masada came down at the feast of unleavened bread on the small town of Engaddi, drove out those who could resist, killed more than 700 women and children who could not flee, and carried the plunder back to the fortress.
https://lexundria.com/j_bj/4.398-4.409/wst

Titus besieged Jerusalem in April 70, around Passover, and the Romans built a wall round the city to starve it. By August 70 they had broken through the last defences, killed much of the remaining population and destroyed the Second Temple; Rome commemorated the victory with the Arch of Titus.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Siege-of-Jerusalem-70

Josephus, who was with the Roman army, writes that people who slipped out of the city to look for food, most of them poor and some of them fighting men, were caught, whipped, tortured and crucified before the walls, about 500 a day and sometimes more. He says Titus pitied them but let it continue because it was not safe to release so many captives and guarding them would tie up his men, and in the hope that the sight would bring the defenders to yield.
https://lexundria.com/j_bj/5.446-5.451/wst

After the fall, by Josephus's account, the soldiers killed the old and infirm; captives over seventeen were sent in chains to the mines of Egypt or to the provinces to die in the arenas, those under seventeen were sold, and 11,000 died of hunger while being sorted. He gives 97,000 captives for the whole war and 1,100,000 dead in the siege, totals that modern historians do not accept as they stand.
https://penelope.uchicago.edu/josephus/war-6.html

The fortress of Masada fell to the Romans under Flavius Silva on the fifteenth day of the month Xanthicus, which this edition dates to 73 (the year is argued; see Disputed). Josephus is the only source for what happened inside: he writes that 960 people, women and children included, died at one another's hands, and that two women and five children who had hidden underground survived.
https://penelope.uchicago.edu/josephus/war-7.html

voices.text: because it had so come to pass, that our city Jerusalem had arrived at an higher degree of felicity than any other city under the Roman government, and yet at last fell into the sorest of calamities again. Accordingly it appears to me, that the misfortunes of all men, from the beginning of the world, if they be compared to these of the Jews, are not so considerable as they were; while the authors of them were not foreigners neither. This makes it impossible for me to contain my lamentations.
voices.who: Josephus (Yosef ben Mattityahu), a priest of Jerusalem who commanded the rebel forces in Galilee, surrendered in 67 and wrote this history in Rome as a client of the Flavian emperors; by 'the authors of them' he means the Jewish rebel leaders, whom he blames for the ruin of the city
voices.date: written about 75–79, on the war of 66–70
voices.doc: Josephus, The Jewish War, Preface, section 4, translated by William Whiston (London, 1737)

voices.text: But what is still more terrible; there was one Jesus, the son of Ananus, a plebeian, and an husbandman, who, four years before the war began; and at a time when the city was in very great peace and prosperity; came to that feast whereon it is our custom for every one to make tabernacles to God in the temple, began on a sudden to cry aloud, “A voice from the east; a voice from the west; a voice from the four winds; a voice against Jerusalem, and the holy house; a voice against the bridegrooms, and the brides; and a voice against this whole people.” This was his cry, as he went about by day and by night, in all the lanes of the city.
voices.who: Jesus son of Ananus, a countryman who cried this in the streets of Jerusalem from four years before the war until a stone from a Roman engine killed him on the wall during the siege, as recorded by Josephus (the narration is Josephus's; he says the Roman procurator Albinus had the man whipped and released him as mad)
voices.doc: Josephus, The Jewish War, book 6, chapter 5, section 3, translated by William Whiston (London, 1737)

voices.text: לגאלת ציון
voices.who: Legend in Hebrew on a bronze coin struck by the rebel government in besieged Jerusalem in the fourth year of the revolt; in plain English: 'For the redemption of Zion'. Bronze coins from the earlier part of the revolt read 'Freedom of Zion'. These few words are the only ones on this card that come from the rebels themselves without passing through Josephus
voices.doc: Bronze coin of year 4 marked 'half' (catalogued by the project as a half shekel), Jerusalem mint, obverse legend, as published by the 'Judaism and Rome' research project (entry by Samuele Rocca)

voices.text: R. Johanan b. Zakkai once went out of Jerusalem, followed by R. Joshua, and seeing the destroyed Temple, R. Joshua said: "Woe to us, that this is destroyed, the only place where the sins of the Israelites were atoned!" R. Johanan corrected him, saying: "My son, do not grieve over it. We have other means of atonement as effective--namely, bestowal of favors, as it is written [Hosea, vi. 6]: 'For kindness I desired, and not sacrifice.'"
voices.who: Rabbinic memory of the years after the destruction: Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai, who by the same text was carried out of besieged Jerusalem in a coffin, and his disciple Joshua, as told in Aboth of Rabbi Nathan, a rabbinic compilation put together centuries after the event
voices.date: set soon after 70; compiled centuries later
voices.doc: Aboth of R. Nathan, in the passage headed 'Upon bestowal of favors', printed as the Tosephtha to Tract Aboth, Mishna B, in Michael L. Rodkinson (trans.), Babylonian Talmud, Book 5 (vols. IX and X), 1918 edition

witness.text: I have heard that the total number of the besieged, of every age and both sexes, amounted to six hundred thousand. All who were able bore arms, and a number, more than proportionate to the population, had the courage to do so. Men and women showed equal resolution, and life seemed more terrible than death, if they were to be forced to leave their country.
witness.who: Tacitus, Roman senator and historian, Histories, book 5, chapter 13, translated by A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb (1876); his account of the siege itself is lost, and the book is hostile to Jewish religion and customs

witness.text: Since we long ago, my generous friends, resolved never to be servants to the Romans, nor to any other than to God himself, who alone is the true and just lord of mankind; the time is now come that obliges us to make that resolution true in practice. And let us not at this time bring a reproach upon our selves for self contradiction; while we formerly would not undergo slavery, though it were then without danger; but must now, together with slavery, chuse such punishments also as are intolerable. I mean this upon the supposition that the Romans once reduce us under their power while we are alive. We were the very first that revolted from them; and we are the last that fight against them.
witness.who: Speech given by Josephus to Eleazar son of Jairus, leader of the Sicarii at Masada, on the night before the fortress fell. Josephus was not there and wrote in Rome under Flavian patronage; ancient historians composed such speeches, and this one is his composition, not a record of Eleazar's words (The Jewish War, book 7, chapter 8, section 6, translated by William Whiston, 1737)
witness.date: written about 75–79, on the spring of 73

witness.text: The populace was stationed below in the court, the senators on the steps, and the priests in the sanctuary itself. And though they were but a handful fighting against a far superior force, they were not conquered until a part of the temple was set on fire. Then they met death willingly, some throwing themselves on the swords of the Romans, some slaying one another, others taking their own lives, and still others leaping into the flames. And it seemed to everybody, and especially to them, that so far from being destruction, it was victory and salvation and happiness to them that they perished along with the temple.
witness.who: Cassius Dio, Roman senator and historian writing in Greek, Roman History, epitome of book 65 (66 in some numberings), chapter 6, in the Loeb Classical Library translation by Earnest Cary, vol. VIII (1925); this part of Dio survives only in a Byzantine abridgement
witness.date: written in the early 3rd century, on the year 70

official.text: Senatus populusq(ue) Romanus Imp(eratori) Tito Caesari divi Vespasiani f(ilio) Vespasian[o] Augusto pontif(ici) max(imo) trib(unicia) pot(estate) X imp(eratori) XVII [c]o(n)s(uli) VIII p(atri) p(atriae) principi suo quod praeceptis patri consiliisq(ue) et auspiciis gentem Iudaeorum domuit et urbem Hierusolymam omnibus ante se ducibus regibus gentibus aut frustra petitam aut omnino intemptatam delevit
official.who: The Senate and People of Rome, dedication of the lost Arch of Titus in the Circus Maximus (CIL VI 944), in Latin with the editors' expansions in brackets. In plain English: the Senate and People of Rome to the emperor Titus, their leader, because on his father's instructions, advice and auspices he subdued the Jewish people and destroyed the city of Jerusalem, which all generals, kings and peoples before him had either attacked in vain or never attempted. The stone is lost and the text survives in a medieval copy; Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BCE and Sosius in 37 BCE, so the claim of a first conquest does not hold (see Disputed)

official.text: But Titus said, that “Although the Jews should get upon that holy house, and fight us thence, yet ought we not to revenge ourselves on things that are inanimate, instead of the men themselves: and that he was not in any case for burning down so vast a work as that was: because this would be a mischief to the Romans themselves; as it would be an ornament to their government while it continued.”
official.who: Titus, commander of the Roman army and later emperor, at his council of war before the Temple was burned, as reported by Josephus, who was in his camp and whose history Titus approved for publication (The Jewish War, book 6, chapter 4, section 3, translated by William Whiston, 1737). This is the Flavian version of events; another ancient account says the opposite (see Disputed)

official.text: It can therefore be nothing certainly but the kindness of us Romans which hath excited you against us. Who in the first place have given you this land to possess; and in the next place have set over you Kings of your own nation; and in the third place have preserved the laws of your forefathers to you; and have withal permitted you to live either by yourselves, or among others, as it should please you. And, what is our chief favour of all, we have given you leave to gather up that tribute which is paid to God; with such other gifts that are dedicated to him.
official.who: Titus, addressing the rebel leaders John and Simon after the Temple had burned, in a speech written for him by Josephus (The Jewish War, book 6, chapter 6, section 2, translated by William Whiston, 1737); it sets out the Roman case that Rome had been generous and the rebels alone were to blame

today.text: After Judaea became a province of the Roman Empire, it was the refuge of the last survivors of the Jewish revolt, who chose death rather than slavery when the Roman besiegers broke through their defences. As such it has an emblematic value for the Jewish people.
today.who: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Brief synthesis' in the statement of Outstanding Universal Value for Masada (Israel), which is on the World Heritage List. This is the listing text of an international body, not a statement made by the State of Israel; it follows Josephus's account of the deaths, which some historians doubt (see Disputed)

disputed: How many died and were enslaved? Josephus gives 1,100,000 dead in the siege, most of them pilgrims caught in the city at Passover, and 97,000 captives in the whole war; he also reports a count of 115,880 bodies carried out through a single gate, and deserters' reports of 600,000 bodies of the poor thrown out at the gates. Tacitus gives the same number with a different meaning: he had heard that 600,000 people were besieged. As Wikipedia's survey reports the scholarship, Menahem Stern rejected the death toll as exaggerated, Seth Schwartz puts the whole population of Roman Palestine at about a million, roughly half of them Jews, and Guy Rogers estimates the siege dead in the tens of thousands, probably 20,000 to 30,000. The scholars cited there all reject Josephus's totals, and no agreed figure has replaced them; that very large numbers were killed and enslaved is not in dispute.

Did Titus want the Temple spared? Josephus says Titus told his council he would not burn it, that a soldier threw a firebrand without orders and that Titus tried to have the fire put out. The Christian chronicler Sulpicius Severus, writing about 400, says the reverse: that some of the council wished it kept as evidence of Roman moderation, but 'others and Titus himself' thought it should be overthrown so that the religion of the Jews and of the Christians might be more thoroughly subverted. Sulpicius may have drawn on the lost part of Tacitus's Histories, and a paper by Kelly Shannon-Henderson treats the passage as a possible fragment of Tacitus. Cassius Dio says only that the soldiers hung back from the Temple out of superstition and went in under compulsion from Titus, and he does not say who wanted it burned. As Wikipedia's survey reports the scholarship, most modern scholars reject Josephus's version (Lester Grabbe calls it unbelievable); some suggest he played down Titus's part to protect Titus's reputation, while Grabbe and Fausto Parente think he wished to discourage Jewish vengeance. Martin Goodman finds an accidental fire plausible in the dry heat of summer, and Doron Mendels holds that the Romans targeted the Temple as the centre of the rebellion. The question remains open.

What happened at Masada? Josephus, the only source, says the 960 defenders burned their goods, that ten men chosen by lot killed the rest and then one another, and that one of the surviving women told the Romans what had been said and done. The excavator Yigael Yadin (1963–65) found three skeletons in the northern palace and 25 in a cave, and suggested that the Romans had thrown the 25 there. Shaye Cohen argued in 1982 that the account is partly invented: the remains show many separate fires where Josephus has one, storerooms holding provisions were burnt although Josephus has Eleazar order the food spared, the 25 in the cave look like people who tried to hide, and the speeches and the orderly unanimous suicide serve literary ends; he concluded that at least some Sicarii killed themselves and that others may have hidden, fought or been killed by the Romans. Jodi Magness holds that archaeology can neither prove nor disprove Josephus; Menahem Stern accepted the suicide as historical. There is no consensus, and the date is also argued (spring 73 or 74).

Who was to blame? Josephus puts the destruction on the 'seditious temper' of the rebel leaders, whom he calls tyrants and robbers, and presents the Romans as unwilling destroyers; that view suited both his patrons and his own position as a commander who had changed sides. He also records Roman provocations himself, including the governor Florus's soldiers killing about 3,600 people in Jerusalem in 66 and crucifying Jews of equestrian rank. Britannica gives the causes as heavy taxation, resentment of imperial rule and conflict between Jews and Gentiles. The Senate's inscription for Titus presents the war simply as the taming of a people and claims a first conquest of Jerusalem, which Caroline Barron's commentary for the 'Judaism and Rome' project calls 'undeniably false', since Pompey took the city in 63 BCE and Sosius in 37 BCE.
stories.blind: Almost everything known about this war comes from one man, Josephus, who fought for the rebels, went over to the Romans and wrote under the emperors who destroyed Jerusalem; the leaders he blames, John of Gischala, Simon son of Gioras and the Zealot and Sicarii commanders, left no account of their own, and the words he gives them are his. What survives directly from the rebels is a few words stamped on their coins. The tens of thousands sold into slavery, sent to the mines or killed in the arenas left nothing, and the women and children of Jerusalem, Engaddi, Caesarea and Masada are counted, not heard. Rabbinic memory of the destruction was written down generations later. The Roman side survives in Tacitus (whose narrative of the siege is lost), in an abridged Cassius Dio, and in two arches of Titus, one still standing in Rome and one known only from a copied inscription. The Greek and Syrian townspeople who killed their Jewish neighbours, and those killed by Jewish raiders, speak nowhere.
reading: Flavius Josephus, The Wars of the Jews, trans. William Whiston (1737; University of Chicago, Penelope)
Tacitus, The Histories, book 5, trans. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb (1876; MIT Internet Classics Archive)
Cassius Dio, Roman History, epitome of book 65, trans. Earnest Cary (Loeb, 1925; LacusCurtius, University of Chicago)
Caroline Barron, The Arch of Titus in the Circus Maximus (CIL VI 944) (Judaism and Rome project)
Shaye J. D. Cohen, Masada: Literary Tradition, Archaeological Remains, and the Credibility of Josephus (1982; extract at PBS Frontline)
stories.warn: Josephus is both a voice of the defeated and a client of the victors: a Jerusalem priest and rebel general who surrendered, tried to talk the defenders into surrender during the siege and says himself, in his Life, that Titus signed his books and ordered them published. His speeches for Eleazar and for Titus are literary compositions, his numbers are not reliable, and he blames the rebel factions throughout. The English is William Whiston's of 1737, in the spelling and punctuation of that printing (chuse, our selves); later printings punctuate differently. The rabbinic passage is from Rodkinson's free and abridged translation (1918 edition) and the story was written down long after the event. The Latin inscription and the Hebrew coin legend are given in the original with a plain gloss, because no public-domain English version was found; the Latin is known only from a medieval copy of the lost stone. Dates vary between sources: Josephus puts the burning of the Temple on the 10th of the month Lous (Ab), Jewish tradition and Britannica on the 9th. The sources describe famine, crucifixion and the killing of children.
stories.note: Research in progress: the Talmud's account of the destruction (Gittin 55b–58a) is not quoted because no public-domain English translation of that tractate was found. Sulpicius Severus is summarised, not quoted. No statement by the State of Israel was looked up; the 'today' entry is UNESCO's. Modern estimates of the dead are taken from Wikipedia's survey of the scholarship, not from the books themselves.

stories.title: The Zanj rebellion
stories.where: The salt flats, canals and marshes of southern Iraq around Basra. The pin marks the modern district of Abu al-Khasib, south-east of Basra on the Shatt al-Arab, which shares its name with the canal (Nahr Abi al-Khasib) on which the rebel city of al-Mukhtara stood; it is approximate, because the site of the city has never been exactly identified
facts: Landowners of Basra had brought enslaved East Africans (the Zanj) to drain the salt marshes east of the city, where they were worked hard and fed little. In 869 Ali ibn Muhammad won over several of the work gangs by promising them freedom and wealth, and the revolt against the Abbasid caliphate lasted until 883.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Zanj-rebellion

Ali ibn Muhammad was not one of the Zanj and was not enslaved. Al-Tabari reports that he claimed descent from Ali ibn Abi Talib, that his real name was said to be Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahim of the Arab tribe of Abd al-Qays, that he grew up in Warzanin, a village near Rayy in Iran, lived for a time in Samarra among men of the caliph al-Muntasir's household, praising them in verse and asking for gifts, and had already tried to raise a following in Bahrain.
https://shamela.ws/book/9783/5418

According to al-Tabari, the leader went from one work site to the next taking the slaves with him (fifty at one, five hundred at another) and, when he had gathered them, swore to them that he would not betray or abandon them. He told the slaves to fetch whips, had the masters and overseers given five hundred lashes each, and released them on their oath not to reveal where he was or how many men he had; the same page says there were fifteen thousand slaves at the works across the Tigris that one of the released men went to warn.
https://shamela.ws/book/9783/5422

The rebels built a fortified capital, al-Mukhtara, in the salt flats, took the port of al-Ubulla, sacked Basra in 871, defeated the caliph's brother al-Muwaffaq in 872 and seized Wasit in 878, and they were joined by soldiers who changed sides and by discontented peasants.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Zanj-rebellion

Basra fell in September 871 and a massacre followed. Theodor Nöldeke (1892) wrote that the lowest estimate put the dead at 300,000, that the captured women and children were carried into slavery, that women of the houses of Ali and of the ruling Abbasid family were sold to the highest bidder, and that many of the rebels were said to have received ten slaves or more as their share; the figure of 300,000 is a medieval one and is not accepted today (see Disputed).
https://archive.org/stream/cu31924027985088/cu31924027985088_djvu.txt

Ali ibn Muhammad did not promise to end slavery: he promised his followers that they would have homes, money and slaves of their own, and the record shows the Zanj enslaving others and plundering villages and towns.
https://daily.jstor.org/what-was-the-zanj-rebellion

Al-Muwaffaq began a great offensive in 879, took the second rebel city, al-Mani'a, drove the rebels out of Khuzistan, and after a long siege of al-Mukhtara crushed the revolt in 883; Ali ibn Muhammad's head was carried to Baghdad.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Zanj-rebellion

Al-Tabari records that in the final fighting many Zanj were killed, drowned or captured, and that of about a thousand who were cut off and turned inland most died of thirst and the survivors were seized and enslaved by Bedouin.
https://shamela.ws/book/9783/5669

voices.text: فسألني عن أخبار غلمان الشورجيين وما يجري لكل غلام منهم من الدقيق والسويق والتمر وعمن يعمل في الشورج من الأحرار والعبيد، فأعلمته ذلك، فدعاني إلى ما هو عليه، فأجبته، فقال لي: احتل فيمن قدرت عليه من الغلمان، فأقبل بهم إلي ووعدني أن يقودني على من آتيه به منهم، وأن يحسن إلي
voices.who: Rayhan ibn Salih, one of the ghilman of the shurajiyyin, the men who ran the salt-flat works (ghilman covers slaves, servants and young men; the page does not use the word 'abd, slave, of Rayhan himself); he carried flour from Basra to his master's ghilman and was, the chronicler says, the first of them to join the leader; as recorded by al-Tabari (died 923), a scholar of Baghdad who wrote under the Abbasid caliphs, from the side that put the rebellion down; the page says only 'it is reported from Rayhan ibn Salih' and names no one who passed the account on. Plain gloss: he asked me about the ghilman of the salt-flat owners, how much flour, parched-grain meal and dates each slave was given, and who worked the salt flats, free men and slaves; I told him; he called me to his cause and I accepted; he said to me: win over whichever of the slaves you can and bring them to me; and he promised to put me in command of those I brought him and to treat me well
voices.doc: al-Tabari, Tarikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (History of the Prophets and Kings), year 255 AH, section 'Khuruj awwal Alawi bi'l-Basra'; ed. Muhammad Abu al-Fadl Ibrahim (Cairo, Dar al-Ma'arif, 2nd ed. 1967), vol. 9, p. 413, as transcribed by al-Maktaba al-Shamela
voices.lic: Public domain (Arabic text of the early 10th century). The wording follows the online transcription of the 1967 Cairo edition; commas and colons are the modern editor's. Quoted in Arabic because the only full English translation (SUNY Press, 1992) is in copyright

voices.text: قد أردت ضرب أعناقكم لما كنتم تأتون إلى هؤلاء الغلمان الذين استضعفتموهم وقهرتموهم، وفعلتم بهم ما حرم الله عليكم أن تفعلوه بهم، وجعلتم عليهم ما لا يطيقون، فكلمني أصحابي فيكم، فرأيت إطلاقكم
voices.who: Ali ibn Muhammad, leader of the revolt (himself neither Zanj nor enslaved), speaking to the slaves' masters whom he had seized, as recorded by al-Tabari, the Abbasid-side chronicler; the page does not name the informant for this speech. Plain gloss: I meant to cut off your heads for what you have been doing to these slaves, whom you treated as weak and crushed; you did to them what God has forbidden you to do to them and laid on them more than they can bear; but my companions spoke to me on your behalf, and I have decided to let you go
voices.doc: al-Tabari, Tarikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk, year 255 AH, section 'Khuruj awwal Alawi bi'l-Basra'; ed. Muhammad Abu al-Fadl Ibrahim (Cairo, Dar al-Ma'arif, 2nd ed. 1967), vol. 9, p. 414, as transcribed by al-Maktaba al-Shamela
voices.lic: Public domain (Arabic text of the early 10th century). The wording follows the online transcription of the 1967 Cairo edition; commas are the modern editor's

witness.text: L'insolence de l'armée des Zendj était telle qu'on y vendait à l'encan les femmes de la famille de Haçan, de Huçeïn et d'Abbas, les descendantes de Hachem, de Koreïch et des plus nobles familles arabes. Une jeune fille se vendait de deux à trois dirhems ; le crieur annonçait sa généalogie en ces termes: «Une telle, fille d'un tel, de telle famille!» Chaque noir possédait dix, vingt et même trente de ces femmes; elles servaient de concubines aux noirs et remplissaient auprès de leurs femmes les fonctions des plus humbles esclaves.
witness.who: Al-Mas'udi (died 956), historian from Baghdad who wrote some sixty years after the war ended, Muruj al-dhahab (Meadows of Gold), in the French translation of C. Barbier de Meynard, Les Prairies d'or, vol. 8 (Paris, 1874), p. 60. Plain gloss: the Zanj army was so insolent that women of the families of Hasan, Husayn and Abbas, descendants of Hashim and Quraysh and of the noblest Arab families, were sold in it by auction; a girl sold for two or three dirhams, and the crier called out her descent: 'So-and-so, daughter of so-and-so, of such a family!'; each black man owned ten, twenty, even thirty of these women, who served the men as concubines and their wives as the lowest slaves

witness.text: The work in such a case is very hard, and the supervision must be strict. The feeling of affection which in the East binds the slave very closely to the family in which he lives and has grown up, is here altogether wanting. On the other hand, among such masses of slaves working together there easily springs up a certain community of feeling, a common sense of embitterment against their masters, and, under favourable circumstances, a consciousness of their own strength; thus are combined the conditions of a powerful insurrection.
witness.who: Theodor Nöldeke, German orientalist, 'A Servile War in the East', in Sketches from Eastern History, translated by John Sutherland Black (London and Edinburgh, 1892), p. 149; an outside historian working from al-Tabari a thousand years later

witness.text: It was not till Monday that the Zenj took full possession. The massacre that followed was frightful. It is even alleged that many inhabitants were induced, by offers of quarter, to gather together at certain places, where they could more easily be cut down. The chief had vowed direst vengeance on the city which had deceived his hopes.
witness.who: Theodor Nöldeke on the sack of Basra in September 871, 'A Servile War in the East', in Sketches from Eastern History, translated by John Sutherland Black (1892), p. 159

official.text: كتب إليه كتابا يدعوه فيه إلى التوبة والإنابة إلى الله تعالى مما ركب من سفك الدماء وانتهاك المحارم وإخراب البلدان والأمصار، واستحلال الفروج والأموال، وانتحال ما لم يجعله الله له أهلا من النبوة والرسالة، ويعلمه أن التوبة له مبسوطة، والأمان له موجود، فإن هو نزع عما هو عليه من الأمور التي يسخطها الله، ودخل في جماعة المسلمين، محا ذلك ما سلف من عظيم جرائمه، وكان له به الحظ الجزيل في دنياه
official.who: Al-Tabari's report of the letter that Abu Ahmad al-Muwaffaq, the caliph's brother and commander of his armies, sent to the rebel leader before besieging al-Mukhtara (Tarikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk, year 267 AH; Cairo edition of 1967, vol. 9, p. 581); al-Tabari gives the letter's content, not its text, and names as his source Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Sahl, reporting from Muhammad ibn Hammad; the date and the source stand at the foot of the preceding page (p. 580, https://shamela.ws/book/9783/5588). Plain gloss: he wrote him a letter calling on him to repent and turn back to God from what he had done, the shedding of blood, the violation of what is sacred, the ruin of lands and cities, the taking of women and property as if lawful, and the claim to prophethood and a divine mission for which God had not made him fit; and telling him that repentance was open to him and safe-conduct ready: if he gave up the things that anger God and joined the community of the Muslims, that would wipe out his great past crimes and he would have a rich share in this world. The page goes on to say that the leader read the letter and gave no answer

disputed: Was it a slave revolt? Nöldeke (1892) called it a 'servile war' and compared it with the slave wars of the late Roman republic, and Britannica describes a revolt of enslaved East Africans. M. A. Shaban (1976) argued that it was not a slave revolt at all but a rising of 'blacks' in which a few runaway slaves joined a majority of Arabs and free East Africans, on the ground that slaves alone could not have sustained so long a war. Ghada Hashem Talhami (1977) sees a religious and social rising of the lowest classes of the Basra region, joined by Bahrainis, Bedouin and others, and says the sources do not show that the Zanj were the majority. The sources cited here agree that the leader was a free man who claimed Alid descent and used Kharijite slogans, and that Bedouin, peasants and deserting soldiers joined him. Against Shaban, al-Tabari's account of the first day counts slaves taken from named work sites by the fifty and the five hundred. There is no consensus on the label.

How many died? Al-Mas'udi wrote that the more moderate estimate of all the dead was 500,000 and that 300,000 were killed in a single battle near Basra, but in the same passage he says that both the high and the moderate figures rest on empty conjecture and that no exact count is possible. Later medieval writers went higher: al-Suli is cited for 1,500,000 and Ibn al-Tiqtaqa for 2,500,000. Al-Tabari gives no total. Wikipedia's article says modern historians consider the medieval figures gross exaggerations. For Basra, Wikipedia's article on the battle says modern historians reject al-Mas'udi's 300,000 as excessive and, citing Alexandre Popovic's monograph, that other authors give 10,000 to 20,000; Adam Ali, a University of Toronto lecturer writing for Medievalists.net, says most scholars agree on that range. Nöldeke judged the 300,000 fighting men claimed for the rebel leader greatly exaggerated, and William Muir called the figures given for the armies and the captives 'clearly fabulous'; neither was speaking of the dead. No reliable total exists.

Who were the 'Zanj'? The older view, followed by Nöldeke and Britannica, takes the word in its geographical sense: people brought from the East African coast. Nöldeke himself noted that the 'Zenj, properly so called' mostly knew no Arabic and needed an interpreter, while other black slaves, from Nubia and elsewhere, spoke it; al-Tabari says the leader's festival sermon had to be repeated by those who understood Arabic for those who did not. Talhami argues that 'Zanj' was used loosely for black Africans in general, and JSTOR Daily cites her for the view that most of those who took part were black slaves of Nubian and Ethiopian origin. Wikipedia's article reports that, because there is little evidence of a large slave trade on the Swahili coast at this date, the word is thought in this case to mean Africans generally, though JSTOR Daily calls the origin of the rebels still a point of scholarly contention. The Arabic sources give no account of where individual rebels came from.

Who was Ali ibn Muhammad and what did he believe? He claimed descent from Ali and Fatima; al-Tabari gives another name and an Arab tribal origin and reports that he changed his claimed genealogy between Bahrain and Iraq, al-Mas'udi calls the genealogy false, and Muslim historians of the period generally rejected it. Britannica calls him a Persian; Wikipedia's article reports that other historians think a Persian origin unlikely. Al-Mas'udi says he followed the Azraqite branch of the Kharijites and killed women, children and the old; Britannica says the movement adopted Kharijite doctrine after it began. Nöldeke thought him 'a man of genius'; al-Tabari, as Nöldeke notes, prefers to call him 'the abominable one', 'the wicked one' or 'the traitor'. Whether he acted from belief or used religious claims to win power cannot be settled from sources written by his enemies.
stories.blind: Almost everything known comes from al-Tabari, who lived in Baghdad during the war and wrote under the dynasty that won it; al-Mas'udi, writing some sixty years after the war ended, is as hostile. The Zanj left no document of their own: no letter, nothing beyond their coins, which carried Kharijite formulas (one was published in 1933 as 'A Rare Coin of the Zanj'), and no account by any of the thousands who cleared the salt flats. Their words reach us only where al-Tabari passes on what former rebels told his informants, as with the slave Rayhan ibn Salih, and the leader's speeches come the same way. Al-Mas'udi says the first history of the revolt was written by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Sahl; al-Tabari cites him by name, but his book is lost. The people of Basra who were killed or sold are heard mainly through the Baghdad poet Ibn al-Rumi's elegy for the city and through the chroniclers. The women held by both sides, and the enslaved people whom the rebels themselves took, do not speak at all.
reading: Theodor Nöldeke, 'A Servile War in the East', in Sketches from Eastern History, trans. J. S. Black (1892, archive.org), pp. 146–175
al-Tabari, Tarikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk, vol. 9 (Cairo edition of 1967, Arabic text, al-Maktaba al-Shamela): the start of the revolt, year 255 AH
al-Mas'udi (Maçoudi), Les Prairies d'or, Arabic text and French translation by C. Barbier de Meynard, vol. 8 (1874, archive.org), pp. 31–33 and 57–61
Ghada Hashem Talhami, 'The Zanj Rebellion Reconsidered' (International Journal of African Historical Studies, 1977, JSTOR)
stories.warn: The Arabic quotations are al-Tabari's text as printed in the 1967 Cairo edition and transcribed online; their punctuation is the modern editor's, and the glosses in 'who' are this site's plain summaries, not translations. The standard English translation (The History of al-Tabari, vols 36 and 37, SUNY Press, 1992) is in copyright and is not quoted. Al-Mas'udi is quoted in Barbier de Meynard's French of 1874. Nöldeke writes in the racial language of 1892: on the same page as the passage on Basra he speaks of 'brutal negro slaves', and he uses 'negroes' throughout. Every account of what the rebels said and did was written by their enemies; the numbers in these sources (300,000 dead at Basra, 500,000 in all, fifteen thousand slaves at one group of works, women sold for two or three dirhams) cannot be checked. The Arabic word ghilman, given as 'slaves' in the facts, also means servants or young men. JSTOR Daily says the leader promised that his followers would enslave their former masters; al-Tabari's page on his festival sermon (vol. 9, p. 415) has him promise slaves, wealth and houses without naming the masters, and on p. 414 he lets the masters go. Spellings vary: Zanj, Zenj, Zendj; al-Mukhtara, Mokhtara; al-Muwaffaq, Mowaffak, Mouaffak.
stories.note: Research in progress: no words of the Zanj survive outside the hostile chronicle, so 'In their own words' has only two entries, both taken from al-Tabari: an account by one of the salt-flat ghilman, reported without a named transmitter, and a speech of the rebel leader, who was a free man and not one of the enslaved. Ibn al-Rumi's elegy on the sack of Basra, in which he says the city's people were struck down by their own slaves, is described but not quoted, because no reliable edition of the Arabic could be read online in the time allowed. The coins the rebels minted, and al-Tabari's account of the final victory in 883, have not yet been added, and nothing is quoted on what the caliph's army did to the rebels in 879–883. The modern figure for the dead at Basra rests on Wikipedia and Medievalists.net, not on Popovic's book itself. The page numbers for Nöldeke agree with the running heads in the scan's text; those for al-Mas'udi were worked out from the scan's leaf numbers and should be confirmed against the page images.

stories.title: The Spanish–CHamoru Wars and the emptying of the northern Marianas
stories.where: Guam and the Mariana Islands (Rota, Tinian, Aguiguan, Saipan and the northern islands called Gani); pin: Hagåtña (Agaña), Guam, where the mission and the Spanish garrison stood
facts: The Jesuit Diego Luis de San Vitores landed on Guam on 16 June 1668 with four other priests, four missionary brothers and 32 soldiers. Kepuha (Quipuha), a chief of Hagåtña, housed the missionaries and gave land for the first church, which opened on 2 February 1669.
https://www.guampedia.com/chiefs-kepuha-quipuha-3/

The first welcome did not last. The Jesuits rejected the veneration of ancestors, ordered the young men's houses destroyed and taught that all the baptised were equal, which cut across the ranks of CHamoru society; a Chinese castaway named Choco, married to a CHamoru woman of Saipan, spread the word that the water and oils of baptism were killing people.
https://www.guampedia.com/father-diego-luis-de-san-vitores/

After a CHamoru leader named Gufac was killed while trying to free an arrested man, Hurao, a high-caste chief of Hagåtña, raised about 2,000 warriors against the mission. The Spanish seized him early in the fighting and San Vitores later freed him; a Spanish soldier killed Hurao on 11 May 1672.
https://www.guampedia.com/chiefs-hurao/

CHamoru fighters also killed missionaries and their helpers. On 2 April 1672 San Vitores and his assistant Pedro Calungsod (Calangsod) entered the home of Matå'pang, a chief of Tomhom (Tumon) who had himself been baptised, without permission, to baptise his daughter; on learning of the baptism Matå'pang and a man named Hirao killed both, and Matå'pang weighted the bodies and threw them into the sea.
https://www.guampedia.com/chiefs-matapang-matapang/

Other deaths on the mission's side included the priest Luis de Medina and his catechist Hipolito de la Cruz on Saipan in early 1670, and Diego Bazan, two Filipino catechists and a Spanish escort in March 1672. From 1674 Spanish commanders answered with punitive raids on villages.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93Chamorro_Wars

Agualin (Aguarin), a chief from Hagåtña, went from village to village raising a second war in 1676; his forces burned a church and mission buildings and attacked the Spanish for months. He was captured on Rota in August 1680 and hanged.
https://www.guampedia.com/chiefs-aguarin/

José de Quiroga, who arrived in 1679, pursued those who resisted, burned villages and canoes, and by 1680 the people of Guam were being 'reduced' into a handful of church villages; on Saipan his men killed more than 200 men in one attack. CHamoru also fought on the Spanish side: in the rising of July 1684 led by Yula (Yura), Ignacio Hineti, a lower-caste clan leader, brought 50 warriors to defend the garrison.
https://www.guampedia.com/jose-de-quiroga-y-losada/

The last resisters were defeated on the rock island of Aguiguan (Aguijan) in 1695, and the people of the northern islands were then forced to move to Guam, with deaths at sea. A Spanish census of 1710 counted 3,539 CHamoru.
https://www.guampedia.com/spanish-response-to-chamorro-depopulation/

witness.text: Ces Européans auroient bien fait, leur disoit-il, de demeurer dans leur païs. Nous n'avions pas besoin de leur secours pour vivre heureux. Contens de ce que nos Isles fournissoient, nous nous en servions sans rien desirer au delà. Les connoissances qu'ils nous ont données, n'ont fait qu'augmenter nos besoins, & qu'irriter nos desirs.
witness.who: A speech Le Gobien attributes to Hurao, a high-caste CHamoru chief of Hagåtña. It was composed in French from mission reports by Charles Le Gobien, a French Jesuit who published in Paris and was procurator of the French Jesuits' China mission; he never visited the islands and wrote from García's 1683 life of San Vitores and the Jesuits' annual letters. No CHamoru wrote or dictated it. Histoire des isles Marianes (Paris: Nicolas Pepie, 1700), p. 140. Plain gloss: these Europeans would have done well to stay in their own country; we did not need their help to live happily; content with what our islands gave, we used it and wanted nothing more; the knowledge they have given us has only increased our needs and sharpened our desires
witness.date: Printed 1700; set in the first war, which modern accounts date 1670 or 1671

witness.text: Ils nous traitent de gens grossiers, & ils nous regardent comme des Barbares. Mais devons-nous les en croire ? Ne voïons-nous pas que sous pretexte de nous instruire & de cultiver nos mœurs, ils les corrompent ; qu'ils nous tirent de cette premiere simplicité, dans laquelle nous vivions, & qu'ils nous ostent enfin nostre liberté, qui nous doit estre plus chere que la vie ?
witness.who: The same speech, which Le Gobien attributes to Hurao; composed in French from mission reports by Le Gobien, a French Jesuit who never visited the islands. No CHamoru wrote or dictated it. Histoire des isles Marianes (Paris, 1700), p. 141. Plain gloss: they call us coarse people and look on us as barbarians, but must we believe them? Do we not see that, on the pretext of teaching us and improving our ways, they corrupt them; that they take us out of the first simplicity in which we lived, and in the end take away our liberty, which should be dearer to us than life?
witness.date: Printed 1700; set in the first war, which modern accounts date 1670 or 1671

witness.text: Il nous est aisé de les accabler par la multitude. Vous craignez peut-estre de les attaquer, & de vous exposer à leurs armes meurtrieres ? Mais une mort glorieuse n'est-elle pas à preferer à la vie honteuse que nous menons ?
witness.who: A speech Le Gobien attributes to Aguarin (Agualin), the CHamoru chief whom he calls the author of the second war against the Spaniards; composed in French from mission reports by Le Gobien, a French Jesuit who never visited the islands. No CHamoru wrote or dictated it. Histoire des isles Marianes (Paris, 1700), livre VII, p. 247. Plain gloss: it is easy for us to overwhelm them by our numbers; perhaps you are afraid to attack them and face their deadly weapons? But is a glorious death not better than the shameful life we are leading?
witness.date: Printed 1700; set in the second war, which began in 1676

witness.text: A war of extermination now began, which lasted twenty-three years, suspended from time to time when the Spaniards found themselves too weak to continue it, but resumed at the arrival of each ship bringing reinforcements, no matter whether in the meantime peace with the natives had been declared or not. Often whole villages were punished for the act of a single man, and innocent natives who had committed no crime whatever were shot down wantonly.
witness.who: William Edwin Safford, botanist and US Navy lieutenant who was assistant governor of Guam from August 1899 to August 1900, just after the United States took the island from Spain; his footnotes here cite García's Jesuit history. The Useful Plants of the Island of Guam (Contributions from the United States National Herbarium, vol. 9, Washington, 1905), p. 15

witness.text: Écrasés, décimés, les Chamorros ne se soumirent pas, mais moururent. En 1710, on n’en compte plus que 3,539; en 1741, il n’en restait que 1,816. Rarement pareille dépopulation sévit sur un pays; rarement aussi modifications plus profondes se produisirent chez un peuple dans un aussi court espace de temps.
witness.who: C. de Varigny, French writer, 'L'Océanie moderne', part V, Revue des Deux Mondes, 3rd period, vol. 85 (1888). Plain gloss: crushed and decimated, the Chamorros did not submit but died; in 1710 only 3,539 were counted, in 1741 only 1,816 remained; rarely has such depopulation struck a country, and rarely have deeper changes come over a people in so short a time. Varigny wrote two centuries later and gives the islanders 60,000 people and bows and arrows, neither of which is established

official.text: Padre Solano, calling together the soldiers of the post, declared to them that though arms used in their proper time and season were the defense of that Christianity, yet wielded intempestively they would be its destruction, since they would not only irritate with reason the Indians, but would become unworthy of the favor of the Lord, without which what could twenty or thirty men do against thirty thousand?
official.who: Francisco García SJ, reporting the address of Francisco Solano SJ, head of the mission after San Vitores was killed in 1672, to the garrison; from García's life of San Vitores (Madrid, 1683, p. 447), here in W. E. Safford's English rendering (The Useful Plants of the Island of Guam, Washington, 1905, p. 16)

official.text: His apostolic zeal and complete dedication to those people in need of spiritual and human promotion characterized the years of this exemplary missionary, who, in imitation of the words of the Master “greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Jn. 15, 13), shed his blood in sacrifice, while asking God to forgive those responsible for his death.
official.who: Pope John Paul II, speaking of Diego Luis de San Vitores in his homily at the Mass of beatification of San Vitores and two other Jesuits (Holy See website, an English paragraph on the Spanish-language page)

today.text: In 1680, Captain Don Joseph de Quiroga was appointed the new governor of Guam and began a brutal campaign to subjugate the island and the rest of the Marianas. He ordered that any rebellious CHamoru be executed and instituted a policy known as reduccíon.
today.who: US National Park Service, War in the Pacific National Historical Park, Guam, in its history of the village of Assan (spelling 'reduccíon' as on the page; Guam has been a US territory since 1898)
today.date: page last updated 5 May 2025, read 26 November 2026

disputed: How many CHamoru were there in 1668? San Vitores wrote of about 100,000 on Guam; the lowest modern estimate cited is 24,000; the Jesuit historian Francis Hezel works from 40,000; Quiroga, looking back in 1720, put Guam at 50,000 at the start of the conquest and 4,000 by then; the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica gave 40,000 to 60,000 for the islands, and the mission superior Solano, in García's account, spoke of thirty thousand. There is no agreed figure. What is agreed is the scale of the fall: a Spanish census of 1710 counted about 3,500 CHamoru, and the numbers kept falling until the later 1700s.

War, disease or removal? Older histories (Safford in 1905, Varigny in 1888, and Guam histories of the 1960s) describe a war of extermination and blame Spanish arms, Quiroga above all. Francis Hezel argues that introduced disease killed far more than fighting did and rejects the word genocide; one count Wikipedia cites him for (his 2015 study was not read) is 917 deaths recorded on Guam and Rota in 1680–83 against about twenty from hostilities. Richard Shell and others answer that the forced herding into mission villages, the destruction of canoes and the removal of the northern islanders spread the epidemics and broke the society, so that disease and conquest cannot be separated. Epidemics are recorded in 1683, 1690 and about 1699–1700. There is no agreed view: Guampedia's survey says the question is still contested, Wikipedia's article calls the wars a genocide, and Hezel rejects that word. The sources also disagree on dates: Hurao's rising is put in 1670 (Wikipedia's summary) or after July 1671 (the same article's narrative), the Yula rising in 1683 or 1684, the fall of Aguiguan in 1695 or 1696.

Did Hurao say it? The speech is printed only by Le Gobien, in Paris, in 1700, twenty-eight years after Hurao's death. Guampedia presents it as recorded as it was told to Le Gobien and says it is often quoted as an example of CHamoru resistance. The historian Carlo Ginzburg (died 2026) argued that so polished a text cannot be an accurate record of a real speech: Le Gobien never went to the islands, and his sources (García's 1683 life of San Vitores and the Jesuits' annual letters) mention Hurao only as a man imprisoned and released. Ginzburg added that those letters do report the islanders' belief that rats, flies, mosquitoes and sickness came with the ships, a complaint Le Gobien put into the speech and mocked in a note, so that an Indigenous argument survives inside a European composition; he also noted that Diderot's Supplément au voyage de Bougainville seems to echo it. The page that reprints his chapter dates the revolt 1685, which does not fit Hurao's death in 1672. The excerpt does not mention Aguarin's speech, which comes from the same book by the same author.

Was Choco a slanderer? The Jesuit accounts make the Chinese castaway Choco the first great obstacle, a man who turned the islanders against baptism with a lie; Safford repeats this, while allowing that many of the baptised did die shortly afterwards. Guampedia's writers point out that many baptised children and old people died soon after, that San Vitores baptised children daily without their parents' permission, and that Matå'pang believed the water would kill his daughter. Wikipedia's article says that, by Spanish accounts of the time, people in places with regular contact with the mission, such as Hagåtña, did not seem to believe the rumour, while villages whose only contact was the baptism of the dying and the newborn may have. Choco's own words are not recorded.
stories.blind: This card has no words written or dictated by a CHamoru of the time, so 'In their own words' is empty. Everything written then comes from the mission's side: Jesuit letters and annual reports, García's life of San Vitores (1683) and Le Gobien's history (1700), plus soldiers' and governors' papers. Hurao, Aguarin, Matå'pang and Yula are known only through men who wanted them defeated, and the speeches printed under their names were composed by a Jesuit in France; the CHamoru who fought for the Spanish, such as Hineti, are known only through the same men's praise. Choco is heard only in his opponents' summary. The people of the northern islands who were shipped to Guam, the women, and the lower-ranking CHamoru left no words at all. The assistants who died with the priests, such as Pedro Calungsod and Hipolito de la Cruz, also left none.
