witness.text: The soldiers of the Khmer Rouge quickly emptied the capital, which had swelled to some 2 million people owing to the influx of refugees during the war. It is believed that many thousands, especially among the aged and the young, died from lack of food, water and medical assistance during forced marches to the countryside. Witnesses reported numerous instances of hospital patients being dragged from their beds and dying on roads out of the city. By the end of the evacuation, the capital had as few as 20,000 residents.
witness.who: The UN Group of Experts for Cambodia (Sir Ninian Stephen of Australia, chairman; Judge Rajsoomer Lallah of Mauritius; Professor Steven R. Ratner of the United States), appointed by the UN Secretary-General in 1998, in their report to him (UN document A/53/850, paragraph 20)

witness.text: The misery caused by the methods used by the Khmer Rouge in implementing its policy of transforming the Cambodian economy constituted the single largest source of deaths during the Khmer Rouge period. Starvation, disease and physical exhaustion, caused by overwork and inadequate food, medicine and sanitation, killed hundreds of thousands. According to witness reports, the Khmer Rouge overseers also routinely killed many thousands who refused or could no longer work, often murdering their family members as well.
witness.who: The UN Group of Experts for Cambodia, report to the Secretary-General (UN document A/53/850, paragraph 23)

witness.text: These deliberate killings occurred on a massive scale, were systematically organised and directed against the Vietnamese. In each case, Vietnamese were targeted not as individuals but based on their membership of the group and their perceived ethnicity. This happened under the umbrella of the CPK’s policy to specifically target the Vietnamese, including civilians, as a group. Until late 1976, the Vietnamese were targeted for expulsion, from April 1977, for destruction as such.
witness.who: The Trial Chamber of the ECCC, a court of Cambodian and international judges, in the summary of its judgment in Case 002/02 read in court (paragraph 32; CPK is the Communist Party of Kampuchea). The copy linked is marked 'courtesy copy - not checked against delivery'; the full written judgment is the authoritative text

official.text: After having led the people’s national democratic revolution to the total and decisive victory of 17 April 1975, the Party continues now to have an absolute monopoly of leadership in all domains of the socialist revolution and in the building of socialism.
official.who: The 1976 Statute of the Communist Party of Kampuchea, the ruling party of Democratic Kampuchea, first page, as read out in court by Duch on 31 March 2009 and printed in the ECCC's compilation of his statements (the court's English translation). Duch, on trial, chose this sentence as evidence for his argument that the Party alone was responsible for the crimes; no printed text of the Statute is linked

official.text: During the S-21 era, I valued my life and the lives of my family as more important than the lives of those who were detained at S-21. During that period I never dared even to think about disputing or opposing the orders from the top, despite knowing that they were criminal. It was a matter of life and death for me and my family. As the director of S-21, I did not dare to seek any alternatives to obeying the orders from the upper echelon, despite knowing that carrying them out would lead to the loss of thousands of lives.
official.who: Kaing Guek Eav, alias Duch, chairman of S-21, in a statement to the ECCC Trial Chamber during his trial, as printed in the court's own 'Compilation of statements of apology made by Kaing Guek Eav alias Duch during the proceedings' (p. 3; the court's translation from the Khmer). In the same statement he says he is still responsible for the crimes
official.date: 31 March 2009 (probable: the compilation prints this paragraph, which begins 'Thirdly', without a date, ahead of the first and second points of his statement of 31 March 2009)

today.text: Following the defeat of the Khmer Rouge regime, the Cambodian Memorial Sites became places of memorialisation to honour victims. As places of reflection and learning, the serial property encourages peaceful coexistence among peoples and fosters a commitment to never repeat such atrocities. The property provides an example of the ongoing process of navigating the joint goals of justice and national reconciliation.
today.who: Not a Cambodian government statement: this is the UNESCO World Heritage Centre's 'Brief synthesis' for the property 'Cambodian Memorial Sites: From centres of repression to places of peace and reflection' (the former M-13 prison, Tuol Sleng and Choeung Ek), in Cambodia, added to the World Heritage List in 2025. Whether the tribunal served justice is contested (see What is disputed)
today.date: page accessed 26 November 2026 (the linked page does not print the inscription date; see the note)

disputed: How many died? There is no agreed count. The UN Group of Experts in 1999 reported scholars' figures of 1.5 million and nearly 1.7 million, about 20 per cent of an April 1975 population of 7.3 to 7.9 million, and said historians had rejected the 2 to 3 million often used by Cambodian governments since 1979. Yale's Cambodian Genocide Program gives about 1.7 million, 21 per cent of the population. The demographer Patrick Heuveline (2015) puts the 95 per cent range for excess deaths at 1.2 to 2.8 million with a median of 1.9 million, of which about 1.09 million violent; he finds Michael Vickery's 740,800 and the post-1979 government's 3.315 million both very unlikely. UNESCO's World Heritage text says one quarter of the population perished in a single decade, a longer period than 1975–79; the US Holocaust Memorial Museum says almost two million. The sources cited here agree on a range of roughly 1.5 to 2 million or somewhat more, not on a number.

Was it genocide, and of whom? The legal finding is narrow: the ECCC convicted for genocide of the Vietnamese and (Nuon Chea only, as a superior) of the Cham, made no genocide finding concerning ethnic Khmer, and judged the deaths in the cooperatives, worksites and security centres as crimes against humanity. It found that Cham were killed on a massive scale; it held that Khieu Samphan was not responsible for that genocide as an aider or a superior. The Supreme Court Chamber upheld the Vietnamese finding on 22 September 2022; Nuon Chea died in 2019 before his appeal was decided, so the Cham finding was never tested on appeal, although the Chamber found no legal reason to vacate it. The UN Group of Experts in 1999 said the Khmer are a national group under the Genocide Convention but took no position on whether genocide was committed against part of them, because that turns on the Khmer Rouge's intent. Inside Cambodia the word genocide has been used for the whole population's suffering since the 1979 trial, which used a wider definition than the Convention's, and the legal scholar Rachel Killean reports that Judge You Ottara's separate opinion called the court's approach overly formalistic. The question the experts left open, whether the killing of Khmer by Khmer (often called 'auto-genocide') meets the Convention's definition, was not decided by the court. Yale's Cambodian Genocide Program uses the word for the whole period.

How much did the American bombing help the Khmer Rouge to power? Taylor Owen and Ben Kiernan (2006) argue that civilian casualties drove ordinary Cambodians to an insurgency that had been small, and that the Khmer Rouge used the bomb damage as propaganda. Their 2006 figure of 2,756,941 tons of bombs (for 1965–73) rested on a database error; in 2010 and again in 2015 the same authors corrected it to about 500,000 tons, close to the 539,129 tons in the US Library of Congress study. The Library of Congress study records the opposing view too: the bombing bought time for the Lon Nol government without stopping the communist advance, the former US officials Emory Swank and General John Vogt disputed William Shawcross's argument that it forged the Khmer Rouge, and the insurgents depended heavily on North Vietnamese help. Estimates of bombing deaths in that study run from 30,000 to 500,000; Owen and Kiernan cite 50,000 to 150,000 civilians. The sources cited here do not agree on the weight to give the bombing against the 1970 coup, Vietnamese support and Prince Sihanouk's alliance with the Khmer Rouge.

Did the tribunal deliver justice? It convicted three people after more than 13 years of hearings, at a reported cost of about 330 million US dollars; of the two other accused in Case 002, Ieng Sary died in 2013 during the trial and Ieng Thirith was found unfit to stand trial, and Pol Pot died in 1998 before any charge. The Open Society Justice Initiative (2020) says Cambodian officials consistently acted to block further cases (003 and 004), reporting that Prime Minister Hun Sen told the UN Secretary-General in October 2010 that Case 003 would not be allowed; it describes the Cambodian and international judges reaching opposite conclusions and the cases as deadlocked. Against this, the court's own record is that the two most senior surviving leaders were tried and convicted and that 185 witnesses, civil parties and experts were heard in public in Case 002/02 alone. Vann Nath told the judges that testifying in public was an honour and that what he wanted was justice for those who died.
stories.blind: The voices here are survivors who lived to speak in a courtroom thirty years later, through interpreters, in answer to lawyers' questions. Of the thousands held at S-21 very few survived; the dead speak, if at all, through confessions extracted under torture, which are not quoted. The Cham and Vietnamese victims are represented by one Cham civil party; no ethnic Vietnamese voice is quoted here, although a civil party whose ethnic Vietnamese wife and children were killed testified in December 2015, and the transcripts of that part of the trial were not read for this card. The people of the cooperatives who starved, the women forced to marry, the monks disrobed and the Khmer Republic soldiers shot in 1975 are present only in the court's findings. The regime is heard only at second hand: one sentence of its Party Statute, chosen and read out by a prison chairman on trial in his own defence, and that chairman's own statement; Pol Pot and most of the leadership never answered in court.

stories.warn: The theme 'Genocide' is used here in the court's sense: the ECCC found genocide of the ethnic Vietnamese and of the Cham. It made no finding of genocide against ethnic Khmer: the mass deaths in the cooperatives, worksites and security centres across the country it judged as crimes against humanity. Whether those were also genocide is disputed (see What is disputed). All the testimony is the court's English interpretation of words spoken in Khmer, printed as spoken, with the transcript's own double hyphens and rough grammar; a reviewed transcript can differ slightly from the live interpretation. The transcripts name guards and describe torture and killing. Duch's statement is the court's translation and is his own account of his motives. The Case 002/02 summary is a courtesy copy; the written judgment of more than 2,000 pages is the authority. Khmer names are spelled several ways (Kroch Chhmar or Krouch Chhmar; Kaing Guek Eav or Kang Kek Iew). The Ba Chuc figure in the note rests on Vietnamese official counts reported in the press.
stories.note: Research in progress: the full trial judgments were too long to read through and only their opening parts, the court's summaries and press releases were used, so no survivor is quoted from the Case 002/02 judgment itself and no ethnic Vietnamese survivor is quoted. The 1970 killings of ethnic Vietnamese under Lon Nol rest on Wikipedia's report of later scholars (Kiernan for the killings, Duncan for the 200,000 repatriated); no better page was found, and the Library of Congress study and Britannica do not mention them. Not covered in the facts: Democratic Kampuchea kept Cambodia's United Nations seat during the 1980s (UN Group of Experts, paragraph 38, https://hrlibrary.umn.edu/cambodia-1999.html). The demographic report written for the court by Ewa Tabeau and They Kheam (2009) could not be opened. No Democratic Kampuchea document was found in a quotable printing other than the Party Statute sentence read in court; the 1976 Constitution and Pol Pot's speech of 27 September 1977 exist online only in modern scholars' translations. The killing of 3,157 villagers at Ba Chuc in Vietnam by Khmer Rouge troops in April 1978 is reported by Wikipedia from press accounts (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba_Ch%C3%BAc_massacre) and was not checked against a primary source. Cambodia's 20 May National Day of Remembrance was confirmed only from Wikipedia. The UNESCO inscription date, 11 July 2025 at the World Heritage Committee's 47th session in Paris, is from Cambodia's state news agency (https://akp.gov.kh/post/detail/341997), not from the UNESCO page; no Royal Government statement was quoted, because the foreign ministry's page (mfaic.gov.kh) refused to open and the others were not checked word for word.
